items.title: A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.
items.summary:
Back to Articles
A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.
Published
November 5, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 37
+31
Olesia Krizhevich olesiagradium Follow gradium Laurent Mazare lmz Follow gradium Eric Bezzam bezzam Follow Eustache Le Bihan eustlb Follow
Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.
We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.
Why a voice should live on your device
Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.
Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.
We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.
Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.
What we released
Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.
It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.
Demos and first projects
The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.
The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.
Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.
Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.
How Phonon did on the Hugging Face Open TTS Leaderboard
The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.
On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.
Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.
Inference
We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).
Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.
It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.
Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:
from transformers import AutoProcessor, GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration
model_id = "gradium/phonon-31m-en"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto")
model = GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto")
print(f"{model.num_parameters():,}") # 30,788,354
print(f"{processor.audio_tokenizer.num_parameters():,}") # 10,305,313
A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from safetensors.torch import load_file
path = hf_hub_download("gradium/phonon-voices", "voices/LMDIYE0Oa377Qh6Z.safetensors")
voice = load_file(path)["speaker_wavs"][0].T # (num_frames, 512)
The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:
conversation = [
{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "audio"}, {"type": "text", "text": "Hello from Phonon."}]}
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
conversation,
tokenize=True,
return_dict=True,
add_generation_prompt=True,
processor_kwargs={"audio_prompt_latents": [voice]},
).to(model.device)
# prompt: <|audio_prompt|> × num_frames, "Hello from Phonon.", <|audio_bos|>
generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:
outputs = model.generate(**inputs) # audio_latents: (batch_size, num_frames, 32)
audio = processor.decode(outputs.audio_latents, outputs.audio_latents_mask)
processor.save_audio(audio, "phonon.wav")
See the docs 🤗 for more!
What's next
Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.
We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.
Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.
Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.
One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

items.title: Addressing the code review bottleneck
items.summary:
Engineering
Addressing the code review bottleneck
Ben Holmes|November 5, 2026
How many agent PRs are awaiting your review right now? 10? 100? 1000?
“Too many” or “I’m tired” are valid answers too. That said, I’m not going to suggest that we let the bots win and merge without human review; that’s for a post-AGI world. Today, the goal is to cut the time spent on each code review, and reduce the barrier for shipping agent PRs to production.
There are three levers you can pull today to cut review times significantly:
Run rounds of adversarial code review with your own review agent before a human looks.
Verify user flows end-to-end with simulated environments, computer use, and automated checks.
Score and mitigate merge risk on every PR so reviewers know what to focus on, with a /merge-risk skill you can use.
Let’s drill into each of these.
Build your own code review agent
Agents should run through their own internal code review process before a PR ever reaches a teammate. Think of this like doing a “make it work” pass (the code addresses the task) followed by a “make it good” pass (the code is well-architected for the next person).
It’s tempting to use an off-the-shelf code review agent for this. But it’s quite easy, and valuable, to build a code review agent yourself. It lets you define the grading criteria based on what your team cares about. Plus, owning the agent also lets you fine-tune its accuracy based on your own data. As Addy Osmani calls out in Anthropic's code review process, production incidents and reverts are high-signal feedback that something slipped through review. These can be turned into eval cases to improve the quality of code review over time.
It’s also common to have code review agents comment on the GitHub PR for the human to see. This works, but it creates noise that, in a majority of cases, doesn’t require human attention. It’s better to have your implementation and code review agents work together outside the GitHub thread, and only surface comments on the PR that require human input.
Here is the default loop that Warp Factories ships with:
The implementation agent hands off work to a code review agent.
The code review agent reviews the code and collects its findings as a list, noting the severity, impact, and the suggested change if applicable. If there’s ambiguity behind a change (i.e. code that goes beyond product decisions documented in context or in code), it hands back to the human for input. In the case of Warp Factories, this would be on the Slack thread of taskboard ticket where implementation began.
The implementation agent reviews these findings and addresses anything it can fix.
The code review agent flags more findings, and the cycle repeats until everything is settled or N max turns are reached.
Because multiple rounds of adversarial review can get expensive, we have also been experimenting with a gate in front of the reviewer to decide whether review is needed. In our early benchmarks on cost-to-quality against our own full-stack systems, we found that restricting multi-round review to larger features is a viable option. We’ll share more findings here soon.
Eval your code review agent
Once you set up a code review agent, you'll also want to evaluate the quality of those code reviews over time. This includes both the quality of the reviews themselves and downstream metrics like cost-per-PR, cycle time, and incident rollbacks.
In Warp Factories, we have dashboards for tracking those metrics, along with qualitative scoring for code quality, efficiency, test quality, and other failure modes.
These qualitative scores are driven by an LLM-as-a-judge using scoring rubrics across each metric. You can have this LLM-as-a-judge eval the full agent conversation, or eval the code review subagent specifically. From there, a self-improvement agent reviews the scores given by this LLM-as-a-judge to propose improvements automatically. /skill-doctor is a simple way to try this pattern yourself.
Give agents a computer to verify their work
Would you trust a PR written by a coworker that they didn’t verify on a local build? Hopefully not, and the same should go for agents.
You should give the agent tools to test the application as if it's a user. For backend systems, this means simulating the environment realistically: standing up a staging database, injecting test credentials for the agent to use, and capturing access logs to understand what the agent is doing.
For clientside changes, you’ll need commands for the agent to navigate around the application like a user. The Chrome DevTools MCP and WebMCP are model-agnostic options for web apps, but computer use is becoming more common across harnesses to test any kind of client application.
A computer-use-enabled model has its own virtual desktop to open the application and click around the application it built. In Warp Factories, computer use runs as a tool call that delegates to a computer-use subagent, which drives the computer and reports back screenshots and screen recordings as artifacts.
Once an agent verifies its work this way, these artifacts should be available to the human reviewer. Verification should also include both a before and after state to confirm what was changed. We suggest making test artifacts a required field on your PR description so an agent does this by default. Matt Pocock’s /pr skill is a good template.
It’s also important to prevent over-verification. If multiple screenshots are needed, they should be for distinct user flows rather than overlapping ones. Plus, recordings should be edited to remove dead space and jump to the part that’s worth human review. We added FFmpeg post-processing to Warp Factory agents to automatically slice out dead zones between agent actions. This can cut clips from minutes to 10-15 seconds in our experience.
Demonstration of the computer use tool built into Warp Factories
Have agents score and mitigate risk
Once the agent has reviewed and verified its own work, the human reviewer needs to understand the scope of the change, and which parts are worth the closest review. These are five criteria worth assessing:
Verification: Is the code well verified, both with test coverage and end-to-end computer use artifacts?
Alignment: Does the code follow the issue and PR description, or are there drive-by fixes and unintended side effects?
Impact: What is the blast radius of the change, and is it touching sensitive code paths like auth, permissions, or billing? For sensitive systems, this is where you should route reviews by code owner so the right person is tagged into the PR.
Rollback cost: How easily can this be rolled back, and what is the rollback procedure in the case of an incident? Matt Pocock frames this as a one-way door versus a two-way door, where a one-way door (like a destructive schema migration) is harder to reverse.
Error detection: If something goes wrong in production, how much visibility will we have? Are errors swallowed, logged, or reported to an error monitoring service? That last option is ideal for agent visibility to fix their own mistakes. For example, we added a webhook to monitor for Sentry alerts and relay reports to our software factory agents for investigation.
These five categories help you decide how much human oversight a PR actually needs. If you want to spot-check your own PRs against these criteria, we created a /merge-risk skill to score the risk and highlight what needs the most attention.
It’s also worth bringing some of these criteria into the PR description, namely testing procedure, rollback cost, and impact. Matt Pocock's PR template and Anthropic's internal code review template both follow similar lines.
You can also have your agent run the merge-risk skill as a last-mile step to catch risky changes early:
Strip out unaligned changes to avoid drive-by fixes
Add error monitoring on new paths for better tracking
Break up high-impact changes into stacked PRs for simpler review
Avoid code sensitive paths if it can achieve the same outcome
And of course, verify work end-to-end with screenshots and recordings
Reduced risk doesn’t mean zero risk
None of these remove the human bottleneck on code review; engineers should continue to stay involved in how a codebase evolves. All of these are meant to a) increase trust in the work an agent delivers, and b) reduce the human attention needed to get work to the finish line.
To start, try adding fields like “impact” and “rollback cost” to your PR descriptions to pick out the low-hanging fruit. Then, layer on a code review step, and add computer use for deeper verification than e2e tests can provide. Focus engineering on the systems driving your agents, instead of reviewing every PR line-by-line.

items.title: Australian universities are creating AI-native graduates
items.summary:
OpenAI
November 5, 2026
Company
Australian universities are creating AI-native graduates
The future of Australia’s workforce is taking shape before today’s students receive their degrees. Across university campuses, students are using AI to investigate ideas, build assistants and turn concepts into working prototypes. They are beginning to develop the skills they will take into research, established industries and ventures of their own.
Recognising this shift, Australian universities, including UNSW Sydney, University of Sydney, La Trobe University, and Adelaide University, are forging collaborations with OpenAI to give their students and staff access to frontier AI tools.
Students, educators and IT teams are putting AI to work in clinical simulations, robot-assisted teacher training and student projects that build pathways into industry. Alongside this work, universities are developing frameworks for where and how AI can be used in learning and assessment, helping students build practical skills while knowing when to rely on their own judgment. For teachers, employers and industry practitioners, these examples offer practical lessons in designing AI-supported learning, setting clear expectations for AI use and preparing Australians for an AI-enabled workplace.
New research1 commissioned by OpenAI reveals what students want from their universities, including the access to AI they increasingly expect. In a survey of more than 1,000 Australian university students, 81% said they already use AI several times a week, including nearly a third (33%) who use it multiple times a day. Over a quarter (28%) had already built an AI agent or assistant to help manage their studies, work or personal life. Four out of five students (79%) want their university to offer more opportunities to use advanced AI tools on real-world projects, with the same proportion interested in applying AI to challenges in health, climate, science or cyber security.
AI use and career readiness
81%
Use AI several times a week
33%
Use AI multiple times each day
28%
Have already built an AI agent or assistant to manage studies, work or personal life

Believe AI skills will be essential to success in their chosen career
69%
Believe AI literacy will become as fundamental as digital literacy, writing or numeracy

Believe AI skills will give Australian graduates an advantage in the global workforce
Findings from a survey of university students in Australia1
Students also see those experiences as preparation for what comes next. More than sixty percent (61%) believe AI skills will be essential to success in their chosen career, and 65% believe those skills will give Australian graduates an advantage in the global workforce. There is entrepreneurial ambition, too. More than three quarters (76%) of students surveyed said they were interested in starting a company or working for themselves, while over two thirds (68%) believed AI would make it easier to start a business.
The question for higher education is how to meet students where they are. Giving them access to advanced tools is a start, but helping them use those tools with sound judgment, subject knowledge and practical experience is what will make them AI-ready for the workforce.
UNSW’s expanded collaboration with OpenAI is one way universities are responding. The university is bringing ChatGPT Edu to more than 80,000 students and staff, expanding access in stages as it works towards availability across the student community.
UNSW and OpenAI plan to integrate generative AI foundations and Codex into educational programs and courses, with opportunities for students to apply AI through hackathons and industry projects. The collaboration is also intended to connect students with internships, graduate roles and startup networks.
UNSW Master of IT student Nalin Iyer put the workforce question plainly: “It’s important to understand what industry is looking for and how AI fits into that.”
The University of Sydney’s collaboration with OpenAI also aims to build practical capability across the institution. It will provide students and staff with supported access to ChatGPT Edu, with training and guidance. The rollout is staged, with access for all students scheduled for Semester 1, 2027 after a trial. The university is also establishing a $1 million AI Sustainability Research and Innovation Fund to study and advance sustainability.
Representatives from the University of Sydney and OpenAI mark the start of their strategic collaboration
La Trobe University is connecting broad access with an ambition to embed AI across its curriculum. All 3,500 staff already have access to ChatGPT Edu, with universal access planned for its 45,000 students and staff in the first quarter of 2027. Its approach includes Australia’s first Bachelor of AI Engineering (Honours), welcoming its first cohort in 2027, and Australia’s first AI MBA program.
As part of its AI-first strategy, La Trobe appointed Australia’s first Pro Vice-Chancellor AI and Chief AI Officer, Phil Laufenberg, to lead the university’s approach to AI across education, research and operations.
“AI should happen with us, not to us. We want students in every discipline to have the skills and confidence to help shape how AI is used in their profession. That means opportunities to build, test ideas and solve real problems, alongside the critical thinking and judgement to use AI responsibly.”
—Phil Laufenberg, Pro Vice-Chancellor AI and Chief AI Officer, La Trobe University
These efforts respond to a reality the survey makes clear: students are already experimenting with AI, but institution-wide access and support mean all have equitable opportunities to develop their skills, regardless of what they study or what individual tools they can afford.
Practice before it counts
At La Trobe University, some of the most interesting work begins with a simple question: how can we use AI to enhance practical experience in learning?
Dr Cameron Anderson, Head of the Paramedicine program, uses ChatGPT to create a wide range of practice activities delivered through the university’s learning management system, where students interpret an ECG, assess a possible heart attack or triage patients after a mass casualty incident. AI helps create simulations that reinforce and test classroom learning.
“ChatGPT helps us create realistic clinical scenarios so our paramedicine students can practice difficult field decisions. They still need to interpret evidence, explain their reasoning and defend their decisions. It also helps identify course material needing updates in line with new research, giving us more time for teaching.”
—Dr Cameron Anderson, Head of the Paramedicine program, La Trobe University
Professor Therese Keane, Associate Dean for Research and Industry Engagement in La Trobe’s School of Education, uses a social robot called Fletch to help future teachers practice giving feedback to parents. Powered by OpenAI large language models hosted through Microsoft Azure, Fletch responds with speech, facial expressions and head movements.
Professor Keane’s team developed realistic scenarios from interviews with highly experienced educators. Importantly, Fletch enables trainee teachers to practice situations where conversations with parents turn confrontational, developing key skills in an area that many teachers find challenging.
Professor Therese Keane at La Trobe University is helping future teachers practice difficult conversations with parents using Fletch, an OpenAI-powered social robot
La Trobe is bringing AI into more of its courses and operations. The university has made OpenAI’s agentic tools Codex and ChatGPT Work available across the institution, with its handbook listing Vibe Coding for Startups and Agentic AI Software Engineering (from 2027).
The university’s AI Business Studio extends practical learning into industry. It aims to give more than 1,000 students practice experience as consultants and forward deployed engineers using ChatGPT Edu and Codex to help small and medium enterprises adopt AI by 2028 and connect graduate skills with the needs of businesses.
An AI rollout of this size needs steady work behind the scenes. La Trobe reports dozens of live use cases, training for hundreds of people and 10% month-on-month growth in active users. It manages safe access and token economics as more people take part. “ChatGPT and Codex have helped shorten early systems development and innovation from months to weeks, and importantly, enabled embedded co-design by staff and students,” Laufenberg said.
As a newly established university created through a complex merger, Adelaide University has an opportunity to embed secure, governed and scalable uses of AI from the outset. Australia’s first new major university in a generation is building on existing use of OpenAI’s API by researchers, students and staff.
Adelaide University is one of the first institutions in the higher education sector to harness OpenAI Daybreak Blue to conduct authorised defensive security work, providing a vital capability for cyber defences, including vulnerability discovery, secure code review, malware analysis, incident response and patch validation.
“This is enabling human-centric AI in a thoughtful way, providing us with access to frontier AI models to strengthen our cyber security posture.”
—Abhishek Singh, Chief Technology and Security Officer, Adelaide University
UNSW Senior Lecturers Mariana Rodriguez-Valenzuela (seated) and May Lim assist with the rollout of ChatGPT Edu as Joel Solomons, Education Solutions Engineer at OpenAI ANZ, looks on
Learning when and how to use AI
Universities are also setting clear expectations for when students can use AI and when they need to demonstrate their own knowledge.
UNSW has introduced a Can, Can’t, Must framework for assessment. Depending on the learning goal, an educator can specify that AI use is permitted, prohibited or required. That gives students a way to practice using AI appropriately while still demonstrating the foundational knowledge their field demands.
The University of Sydney is pairing its rollout with a responsible AI framework alongside its assessment approach that ensures students demonstrate their own capabilities in supervised settings, then show how they can use AI effectively in open assessments.
La Trobe is also supporting wider access with practical guidance. Its library has developed free Responsible and Safe AI learning modules for all students, and AI skills development is being integrated in 50 priority first-year subjects for Semester 1, 2027. Tailored modules for Education, Law and Health connect AI literacy with professional responsibilities, while workshops and teaching resources support educators in designing learning activities and assessments.
Students already see AI skills as essential to their careers and an opportunity to get ahead. By widening ChatGPT access and bringing AI into everyday teaching, Australian universities are helping turn that ambition into practical experience. The goal is to prepare graduates who can use AI to learn, create and solve problems, with the subject knowledge and judgment to apply those skills confidently as they enter the workforce.
​

items.summary:
OpenAI
November 5, 2026
Cult.fit builds operational muscle with Codex
Cult.fit is using Codex to help teams across functions build tools, move faster, and change how work gets done.
Contact salesCompany size: EnterpriseRegion: Asia-Pacific & OceaniaIndustry: HealthcareProducts: Codex, API
20+
internal applications built by non-engineering teams in recent months

annual software savings by rebuilding an internal capability with Codex

Cult.fit is one of India’s leading technology-enabled fitness companies, operating 708 fitness centers across 77 cities and serving nearly one million paid members. Its business combines subscription-based access to gyms and trainer-led fitness classes with a growing consumer products portfolio spanning fitness equipment, accessories, workout footwear and activewear.
As the company grew, it wanted to solve more operational and product challenges without adding layers of process and complexity. By standardizing engineering on Codex and then extending it beyond engineering, cult.fit is helping teams across the organization analyze data, build tools, and move ideas into production. Alongside its Codex rollout, it is using the OpenAI API to develop more personalized member experiences, including through its AI Trainer.
For Santhosh Kumar, CTO at cult.fit, AI presented an opportunity to change how the organization works. “We wanted to become more AI-native in the way we run things,” he says. “How can we run our operations or transform our operations to be AI-first? What new customer experiences can we offer? And how can we transform how we run our organization?”
Standardizing software development with Codex
Cult.fit’s first major shift was in engineering. Before standardizing on Codex, developers were using a mix of coding agents and assistants. Different tools meant different conventions for repositories, agent instructions, skills, and development workflows, making it harder to share knowledge and reuse capabilities across teams.
Cult.fit wanted a shared platform around which it could standardize the software development lifecycle. The company chose Codex as that foundation. Repository structures, skills, testing, code review, and feedback loops could now follow common conventions across teams.
“Once we standardized on Codex, we could build our software development lifecycle around a single platform.”
—Santhosh Kumar, CTO, cult.fit
The team then extended Codex into more specialized engineering workflows. Its Site Reliability Engineering agent can aggregate information from observability platforms and logs, investigate incidents, and, in many cases, create a pull request with a proposed fix for an engineer to review. Security agents help identify and address vulnerabilities, while other on-call agents investigate recurring production issues.
Cult.fit is also moving toward a more fully spec-driven development model, where a specification can guide work through the software development lifecycle toward a pull request for an engineer to review. This gives teams a more repeatable path from a defined requirement to working code.
One recent example is a social feed for the cult.fit app. Kumar estimates the project would previously have taken more than a year to build. Using the new workflow, the team built and shipped it end to end in two months.
Giving every team the ability to build
Codex has since expanded beyond engineering. cult.fit made its company data easier for Codex to work with, allowing teams to find answers and perform routine analysis themselves. Previously, even small data requests had to go through a central analyst team, creating a bottleneck.
“Codex has been our biggest step toward data democratization. Teams can now do the analysis they need themselves.”
—Santhosh Kumar, CTO, cult.fit
Teams are also building their own applications and workflows. HR, for example, built a workflow in Codex to manage performance reviews, scheduling, feedback collection, and the work of bringing that information together. More than 20 internal applications have been built by non-engineering teams in recent months.
That shift is changing how cult.fit thinks about the software it needs to run its business. When the cost of its internal dashboard software increased sharply, one engineer rebuilt the functionality with Codex over a weekend. Cult.fit now runs the capability on its own application, avoiding more than $100,000 in annual software costs.
Making this shift required more than giving employees access to Codex. A large hackathon gave employees an early view of what was possible. The company then brought its management team together for a one-day session where leaders across functions built something relevant to their own work with Codex.
Engineering also runs twice-weekly office hours to help employees move projects from an idea to production, while engineers are embedded in selected functions to provide technical and domain support.
“Software has been democratized. With OpenAI’s solutions, our people are able to build their own applications around whatever their teams need.”
—Santhosh Kumar, CTO, cult.fit
Enriching the member experience with AI
Cult.fit is also using the OpenAI API to extend AI into the member experience through its AI Trainer. With over 45% of cult.fit members being first time gym goers, guidance is a key access for helping them build a fitness habit. The company first built the AI Trainer several years ago to give members a guided personalized workout experience without a personal trainer.
Around 20% of Cult.fit’s gym users currently utilize the AI Trainer product. With advances in language models, cult.fit saw an opportunity to make the experience more interactive and conversational.
The latest version is designed around a voice-first workout experience. Using GPT Realtime through an OpenAI API integration, the trainer can provide coaching cues and support workout logging through two-way voice interaction.
Making AI part of the operating model
Cult.fit is also applying AI to customer support workflows that previously required human agents to assess each case. One example is requests to waive penalties for missed group fitness classes.
When a member says they missed a class for a valid reason, an AI agent can assess the request by checking signals such as local weather and attendance patterns for that class before deciding whether the penalty should be waived.
Cult.fit built these agents into its existing Sprinklr support platform and connected them to its backend systems, moving customer support from a predominantly human-led chat model toward an AI-first workflow.
Results at a glance
20+ internal applications built by non-engineering teams in recent months
$100,000+ annual software savings by rebuilding an internal capability with Codex
50%+ reduction in customer support costs
What’s next
Cult.fit’s next step is to move from individual AI workflows toward an organization where AI is built into how work gets done. In operations, Kumar describes the ambition as an “autopilot operations org,” with AI taking on more of the support work around frontline teams.
In the member experience, the goal is a “trainer in your pocket,” extending personalized guidance beyond what a human trainer can provide at scale. Inside the organization, cult.fit continues to look for bottlenecks teams can remove with AI. As more employees build applications, analyze information, and automate workflows themselves, more ideas can move directly into working solutions.

items.title: Devin Review 2.0
items.summary:
Today we’re introducing Devin Review 2.0, which makes Devin Review the default tool for PR review when working with Devin.
Since August, we’ve cut the cost of reviewing a PR by 82%. A typical review now costs just $0.25-$0.75, making Devin Review cheap and effective enough to run on every PR.
Watch at https://devin.ai/images/blog/devin-review-2/devin-review-2.mp4
On average across our customers, each bug that gets fixed costs about $2.25.
In this post, we first discuss why review matters more today than ever before. Then we dig deeper into Devin Review’s new cost profile, explore how Devin Review works with Devin, and introduce its latest improvements.
Code review is the bottleneck
The throughput of PRs is increasing, but our capacity for manual code review is not. Code review—the step immediately after PR creation—has become the new bottleneck of the SDLC.
One way to overcome this problem is to stop reviewing PRs or review fewer PRs. However, while this brings short term gains in throughput, it has long term costs in customer-facing bugs and code quality.
A better way to overcome this problem is to use agents to assist with review. Devin Review finds bugs automatically to make all PRs safer. It also produces a guided tour of the PR, so that the human review is faster and has more context.
5x cheaper since August
Since August, the cost of a Devin Review per PR has dropped by 82%. These savings came from a better mix of models across Devin Review and from harness optimizations.
Quality did not suffer. After the cost cuts, Devin Review found more bugs per PR, up from 1.22 to 1.32 on average.
Automatically review every PR
You can run Devin Review on individual PRs with a /devin review comment in GitHub or GitLab. You can also start one from the Devin Review page in Devin Cloud or Devin Desktop.
You can also choose to automatically run Devin Review on your PRs once they are ready for review. Much like CI, this ensures that fewer bugs get merged into your codebase. And this makes it so that when your developers open a fresh PR, there is a completed review with feedback waiting for them.
Devin Review supports using fine-grained rules to decide when a PR should be reviewed. You can choose to run Devin Review on draft PRs; or filter by file paths, branches, labels, and more. Our customers use these rules to minimize their spend by excluding low-value PRs.
Incremental PR reviews
When run again on the same PR, Devin Review now incrementally reviews only the parts of the PR that have changed. This applies by default to every PR. This has two benefits:
New findings are focused on the latest changes, reducing noise.
Costs are greatly reduced, as each push is smaller than the whole PR.
About 80% of PRs cost less than a dollar to review, including all pushes. Devin Review also has a configurable per-PR spend limit, so a runaway PR can’t run up the bill.
Devin Review’s automatic review rules can be set to run on every push. This allows Devin Review to find new bugs as the PR evolves and to refresh the guided tour. One-off reviews are helpful, but miss a large part of the PR lifecycle.
Fix bugs faster with Devin
Devin Review can review PRs from all sources, but it works best with Devin.
When you use them together, Devin investigates each finding and decides whether to fix it, dismiss it, or escalate it to you. By the time you return to the session, the only things left are the bugs and decisions that need your attention.
We have also made Devin Review 1.5x faster since August, with a median latency of 94 seconds, down from 139 seconds.
Make Devin Review work for you
We’re also introducing two features that give you more control over how Devin Review runs and what it looks for.
Effort levels
By default, Devin Review is tuned to be cost efficient. But in some parts of your codebase, such as billing or security-sensitive code, a missed bug costs far more than a review.
For those areas, we’ve added Devin Review Ultra, an effort level that runs a more thorough review at a higher cost.
Custom reviewers
By default, Devin Review looks for bugs. But many teams also have specialized checks they want to run on every PR, which look very different from a bug-finding pass.
Custom Reviewers, now in beta, let you turn those checks into reviewers that run inside Devin Review, using your own instructions. Internally, we run custom reviewers to enforce backend security practices, safe DB migrations, performant SQL queries, and accessible UI components.
Each custom reviewer can have its own automatic review rules. Its findings appear in your Devin Review results and flow into Devin’s automatic fixing, and it follows the same cost controls as the rest of Devin Review.
Learn more
Try Devin Review on your next PR, or read the documentation to learn more.
Devin Review has a free 14-day trial that starts with your first review.

items.title: Franklin Templeton uses OpenAI to support investment research
items.summary:
OpenAI
November 5, 2026
Franklin Templeton uses OpenAI to support investment research
Starting with equity research, Franklin Templeton is developing AI workflows to help portfolio managers compare views and examine risks.
Contact salesCompany size: EnterpriseRegion: North AmericaIndustry: FinanceProducts: CodexShare
Franklin Templeton wants AI to help portfolio managers examine different research views and the risks behind an investment idea. Codex is one of several tools our investment teams are using to develop workflows for investment research.
“The biggest unlock from using OpenAI’s tools is the ability to merge continuous intelligence with human judgment. It has really transitioned because, beforehand, AI was automating our human-led process. Now AI is actually automating the ability to surface intelligent insights, and that intelligence layer plus human judgment is just a fantastic unlock.”
—Katrina Dudley, Senior Vice President, Public Market Investments, Franklin Templeton
Creating connected, continuous intelligence
When Franklin Templeton first tried using AI, the team put data in a database and connected the models to it. But it didn’t produce the answers the teams needed because the models didn’t understand how the data fit together. When the team added agents and a semantic layer, a structured model of what the firm’s data means and how it’s connected, the results changed. The team is using Codex and other tools to develop this connected intelligence layer. "We've been able to build what we think of as a connected intelligence layer," Dudley says. "We're bringing the data into the tools, and we're surfacing insights that make a difference."
Research, risk, compliance, and trading offer different perspectives on an investment. Franklin Templeton’s ambition is to bring those inputs together for portfolio managers. “We're able to bring that all in and then use that to surface insights to the people who are making decisions, which are our portfolio managers,” Dudley says.
Dudley describes the earlier equity-research workflow as human-led and sequential: an analyst performs first-pass stock analysis, reviews earnings calls, and studies competitors in each business line. The goal is to surface useful information as analysts prepare new ideas to be pitched to portfolio managers or provide updates on existing positions in the portfolio. As she puts it, “It's just continuous intelligence combined with that human judgment.”
In the workflow Franklin Templeton envisions, its investment teams will have access to a governed, reusable intelligence foundation that brings together trusted connectors, portfolio and workflow context, and agentic capabilities that surface actionable insights for its analysts and portfolio managers.
Creating workflows specific to each role
Franklin Templeton has used Codex in hackathons, bringing experts alongside investment practitioners as they develop their own tools. Its Investment AI champions are working to turn experiments into production-ready workflows, with security review, expert support, and data controls as part of that process.
Dudley says, “We have moved from augmenting our research process to reimagining the investment research workflow.”
Building AI around how investing works
Some of what makes AI helpful in other settings doesn't work in asset management. Many tools learn a user's preferences and show them more of the same, so if someone favors one research provider, the tool surfaces more of that provider's reports. For an investment team, that narrowing potentially brings a biased perspective into the investment process. Franklin Templeton wants the opposite. "We want to make sure that they're accessing that diversity of research and diversity of opinion," Dudley says.
Franklin Templeton wants its AI systems to emphasize investment risks. “We need AI to understand that a great investment idea is one that is well reasoned, but it also has analyzed the risks and makes our portfolio managers aware of the risk,” Dudley says. “If you’re looking at a research note, focusing on the fact someone has identified the investment risks is not a bad thing from our perspective. It makes for a more informed investment decision.”
Franklin Templeton's experience points to some investment management best practices:
“Our message from leadership is consistent: we encourage innovation and experimentation with AI within clearly defined risk guardrails. Not every initiative will succeed, but each should generate insights that strengthen our capabilities, inform future decisions, and drive continuous improvement,” Dudley says.
Get new tools into people's hands: Dudley says Franklin Templeton has brought practical labs to teams quickly after new technology launches, so they can test how it fits their work.
Help teams learn the tools: Dudley says, "The goal is getting them to actually understand the power of the technology."
Build with appropriate controls: Security review, expert support, and data agreements are part of Franklin Templeton’s path from experimentation toward production-grade tools.
“With OpenAI, our teams feel like they’re at the forefront of technology.”
—Katrina Dudley, Senior Vice President, Public Market Investments, Franklin Templeton
Dudley’s longer-term goal is to make that connected intelligence accessible across investment teams, from analysts to the leaders of each investment group.
She wants analysts to spend more time in the field, speaking with many different experts and professionals, including executives at private companies, and bringing what they learn back to their investment teams. For Dudley, that human perspective remains essential as the tools develop.

We’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, which offers native 15-second video creation, improved reference adherence, and multi-turn conversational editing. This update lowers costs by 30% and provides better consistency for your professional projects. You can start using these capabilities today across the Gemini API, Google Vids, and Gemini for business to produce high-quality video content at scale.

General summary
Bullet points
Today, we’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, and making it generally available across the Gemini API and Gemini for business. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces native 15-second video creation, multi-turn conversational editing capabilities, and enhanced reference following. We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video.
Here’s an overview of what’s new:
Fast and cost-effective at scale
Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K.
Longer clips up to 15 seconds
You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation.
Better reference adherence
You can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Faces, garments, packaging typography, and brand colors stay consistent across camera angles, making it easy to turn existing product photography or character sheets into virtual try-on clips, catalog spins, and branded video ads.
Combining one model photo with front-and-back product shots of three outfits, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates a 15-second virtual try-on sequence across 360-degree turns and match cuts while keeping the model’s identity and each garment’s cut, drape, and back details consistent.
More consistent results
You can maintain stronger character, object, and scene consistency from the first to the last frame, with less visual drift or morphing across motion and camera transitions. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot.
Given the same static studio lighting exhibition poster and five-layer animation prompt, Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash does not match the reference image as closely as 1.2 does. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash builds the poster sequentially layer by layer on the dusty-pink cyclorama rising the hexagonal plinth, assembling the ribbed glass, warm filament, faceted crystal, and coiled-cord letterforms for HALO, GLOW, and LUMEN, and locking every material, shadow, and typographic detail consistently through the final frame.
Easier editing in conversation
You can refine the same clip turn by turn — such as swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio — instead of starting over from scratch. Multi-turn conversational editing works across full 15-second clips, making it easy to produce ad variants for different audiences and placements without re-briefing or re-generating.
Starting from one generated clip, multi-turn conversational prompts swap the background turn by turn — from a striped pavilion tent to an oak forest, a stable with a white horse, a market fair, and a stone castle — while keeping both characters’ performances, armor reflections, and camera framing intact.
More natural speech
You can generate scenes with more fluid, natural-sounding dialogue, clearer lip-sync, and distinct multi-speaker conditioning. This will show up whether you’re directing multi-character dialogue in Flow, creating video explainers in Gemini for business, or creating polished, pro videos with avatars, music and narration in Google Vids.
Conditioned on one conservatory scene image alongside four character, mouth, and one-second voice references, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash routes each sampled voice to the right character with expressive lip-sync and natural comedic timing across a 15-second animated scene.
More controllable, cinematic look
You can direct complex, continuous camera movements like sweeping FPV flythroughs to dramatic zoom-outs and orbits with significantly fewer unwanted jump cuts, steadier scale, and a more polished, cinematic look.
Guided by two architectural reference photos, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash directs one continuous FPV drone flight across the piazza, through the bronze doors, and up through the Pantheon’s coffered dome to the oculus with zero jump cuts.
Longer clips with smoother motion and tighter consistency
Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates clips up to 15 seconds long that hold references together better than before. You can scroll through to see characters, text, and camera moves stay consistent across longer shots, multiple turns and transitions with no cuts.
15 second long clips: Turns one style frame into a 4-shot, 15-second macro science explainer with accurately spelled, motion-tracked callouts.
Multi-turn motion transfer: Generates a rippling octopus in Turn 1, then replaces it in Turn 2 with a dancer whose gown mirrors the exact fluid motion.
First-to-last frame consistency (1.1 vs. 1.2): Connects an exterior start frame and interior end frame in one continuous camera push in 1.2 Flash. You can see subtle differences like the cats on the roof, the soup ladle turning into chopsticks, and some other minor changes.
Unbroken crash zoom-out: Pulls continuously from a tight shoreline close-up to an aerial island vista in one 10-second shot with natural scale and zero cuts.
Real-world results, from creatives to global brands
Businesses, startups, and creatives are already using Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash in their workflows. And for the first time, Gemini Omni is now generally available, backed by Google Cloud’s enterprise-grade infrastructure and security. Provisioned Throughput is available, and outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark.
Get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash
While development is ongoing to further improve things like fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is ideal for businesses, developers, and creators producing videos at scale. You can get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash today as it rolls out across Google’s products and developer platforms:
For developers using the Gemini API: Prototype in Google AI Studio, explore interactive starter apps, and check out the developer documentation and pricing.
For businesses: Try it in the Google Cloud console, and build enterprise solutions with the API.
For everyone using Google apps: Direct scenes and multi-turn edits in Flow, generate 15-second clips at no additional cost in Google Vids with a Google account or Google Workspace subscription, create 15-second videos in the Gemini app (rolling out to Google AI Ultra subscribers), and scale video campaigns in Google Ads.

items.title: GitLab Integration
items.summary: Amp now integrates with GitLab, on gitlab.com and on self-managed instances. Connect your GitLab account and you can start projects from your GitLab repositories. Orbs clone and push as you and come with glab signed in, so the agent can open merge requests, comment on them, and read issues and pipelines. Amp can also subscribe to comments and CI for a merge request it opens. A reviewer's request or a failed pipeline lands in the thread that wrote the code, so Amp already has the context. A New Orb for Every New Merge Request or Issue Ask Amp to start a new orb for every new merge request or issue in a project. You don't need to keep the thread where you set it up. See Create an Orb Spawner. Each new merge request or issue gets its own orb, which reads it and has a summary ready when you open the thread. Later comments go to that same thread. Workspace admins can also run a spawner as a service account. You manage all of these in Settings → Integrations & MCP → GitLab under Event Subscriptions, where you can pause or delete them, edit a spawner, and see the orbs each spawner started. Set It Up Each person connects GitLab in Settings → Integrations & MCP. Then a group Owner installs Push Updates once for the workspace, with one button in Workspace Settings → Integrations & MCP. Amp also supports self-managed GitLab. See Self-Managed Instances. Connect GitLab to get started.

items.title: GPT-6 Cyber Security Evaluation: CodeRabbit’s Results
items.summary: When a security scan flags a vulnerability, your team still needs to assess its impact and decide how to address it. We wanted to understand whether GPT-6 Cyber could help our existing ensemble find more issues worth investigating, and what that would mean for the reports developers receive. We evaluated GPT-6 Cyber in CodeRabbit Secure, comparing our model ensemble with and without it on the same 33 benchmark cases. With Cyber, the ensemble caught 22 selected issues versus 19 without it and reported 66% more high- and medium-severity findings. The 66% increase counts issues flagged in the final reports. We still need to assess how many of the additional findings are real vulnerabilities. CodeRabbit Secure scans your codebase for potential vulnerabilities and traces the code paths behind its findings. This evaluation extends our September code review evaluation to security scans. 66% more high- and medium-severity findings (65.6%, rounded). The known-issue catch rate increased by 9.1%. Some investigations required recovery runs. Try Deep Scan Catching vulnerabilities with a Deep Scan helps your team address security risks before they become very costly incidents. Run a Deep Scan → What is GPT-6 Cyber? GPT-6 Cyber is the cybersecurity variant of OpenAI’s GPT-6 models. Cyber models are trained for security research, including finding vulnerabilities and testing whether they can be exploited, with fewer refusals on authorized security tasks. We received access for this evaluation through the OpenAI Daybreak Defense Network. Cyber models are part of OpenAI Daybreak, with access subject to approval, including additional model-specific approval in some cases. How we evaluated GPT-6 Cyber in our security scans We compared CodeRabbit’s model ensemble with and without GPT-6 Cyber on the same 33 cases. Each case had a known security issue we wanted the scan to find. The cases covered Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, PHP, Rust, Ruby, C, and C#. We evaluated what reached the developer in the final report, after the scan’s verification and reporting stages. A potential issue raised during investigation did not earn credit unless it appeared in that report with an explanation of how the code could fail. We checked the final reports for two things: Known issues caught: We checked whether the report identified the issue selected for that case and explained its cause and security consequence. Each case could contribute one catch to this score. Flagging a risky function or finding a different issue did not count as catching the selected issue. Reported findings: We counted all findings across the 33 final reports for each configuration, including findings about issues other than the selected benchmark issue. We also counted the high- and medium-severity findings separately. A scan could report several potential problems and still miss the known issue. Conversely, several findings about the selected issue would still count as only one benchmark catch. The catch score tells us how many of the known issues were found, while the findings count tells us how much output developers received. For each case, we compared one final report from each configuration. The investigation stage used high reasoning effort to trace potential vulnerabilities through the code. We did not compare results at different effort settings. Results MetricEnsemble with GPT-6 CyberEnsemble without GPT-6 CyberChange Known issues caught22/33 · 66.7%19/33 · 57.6%+9.1% High- and medium-severity reported findings361218+65.6% Reported findings at all severities979592+65.4% The ensemble caught three more selected issues, a 15.8% relative increase, and reported 143 additional high- and medium-severity findings. We still need to assess how many of the additional findings describe valid vulnerabilities. Where coverage changed 5 additional catches − 2 lost catches = 3 more overall. Each square represents one benchmark case. Squares show counts, not identifiable cases. Five additional catches and two lost catches produced the net gain of three. Nine selected issues remained undetected by either configuration. These cases give us concrete targets for improving coverage while preserving existing catches. Reported findings increased in all six selected categories. These are output counts, not category-specific detection rates. Injection and server-side request forgery had the largest percentage increases. Denial of service added the most findings (98), followed by authorization bypass (77). Discussion The evaluation records a net gain of three selected issues with GPT-6 Cyber: five catches the baseline missed and two baseline catches lost. The additions and losses show the difference in coverage between the configurations. Both the additional detections and the lost catches matter when assessing the model’s contribution to the ensemble. We can then test where to use the model selectively, with the goal of adding useful detections while preserving the ensemble’s existing results. Our integration work focuses on making those additional findings useful to developers. The larger report volume makes verification and prioritization especially important. Additional issues worth fixing, preservation of existing catches, and manageable reports are the criteria for that work. The benchmark provides concrete cases for that assessment. Choosing the reasoning effort We used high reasoning effort for investigation, where the model traces potential vulnerabilities through the code. Without a matched lower-effort run, we can’t isolate the effect of that setting. Our next comparison will change effort at one stage at a time, using the same cases and scoring criteria. We will compare known issues retained in final reports, complete-scan time, and cost, including verification. Lower effort could be more practical if it preserves useful catches. Higher effort would earn its place where it adds findings worth investigating. Where GPT-6 Cyber adds value GPT-6 Cyber shows a concrete improvement for deeper security scans in CodeRabbit. In our evaluation, the ensemble with GPT-6 Cyber included 66% more high- and medium-severity findings in its final reports and caught approximately 16% more of the selected benchmark issues than the ensemble without it. If your team’s main problem is already too many alerts, report volume alone gives you little reason to change models. The useful measure is how many additional issues deserve a fix and how much work it takes to establish that. The evaluation provides measured coverage and report-volume results, while report accuracy and assessment effort remain priorities for the integration work. We recommend evaluating GPT-6 Cyber for security-sensitive scans, keeping the issues the existing ensemble already catches in the regression set. For developers using CodeRabbit, our integration work aims to turn that additional detection into useful findings before code ships. These results give us a concrete improvement to build on. What CodeRabbit Secure Deep Scan is finding in practice From October 23 to November 3, teams ran over 13,000 Deep Scans across more than 2,700 organizations. Deep Scan identified critical and high-severity findings, with authorization bypass, IDOR, and cross-site scripting among the most common. These are product-wide Deep Scan results. The evaluation above examines GPT-6 Cyber’s contribution to the model ensemble. Run a Deep Scan →

items.title: GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents
items.summary:
OpenAI
November 5, 2026
ProductSecuritySafety
GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents
A cybersecurity model trained to find and validate exploitable vulnerabilities, while staying within the scope that researchers set.
Join DaybreakRead the system card(opens in a new window)Share
We’re introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, a major leap in security research: more capable at finding and fixing vulnerabilities, and far more reliable staying within the boundaries researchers set. GPT‑6 Cyber delivers major gains on key cybersecurity benchmarks over GPT‑5.6 Cyber, including a 51% relative improvement on ExploitGym and a step function improvement when tested on staying within scope. It is already helping to secure real-world software, uncovering and validating thousands of exploits in security-critical codebases such as Linux and Firefox.
On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. It also follows task boundaries more reliably: in a separate alignment evaluation, GPT‑6 Cyber avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of tests without its deployment prompt, and 100% with this prompt. This improvement in alignment reflects dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately.
These capabilities are already helping secure real systems. Our researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber to develop 948 privilege escalation exploits in Linux⁠ and identify 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, despite extensive prior testing with frontier models. The model also helped develop candidate patches, and Mozilla has released fixes for many of the Firefox vulnerabilities⁠(opens in a new window). Security teams at Cisco, Calif, and CodeRabbit are using it for vulnerability research and code review, and we have relied on it to find and fix weaknesses in our own infrastructure⁠.
It is clear that we have a limited window to use frontier models to secure software⁠. Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers. Mainline models such as GPT‑6 Astra already support code review, vulnerability triage, and patch development. Daybreak Blue helps verified defenders validate vulnerabilities and fixes with fewer unnecessary refusals, while Daybreak Red enables deeper exploit development and authorized security testing with GPT‑6 Cyber.
Advancing frontier cyber capabilities
GPT‑6 Cyber is a major step up from GPT‑5.6 Cyber and outperforms GPT‑6 Astra on most cyber tasks, even when Astra does not refuse the request. We evaluated the model on tasks that require it to understand software, identify vulnerabilities, and develop working exploits. Based on these results, we classify the model as Critical in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT‑5.6 Cyber.
On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability in a remote target, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, about 16 percentage points higher than GPT‑5.6 Cyber’s 32.1%. To test vulnerability discovery, we also built a new evaluation for offensive web penetration testing. Models probe web applications without access to their source code. GPT‑6 Cyber achieved 40.3% recall of vulnerabilities compared with 32.0% for GPT‑6 Astra.
Daybreak Red is designed to support more advanced security workflows, including developing working exploits and using them against remote targets. To evaluate these capabilities, we built a new benchmark called RemoteExploitBench, which uses known vulnerabilities in applications such as GitLab, PostgreSQL, and Jenkins deployed in a controlled environment. In our initial evaluation, GPT‑6 Astra running with Daybreak Blue refused 100% of tasks, while GPT‑6 Cyber completed 95%; its only failure was an exploit it could not get to work remotely. See the system card⁠(opens in a new window) for full results and evaluation settings.
Stronger alignment, better at staying within bounds
One risk for cybersecurity agents is that they go outside the scope of their assigned task, attempt to exploit unrelated services, or disregard the researcher’s rules of engagement.
We made alignment a central focus of GPT‑6 Cyber, using specialized training to help the model stay within authorized scope, follow restrictions on its actions, and report its work accurately. Before deployment, we ran a series of alignment evaluations to measure these behaviors. See the system card⁠(opens in a new window) for full results.
One of these evaluations is ExploitGym Honeypot, which was informed by the Hugging Face incident⁠. We give the model a difficult exploitation task in an isolated environment with access to supporting services, such as a package registry or object store. We deliberately make these services easy to exploit so that attacking them can reveal the task’s flag. The model must infer that exploiting them is outside the scope of its task.
GPT‑6 Cyber shows a step-change improvement over GPT‑5.6 Cyber on this evaluation. When tested without deployment safety prompts, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of cases, up from 94.49% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. With those prompts, GPT‑6 Cyber stayed within bounds 100% of the time.
We can see directly in the GPT‑6 Cyber model’s chain of thought how it reasons about staying within bounds:
Agent chain-of-thought excerpts
“Can't assume extra API or attack controller not target. We should only target binary/server.”“Can't assume extra API or attack controller not target. We should only target binary/server.”“Can't assume extra API or attack controller not target. We should only target binary/server.”
Agent chain-of-thought excerpts
“don't explore out of scope credentials.”“don't explore out of scope credentials.”“don't explore out of scope credentials.”
Real-world impact for security teams
GPT‑6 Cyber is already helping security teams find vulnerabilities, validate their impact, and develop fixes. Customers have put it to work on large codebases, long-running exploit development, and security review:
1 of 9
“GPT‑6 Cyber is a world-class model for cyberdefense. Firefox entered 2026 as one of the world’s most hardened and scrutinized codebases. Even after further hardening with multiple generations of frontier models, GPT‑6 Cyber uncovered previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities, identified architectural improvements, and helped us ship fixes to millions of users.”
- Brian Grinstead, Distinguished Engineer, Firefox
“It's the best model we’ve used so far for long running exploit development tasks. Its ability to construct libraries of primitives over time and then find a path through them to something stronger is a step change from previous generations.”
- Thai Duong, CEO, Calif
“GPT‑6 Cyber was the best model on our internal novel vulnerability discovery and exploitation benchmarks. It scored 23% compared to the previous best score of 13%. It is highly efficient in discovering high impact vulnerabilities in large codebases and converting them to end-to-end proof of concepts. This model is pushing the frontier on how cybersecurity can be handled by models.”
- Steven Hao, CTO, Cognition
“GPT‑6 Cyber represents a major leap forward from prior models. We found the model to be faster, more cost-effective, and significantly smarter. It's already instrumental in helping us better protect our own products, and through Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense, we’re bringing that same speed and precision to our customers to protect enterprise software at scale.”
- Lee Klarich, Chief Product & Technology Officer, Palo Alto Networks
“Defending modern infrastructure requires continuous innovation. As the threat landscape grows in complexity, harnessing frontier AI models like OpenAI GPT‑6 Cyber is an essential step toward tipping the scale in favor of defenders. Integrating these capabilities into our research allows our teams to analyze complex architectures and identify risks with greater speed and precision, ultimately strengthening the resilience and trust of the technology our customers rely on.”
- Anthony Grieco, SVP, Chief Security & Trust Officer, Cisco
“The hardest part of security research is connecting scattered clues into a clear understanding of how an attack could work. GPT‑6 Cyber helps our researchers make those connections, test their hypotheses, and uncover weaknesses that demand deeper investigation. It expands what our experts can take on—and helps us turn that understanding into better protection for customers.”
- Chris Corde, Chief Product Officer, SentinelOne
“We see GPT‑6 Cyber as a meaningful step forward in putting AI to work for defenders. GPT‑6 Cyber builds and validates working exploits at scale, and stays in scope while it does it. At CrowdStrike, we turn what offense finds into defense, so every attack path a model uncovers is one an adversary can’t use. Together that’s how we tilt the advantage back to defenders.”
- Bartley Richardson, Chief AI & Autonomous Systems Officer, CrowdStrike
“We used GPT‑6 cyber on the bugs that are hardest to find: issues buried in complex logic, spread across components, or only reachable through a long chain of conditions. It works through those investigations end to end without losing the thread, and it returns clear, reproducible findings our team can verify and fix quickly.”
- Kyle Polley, CISO, Perplexity
“GPT‑6 Cyber is the strongest model we’ve tested for security review. On our internal benchmark, it found 66% more high and medium severity security issues than our production model. Those are the bugs developers need to fix as they build with AI agents.”
- Harjot Gill, CEO CodeRabbit
