We have also relied on GPT‑6 Cyber to secure our own systems. It was one of the main models behind the work we recently shared on hardening the infrastructure used to train frontier models⁠. In controlled red-teaming campaigns, agents using GPT‑6 Cyber and other OpenAI models chained vulnerabilities to escape microVMs and execute code on the underlying hosts. We used the findings to patch software, tighten network restrictions, and report issues to maintainers and vendors.
Our vulnerability researchers also use GPT‑6 Cyber to find and validate vulnerabilities in open-source software at scale. This work has uncovered previously unknown flaws in software that has been scrutinized for years:
Found 81 novel Firefox vulnerabilities. GPT‑6 Cyber can be suitable for use in autonomous workflows for finding vulnerabilities and proposing high-quality patches at scale. During a vulnerability research campaign, GPT‑6 Cyber produced evidence and reproducible tests for 81 novel vulnerabilities classified by Mozilla as high severity, and showed that an additional 30 known issues were more severe than previously reported. We disclosed the findings to Mozilla, along with proposed patches to help its engineers develop fixes. Mozilla was supportive of this work, and began landing fixes shortly after receiving the reports⁠(opens in a new window).
Developing exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities⁠. GPT‑6 Cyber reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948—more than five times the 166 exploited by GPT‑5.6 Sol using the same research harness. Following the Linux community's guidance, we disclosed 304 critical findings to maintainers with candidate patches and are in the process of getting other vulnerabilities fixed.
Demonstrating critical RCE vulnerabilities. We recently discussed a critical vulnerability in Brotli⁠(opens in a new window), a compression library used by Node.js and other software. Our security researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber alongside other OpenAI models to develop and validate exploits showing how the flaw could enable remote code execution in downstream applications.
Detecting misuse and blocking high-risk activity
As models become more capable and uncover more security vulnerabilities, we are also seeing more attempts to use them to cause harm. These attempts include efforts by malicious cyber actors and adversarial groups seeking to distill our models. We have thus paired GPT‑6 Cyber’s stronger capabilities with stronger safeguards to detect and disrupt misuse and keep the model’s actions within the user’s intent and authorization.
We added and strengthened these protections alongside the release of GPT‑6 Cyber (see the system card⁠(opens in a new window) for full information):
Cyber-specific misalignment monitoring. We monitor whether actions match the user’s authorization, while recognizing legitimate exploit development and testing.
Targeted monitoring for emerging threats. For example, during the coordinated disclosure of critical PHP vulnerabilities, we set up targeted monitoring for attempts to develop exploits against live PHP servers, while preserving support for defenders patching affected systems.
Private Safety Processing (PSP). We use automated checks to review related interactions for misuse. Standard retention remains the default. API customers using Zero Data Retention⁠(opens in a new window) generally must use PSP⁠(opens in a new window), which reviews encrypted records retained in customer storage for 30 days without exposing prompts and responses to OpenAI personnel.
Protection against stolen credentials. We require IP allowlisting for Daybreak Red API access by default, restricting requests to approved networks with limited exceptions. We also monitor credentials for compromise.
Sandboxing and oversight. As with past models, we recommend sandboxing⁠(opens in a new window), action review⁠(opens in a new window), and human oversight for high-risk workflows.
Protections against high-risk cyber assistance. We use new checks to block high-risk activity involving critical systems (see below for more).
Defending critical infrastructure
Protecting critical infrastructure has been a key consideration in designing GPT‑6 Cyber’s safeguards and access, including power plants, water treatment facilities, and the operational technology and industrial control systems (OT/ICS) that underpin them. We simultaneously want to give the teams defending these systems access to our most capable models while also strengthening our safeguards to prevent unauthorized attacks.
First, to equip these defenders, our $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders⁠ grant program subsidizes access for resource-constrained teams such as government organizations and essential service providers. We’re also introducing a new group within Daybreak Red (Daybreak Red for Critical Infrastructure) for approved critical infrastructure defenders, which gives them permissions to conduct authorized testing of critical systems while retaining safeguards against model misalignment.
Second, to prevent misuse of the Daybreak Red and Blue platforms, we have refined safeguards against assistance and capability development that could compromise industrial controls or safety-critical systems, interfere with equipment, or cause serious injury, catastrophic physical damage, or life-endangering service disruption. The figure below compares safeguard label rates across four access configurations, before and after the recent updates we’re rolling out alongside GPT‑6 Cyber.
Higher safeguard block rates are not always better. Many of the techniques in this evaluation are also essential to legitimate security work: understanding systems, finding vulnerabilities, and verifying that fixes withstand attack. We therefore assess these rates alongside support for legitimate research and patching, rather than aiming for 100%.
To evaluate how our models can help defend critical infrastructure, we partnered with Dragos, the global provider for extended operational technology (xOT) cybersecurity. Dragos ran evaluations using cyber-permissive Daybreak Red models in a controlled lab environment. The evaluations covered requests progressing from network discovery and asset enumeration through targeted reconnaissance, sensitive data exfiltration, and unauthorized, potentially dangerous device actions.
“Dragos put a frontier model on a mock power plant range and told it almost nothing. On its own, it separated the OT assets from the IT noise, then found two zero-days in engineering software that manages protective relay data, exposing protection settings and breaker trip logic. That’s the map an adversary wants before touching anything physical. The skill floor is dropping for the reconnaissance and vulnerability research needed before an attack. Working with OpenAI on this shows them the adversary’s path through an OT network before real adversaries take it, so safeguards get built around how these attacks could unfold, while the models stay useful to the people defending these systems.”
—Rob T. Lee, Chief AI Officer, Dragos
We used feedback from Dragos to refine our safeguards, aiming to block harmful assistance without unnecessarily restricting authorized testing. See their final report⁠(opens in a new window) for details on the evaluations. We’re also working to expand partnerships with other offensive security providers and purple teams on penetration testing and red teaming with AI, and with energy companies, other critical infrastructure operators, and national labs to assess our models’ effectiveness and safeguards in industrial defense. We have also increased our investment in threat investigations to detect model usage involving OT/ICS. We’ll continue refining our safeguards with input from partners and the security community, including reports through /feedback when safeguards miss harmful activity or interrupt legitimate work.
Expanding access to trusted defenders
GPT‑6 Cyber is initially available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers. items.title: Introducing Personal Finance in Claude
items.summary:
Introducing Personal Finance in Claude
Ask Claude about your money and get straight answers from the accounts you connect.
CategoryProduct updates
DateNovember 5, 2026
Reading time5 min
ShareCopy link
Getting answers about your money no longer means opening every banking app and doing the math yourself. With Personal Finance in Claude, you can securely connect your bank and card accounts and ask in your own words. Access is read-only, and Personal Finance can’t move, manage, or invest your money.
Claude gives you answers in everyday language, from your balances and transactions, and explains any term that's new to you. Like the rest of Claude, Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it doesn’t offer credit cards, loans, or savings accounts of its own, so your money questions get a straight answer.
Personal Finance starts rolling out in beta this week, on the Pro, Max, and Ultra plans in the US.
What it looks like
Say it's late in the month and payday is still 10 days away. When you ask Claude, "Where did my money go this month?" it adds up your spending across the accounts you connected and sorts it by category. In this example, that comes to $4,309.37, with more than half going to rent and utilities and $1,024.51 to food and drink.
From there, you can dig deeper: "Is that more than usual?" "Anything else I'm missing?" "So what's left before payday?" Claude checks the previous months and points to a membership renewal. Then Claude tells you about four payments that will come out of your checking account before payday, and what you’ll have left: $1,393.22.
If you ask whether anything looks off, Claude reads across every account you've connected and can point to what's easy to miss, like charges that hit twice, unexpected fees, or a bill that’s crept up all year. You can also ask bigger questions, like "Am I spending more than I make?" or "What's an APR, and what has mine cost me this year?" Claude explains the term, then adds up the interest you've been charged.
Ask for a weekly spending chart, a calendar of what's due, or a dashboard of the numbers you choose, and Claude builds one you can keep adjusting.
Security and privacy
Claude's access is read-only. Personal Finance helps you understand your money, and it isn't designed to give investment advice. Claude can make mistakes in its answers, so ask which transactions are behind a number, and check important figures with your bank.
Your accounts are only connected once you sign in to your bank yourself through Plaid, a service that connects apps to banks. That's where you agree to its terms and approve Claude's read-only access, so Claude doesn't ask for or see your bank password.
For the accounts you choose to connect (and only those), Claude sees the bank's name, each account's name, type, and last four digits, balances and credit limits, and up to two years of transactions. When you chat with Claude in the Personal Finance hub, those conversations aren't used to train our models. For anything you share with Claude outside the hub, your privacy settings apply. You can unlink an account anytime, and then Claude can no longer see its data. More details can be found in our Privacy Center.
Getting started
When you see Personal Finance in Claude's sidebar, open it, connect one account, and ask a single question, like "Can I afford a trip this spring?" or "How much could I save each month?" You'll find the setup steps, and how your data is used and kept, in the Help Center. (opens in new tab)
What’s next
Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust. We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it.

items.title: LangSmith BYOC is now available on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud
items.summary:
LangSmith
LangSmith BYOC is now available on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud
Karthic SubramanianNovember 3, 20265minGo back to blogCreate agentsCreate agentsShare
LangSmith Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) now runs on AWS (GA), Azure (Beta), and Google Cloud (Beta). Your traces, evals, datasets, prompts, and agent deployments stay in your own cloud account, on the cloud you choose, and LangChain manages the data plane for you, from orchestration and scaling to platform updates.
How BYOC splits LangSmith
By splitting the control plane and data plane in two, BYOC provides greater flexibily to decide where agents run and where telemetry lives, without taking on the work of running LangSmith. LangChain runs the control plane, which holds auth, org and workspace config, billing metadata, hashed API keys, and static UI assets. You own the data plane, which holds everything sensitive, from traces, prompts, and datasets to experiments, agent deployments, and workspace secrets.
‍
An organization can hold several data planes, each in its specific account and region, and each data plane holds its workspaces. This lets you split data planes by region, environment, or business unit.
For example, a platform team might run production and staging data planes in separate AWS accounts, while a business unit that standardized on Azure runs its own, separate BYOC deployment on Azure. Each team's traces land in the account that team owns.
Why we built BYOC
Until now, teams with strict compliance boundaries deployed and maintained self-hosted LangSmith. This kept their data inside their own boundary, but it took dedicated platform engineers to patch stateful services, configure databases, and run schema migrations.
With BYOC, LangChain provisions and operates LangSmith inside your own virtual network. Consider a team running agent applications across several environments. With self-hosted, every update to the execution components meant coordinating downtime and managing custom Helm rollouts in each environment. With BYOC, the data in your data plane stays in your VPC while LangChain handles scaling, schema updates, and runtime dependencies.
While self-hosting continues to be a reliable deployment option for customers who require complete control, BYOC provides the best of both worlds for customers who need it.
What AWS customers have seen
Since we launched BYOC on AWS in August, many teams have chosen to run LangSmith in their own cloud with BYOC. They point to three main benefits:
Continuous upgrades. LangChain rolls out platform updates, so teams no longer plan maintenance windows or manage Helm upgrades.
The latest LangSmith features. New features reach BYOC data planes soon after they ship on LangSmith Cloud, without waiting for the next self-hosted release.
Automatic scaling. Services scale with load, so teams get consistent uptime and a smooth experience as usage grows.
By expanding LangSmith BYOC to Azure and Google Cloud, more teams can get access to this experience while choosing their preferred cloud vendor.
What BYOC looks like on each cloud
Each cloud has its own network policies, identity model, and security requirements, so BYOC is built from each cloud's own building blocks. While built on each cloud’s building blocks, the core LangSmith experience is common across clouds and deployment options:
Traces, trajectories, evaluations, and insights run on the data plane.
LLM Gateway is runs in the data plane with support for bringing your own provider keys.
LangSmith deployment runs in your cluster.
Engine runs over your data on your own model providers.
Sandboxes for isolation within your private cloud
On all three clouds, BYOC data planes also run Managed Deep Agents endpoints.
Azure: BYOC runs the data plane inside a dedicated virtual network with a private AKS API endpoint. We deploy Istio and KEDA with Helm for ingress routing and event-driven scaling, and system telemetry goes to Azure Monitor.
Google Cloud: At launch, Google Cloud data planes can run in any region and are managed from LangSmith's US control plane. Resources use namespace-scoped names, so they don't collide with your existing infrastructure.
AWS: BYOC runs inside your existing VPC, with the database in subnets you choose. Security teams can attach their own security groups to each application role, so the data plane fits the ingress and egress inspection policies you already run.
Move from self-hosted without starting over
Self-hosted LangSmith gave you full control of where your data lives, but required significant maintenance overhead. BYOC keeps the data in your account while we run the infrastructure, and you can bring your existing self-hosted data with you. Both deployment options run LangSmith reliably, and the choice depends on your specific needs.
The migration happens in two steps. Step 1 is provisioning the BYOC data plane. In step 2, workspace resources move using our open source migration tool, which reads from your self-hosted instance but does not result in downtime or data changes on it. On every cloud, it covers users and roles, datasets, experiments, and prompts. It also brings over annotation queue config, automation rules, and dashboards.
Your traces, runs, and feedback move as a separate step that LangChain runs for you with internal tooling. Trace migration is available on AWS today.
Flexible, Open Platform
LangSmith gives you an open, flexible platform for building and running agents without vendor lock-in. You can build with open-source frameworks like LangChain, LangGraph and Deep Agents, while retaining complete ownership of your data, models, and infrastructure. The LLM Gateway connects to 11 model providers out of the box, plus any OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible endpoint. With this expansion, LangSmith BYOC runs across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, using public Terraform modules hosted at github.com/langchain-ai/terraform and an open-source migration tool.
Get started
Contact sales to provision a BYOC data plane on AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud. The docs cover the architecture, the shared responsibility model, migration, usage, and common questions in the FAQ, with the Create Data Plane API in the API reference.

items.title: Merge builds product and business tools with OpenAI technology
items.summary:
OpenAI
November 5, 2026
Merge builds product and business tools with OpenAI technology
The integration platform uses GPT‑6 Astra, ChatGPT, and Codex for product reviews, marketing, and business development planning.
Join the communityCompany size: StartupRegion: North AmericaIndustry: TechnologyProducts: ChatGPT, CodexShare
Merge helps companies build connected software and AI products, from syncing customer data to enabling AI agents to take action across business systems. Its products span customer-data integrations through Merge Unified, secure tool access for AI agents through Merge Agent Handler, and model routing and cost controls through Merge Gateway. Merge for Workforce brings those capabilities inside companies, helping teams manage which models, tools, and business systems employees can access. Together, these products support both the software companies build for customers and the AI-powered work happening inside their organizations.
Inside Merge, CEO and Co-founder Shensi Ding uses Codex to review product code, including work on a new setup interface for configuring tool access in Merge for Workforce. Her colleagues use GPT‑6 Astra for product testing and marketing. The team also uses AI for the work of running the company, from preparing sales updates to planning customer dinners.
“We use it honestly for everything. Integrations obviously, but we also use it to automate different workflows, to help make our product better overall, to incorporate any feedback from our customers, and to build end-to-end features.”
—Shensi Ding, CEO and Co-founder, Merge
Inside the rollout
Merge launched a tool for adding connectors to AI products, with reliability a priority for Ding: “We’re pretty proud of the quality. Tool calls through Merge succeed 99.9% of the time, compared to public MCP servers, which are around 60%.”
For its own product development, Merge uses GPT‑6 Astra. “It’s really fast, and it was much better at code reviews,” Ding says. “They also liked the personality of GPT‑6 Astra, which goes a long way. It was also clear that Codex had improved a lot. Merge lets employees choose their own AI tools, and which one to use has become a lively internal debate.”
Ding used Codex to review a proposed implementation of the new provisioning tab in Merge for Workforce as the team evaluated how customers would configure tool access. They discussed making the “Add tool pack” action a clearer link that opens separately to make setup less confusing. Codex supplied code-review feedback; Merge’s team made the product decisions and implementation changes, with engineers responsible for validating and shipping them.
“Other AI systems would end up forgetting what I told them and only doing the last thing that I said. GPT-6 Astra continues to execute on every single task really well, and it fills in the gaps for what I did not explicitly say using common sense.”
—Shensi Ding, CEO and Co-founder, Merge
The dinner bot
Merge hosts executive dinners for customers and prospects to build relationships and create opportunities for follow-up product conversations.
For one dinner in Dallas, Merge started with the city and the kinds of people it wanted to bring together. The bot pulled potential guests from the CRM and Apollo, checked previous invitations and responses, and helped prepare outreach from Ding’s email. It also maintained the attendee tracker, proposed a seating chart, and created calendar notes where sales and customer success could add context about each guest.
The model handles reasoning and drafting, while Merge’s connectors provide access to the business systems. Ding reviews the output, rewrites anything that sounds off, and curates the guest list using relationship context the bot does not have.
In October 2026, Merge reported that preparing guest lists and outreach and maintaining the attendee tracker had gone from dozens of hours across the company to about 30 minutes per event. The comparison covers the same planning tasks, measured over the preceding three months. The team still handles hosting, relationship-building, and on-the-ground logistics.
Merge ran 16 executive dinners in Q3, up from eight in Q2, and plans to host more than 30 in Q4. After the Dallas dinner, the team reported positive feedback on the invitations and opportunities for follow-up demos.
“With GPT‑6 Astra, the dinner bot connects to our Salesforce, Gong, Google Sheets, and Gmail, and it’ll send emails on my behalf to people in our network,” Ding says. “It gives me recommendations for people who are a good fit for each dinner, and it surfaces new potential attendees.”
Everyone is a builder
Ding says, “It’s been especially great for team members who aren’t in engineering, because now they can build anything.”
Charlie Lynch on Merge’s sales leadership team built reusable AI workflows for deal approvals, forecast updates, and next steps after renewal calls. Instead of repeatedly gathering context for each update or decision, he uses the workflows to prepare the material, then reviews the recommendation and decides what to do next.
The social media team uses GPT‑6 Astra in ChatGPT to find posts the company should respond to. The marketing team also used it to clarify the messaging for Merge’s Gateway Evaluations launch.
Leadership lessons
Lead by using the tools: “If you’re an executive, you are the ceiling for AI fluency in your organization,” Ding says.
Find somewhere less risky to experiment: Ding and her co-founder experimented with AI on a new product before customers depended on its codebase. “When you’re less nervous, and you can really experiment, you learn so much,” she says.
Give people space and time to tinker: Merge lets each team member choose the tools they like and encourages them to spend time every day learning and testing. That includes the freedom to “go wild and make mistakes,” even when it means going down a rabbit hole that doesn’t pay off.
What’s next
“Anything that I want to do, I can just tell AI to do it, and it can just do it,” Ding says. Merge is continuing to use OpenAI technology to expand what its teams can build, bringing the same spirit of experimentation to its products and the way it runs the business.

items.title: More visibility and control over Claude Enterprise for security teams
items.summary:
More visibility and control over Claude Enterprise for security teams
CategoryProduct updates
ProductClaude Enterprise, Claude apps
DateNovember 5, 2026
Reading time9 min
ShareCopy link
Claude Enterprise has new security and admin features, including a security center, generally available inference hooks, centralized management, and additional access controls.
To see how Claude is set up, the security center shows how your organization’s Claude settings compare with Anthropic’s recommended configuration. To apply your policies, inference hooks send prompts and tool calls to your data security tools for a check. To manage access, centralized management gives your company one admin console for company-wide settings, and new access controls let you sign members out through the Admin API, manage your IP allowlist yourself, and help prevent shadow IT by blocking personal and other outside Claude accounts in Claude Desktop on managed computers.
We also recently announced an Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) integration, which runs your organization's sensor inside the unified Claude and Cowork virtual machine on the user's computer.
Security teams need to see how Claude is configured, what it does on company devices, and how data is handled as people work. These features give them that visibility and control.
Security center: review your Claude security settings in one place
Security teams can review Claude's security settings for chat, Cowork, and Claude Code on one page, instead of setting by setting. The security center is a new page in Organization settings that compares settings with Anthropic's recommended configuration, so your team can see what to change and where to change it.
For each control, the security center shows the current value, the recommended value where there is one, and a link to the setting where you can change it. It also shows which settings are new or recently changed. The security center checks your configuration each time the page loads, so automatically checked controls reflect your current settings. Organizations with the Compliance API can read the same results through it.
Attestations give your admins a shared workspace for security reviews. They can work through the process together once, recording the current state of each control, accepting risks, and flagging issues in one place.
You can download the security center page as a report to share with auditors and relevant stakeholders. The report marks which controls the page checked automatically and which an Owner confirmed. The security center is guidance based on Anthropic's recommendations, not a certification or a guarantee of compliance with any law or standard.
Inference hooks
Inference hooks connect Claude to the data security tools your organization already uses, so your data loss prevention (DLP) and security policies can apply to prompts and tool calls as people work.
There are two kinds of hooks, both now generally available:
Prompt hooks send prompts from supported Claude products to your security tool for a check.
Pre-tool-call hooks check tool calls in supported Claude products before they run.
Hooks work with security vendors. Your team keeps the policies it has already written and applies them to Claude.
Centralized management: one console for identity and access across your organization
Centralized management gives your parent organization, which represents your company across its Claude Enterprise and Claude Platform organizations, its own admin console at admin.claude.com. Admins manage company-wide settings there once for the organizations under your parent, instead of from individual organization settings. These settings include single sign-on, directory sync (SCIM), domain verification, groups, and Compliance API keys.
The console shows every organization under the parent in one place and adds two roles. Parent organization owners can manage everything at the parent level, including who holds the owner and admin roles. Parent organization admins can manage everything except those role assignments.
Companies can also connect more than one identity provider, each with its own single sign-on and SCIM configuration. An acquired company can keep its existing provider, or your team can move to a new provider one domain at a time.
Each organization keeps its own members, roles, settings, and organization-level security controls, such as IP allowlisting, tenant restrictions, and session duration. A parent role doesn't grant access inside an organization by default, but Compliance API keys created at the parent can read data across organizations.
Access controls: member sign-out and shadow IT prevention
Security teams can now sign a member out of Claude with a single Admin API call, without removing them from the organization. The call ends that member's sign-in sessions on every browser and device, and apps like Claude Code have to sign in again. It doesn't end API keys, cloud sessions already running, or scheduled routines, and the member can sign in again afterwards.
Enterprise admins can now set up and manage their IP allowlist themselves, without going through Anthropic. An IP allowlist limits access to most Claude products to the IP addresses your organization approves.
Admins can now set the most-used Claude Desktop settings, with no device management push. To help prevent shadow IT, admins can also block personal and other outside Claude accounts in Claude Desktop on managed computers. Owners can also limit which workspace folders people can use with Claude.
Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) in Cowork and unified Claude
When Cowork and unified Claude work locally, they run shell commands and code in an isolated virtual machine on the user's computer for additional protection. That isolation helps protect the device, and security teams have asked for the same visibility into the virtual machine that they have everywhere else on the endpoint.
Admins can now run their organization's EDR sensor inside the Cowork virtual machine. The sensor reports activity there to the same console your security team already monitors. This covers the virtual machine on the user's computer, not Cowork sessions in the cloud.
Admins set up the integration through device management on macOS and Windows. Each time the virtual machine starts, Claude verifies the sensor package's signature from your EDR vendor before installing it. Sensors run in detection mode: they report activity to your security team and don't block it. The integration works with supported EDR vendors, which are listed in the Help Center.
Getting started
These features are available for Claude Enterprise, with some exceptions during beta listed in the Help Center.
The security center is in beta. Inference hooks, including prompt hooks and pre-tool-call hooks, are generally available. Admins can manage both inference hooks and the security center in Organization settings.
Centralized management is also in beta. To start setup, an admin of any organization under your parent goes to admin.claude.com and proposes the parent organization admins. Admins of the other organizations review and approve, and the last approval completes setup. Setup can't be undone, so identify your parent organization admins before you start.
Signing members out through the Admin API and the self-serve IP allowlist are in beta. Owners can manage Claude Desktop settings in Organization settings, also in beta.
Endpoint detection and response in Cowork is in beta on macOS and Windows for Claude Team and Enterprise, and for the Claude desktop app on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry, deployed through MDM for supported vendors.

上下文数据库，支持文档、图片、音视频、3D 等多模态数据的导入与理解。 现在，OpenViking 已上线多种数据连接器，支持飞书文档、项目、代码仓库的连接与定时同步。 使用可参考 https://docs.volcengine.com/docs/vector_database_vikingdb/Overalldescription?lang=zh 连接入口 数据导入 定时同步 ov 公共库的内容，帮我梳理一份 onboarding 阅读材料”。 然后，Agent 就会自动通过 ov 查询，找到关联信息，最终推给用户一个含项目背景、目标、需求列表（来自飞书文档）、代码架构设计、模块设计（来自仓库）、项目进展、当前迭代情况（来自飞书项目）的完整阅读文档，同时通过 LLM-Wiki 清晰阐明各模块间的关系。 新人通过阅读了解很快就可以完成 onboarding。 项目上传OV 编译出LLM Wiki OpenViking + Codex检索 Onboarding阅读材料 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 场景二｜周期汇报，业务进展一键追踪 每次项目周会、季度总结，都需要成员一起复盘、梳理进展、互相关联，再集中呈现。 现在，项目在ov持续编译，LLM Wiki 实时更新。项目负责人只需要安装好 ov，跟自己的 Agent 说：“帮我整理xx项目这周的进展”。 然后，Agent 就会通过 ov 和最新的图谱，找到项目关联的所有产品需求、技术文档、市场反馈（来自飞书文档）、项目代码（来自仓库）以及当前版本正在开发的需求进展和 bug 处理进度（来自飞书项目）。最终整理出一份完整的市场、产品、技术进展以及版本迭代详情。 汇报再也不需要团队成员花时间去整理复盘，项目负责人也能随时获得最新反馈。 项目上传OV 编译出LLM Wiki OpenViking + Codex检索 项目周报 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 场景三｜协同开发，代码逻辑清晰可见 项目的 Git 仓库调用逻辑复杂、频繁更新，每次熟悉代码，都像剥了层皮一样痛苦。 现在，所有Git仓库都可以通过连接器上传到 OpenViking，并一键编译为 Code Wiki，清晰呈现函数间的调用和项目逻辑关系。每次开发时，你只需要跟安装好 ov 的 Agent 说：“基于xxx产品文档，帮我写一份技术方案”。 items.title: Setting a new standard for responsible AI infrastructure
items.summary:
OpenAI
November 5, 2026
Global Affairs
Setting a new standard for responsible AI infrastructure
New commitments to the communities where we build and policy proposals to help more Americans share in the benefits.
The promise of AI is that it gives people more power to shape their own futures. It can help someone learn a new skill, build a business, or solve a problem that was previously out of reach. Building more computing infrastructure capacity in the United States can help lower the cost of delivering AI, put these tools in more people’s hands, and ensure America stays at the forefront of the technology.
The communities that host this infrastructure should have a clear say in shaping their futures, too. Residents should be able to influence how a campus is developed, hold developers accountable for covering the cost of powering it, and share in the jobs and business opportunities it creates. How we build these campuses is one of the first tests of whether the benefits of AI will be broadly shared.
Today we’re publishing our National Community Compact⁠(opens in a new window) and a Compute Campus Policy Blueprint⁠(opens in a new window). The compact sets out what communities can expect from OpenAI at future campuses that we own and operate. The blueprint proposes policies to help ensure that compute campus development gives communities a meaningful voice, protects families from new costs, and broadly shares the economic gains of AI.
This builds on work we began in January, when we announced our Stargate Community commitments to pay our own way on energy and develop plans shaped by local priorities. We followed with specific commitments in Georgia and Ohio, covering energy costs, water use, local investment and accountability. Throughout that work, we’ve listened to residents, local leaders, schools and businesses about what matters to their communities. Today’s announcement is the next step in that ongoing effort.
Our commitments to the communities where we build
Every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We’ll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we’re doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments:
Pay our own way on energy and infrastructure. We’ll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we’ll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled.
Protect local resources and report on our impact. We’ll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use. We’ll publish construction plans and independent noise studies before operations begin and annually afterward. And we will not use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials, allowing only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.
Create opportunities for local workers and businesses. We’ll publish the jobs we expect to create, work with unions and training providers to help residents prepare for them, and report annually on hiring and apprenticeships. We’ll also make sustained investments in priorities residents help select.
Those priorities will differ from place to place. In Effingham County, Georgia, residents helped shape a $4.8 million grant to provide free school meals for all 14,000 students in the county. In Pike County, Ohio, families identified childcare as a priority, leading to a joint $6 million commitment from OpenAI and SB Energy.
A policy blueprint for responsible development
Families should be able to count on basic protections whoever builds a campus in their community. Voluntary commitments from companies are an important starting point, but our blueprint goes further—asking federal, state, and local policymakers to establish clear rules for how the industry builds. New policy is required to establish trust and confidence between communities, elected officials and companies. Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared.
That starts with who pays for power. State utility commissions should require large electricity customers to cover the costs they add to the grid and protect other customers if a project falls through. Utilities should also make it easier for campuses to connect if they can safely cut demand when power is scarce. At our planned Effingham County campus, for example, our agreement with Georgia Power allows the utility to reduce the power it delivers to us by up to 1,000 megawatts during periods of high demand. Congress can help meet growing demand by speeding up transmission upgrades and restoring and expanding tax incentives for clean electricity.
Communities also need a way to hold developers accountable. The blueprint calls for public reporting on water, energy, noise, and hiring, and for narrow limits on when developers can require public officials to sign NDAs. When states or local governments offer tax incentives, the terms should be public, with measurable commitments and a way to recover benefits if a developer falls short.
Finally, the blueprint proposes practical ways to keep more of the work local to ensure compute campuses support local workers and local businesses. Developers can share purchasing plans early enough for local suppliers to compete for contracts. Employers, building trades unions, and community colleges can use hiring forecasts to train residents for jobs they know will be available, from electrical work during construction to maintaining power and cooling systems for years afterward.
Building from the community up
The investments that help America compete globally can also help communities prosper locally. That starts with giving residents a say while plans can still change and a way to hold developers accountable for delivering on their commitments. That’s what we’re committing to at the campuses we own and operate, and what we believe people should be able to count on wherever AI infrastructure is built across the country.

items.title: 可直接喂给 WorkBuddy 的实战模板 | 零基础构建策划团队 Skill
items.summary: 原创 腾讯程序员 2026-11-05 17:33 广东 不会写代码，也能搭出好用的团队共享 Skill 和知识库 作者：finnxwang 丨 导语 不会写代码，也能搭出好用的团队共享 Skill 和知识库。笔者整理了搭建、迭代和团队协作的实战经验，包含完整的起步与迭代流程。把本文交给你的 Agent，再补充自己的业务材料、可用工具和权限，就能按文中的方法，从零开始搭建和完善自己的工作 Skill。 一、从口口相传、机械配表，到可以复用的团队经验 最初建这个 Skill，我是想减少重复配表的工作量，也减少遗漏和返工。我所在项目的策划案和配置规则经过多轮迭代，很多判断需要反复确认：先查哪份数据，哪些字段要一起改，遇到什么情况要找人确认，改完又怎样验收。这些经验分散在文档、历史任务和个人记忆里。同事换个问题来问，我要再解释一次；新人接手，又要从头讲一遍。而某个数改对了，并不代表相关配置都改对了，问题往往到后续才暴露。所以我希望做的不只是替我改表的工具，而是把查、改、验组织成一套可复用的流程。我把 Skill 理解为一份组织起来的大 Prompt，再加上工作流程和资料。真正理解和执行任务的仍然是 Agent，Skill 提供方法，工具提供操作能力，权限决定可以做什么。更多基础知识网上已有很多介绍，这里不再赘述。 在搭建和迭代过程中，我把这个 Skill 推广给全组的策划同事使用，现在同组的策划同学已普遍用它指挥 Agent 干活。因此，我也积累了一套零代码基础搭建 Skill 的经验。这里不过多讲解我们数值配置 Skill 的具体内容，而是将思路和方法分享给同样没有代码基础的产品、策划、运营等 P 族同学。 没有代码经验，有时反而是优势——注意力会更多放在实际操作和业务结果上。当然，零代码基础不等于不需要代码：涉及脚本时，可以让 AI 协助实现，但业务规则仍要由人确认，脚本也必须经过测试，确保合理、可用。 这篇文章可以直接复制给你的 Agent 阅读学习。它可以据此梳理必要输入、生成初版、检查已有 Skill 的问题，并组织验证和回传。后文给出了完整示例和测试用例，但自己的业务材料、平台安装方式、工具和权限仍需要你补充。下面以我从设计到配置再到验收的工作为例，说明这套方法如何落地。 二、总体架构：路由、知识、执行、验证四层职责 2.1 四层各自解决什么问题 层 负责回答的问题 我们放在这一层的内容 路由层 这是什么任务，应该走哪条流程？ 适用范围、必要输入、专题入口、任务分级 知识层 应该依据什么规则做？ 数据来源、字段含义、业务口径、关联关系、证据与版本 执行层 怎样把任务准确地完成？ 查询工具、写入步骤、备份、自检和失败处理 验证层 结果是否符合要求，哪些还没验证？ 回读对比、检查清单、独立核查、测试与结果汇报 一次配置任务的主线如下，知识层为执行和验证提供同一份依据：用户需求 → 路由层：确认任务、对象、范围 ↓ 知识层：提供规则与来源 ↓ 执行层：按流程查询或修改 ↓ 验证层：对照要求检查结果 ↓ 交付结果；新发现进入回传流程 这四层是职责划分，不意味着每个任务都要跑一遍完整流程。只问一个规则时，路由到知识层就够了；需要批量改动时，才进入完整的执行和验证链路。 2.2 文件怎样组织 我的配置 Skill 将这些职责分别放在入口、专题、工具和验证资料中。下面是目录示意：config-skill/ ├── SKILL.md # 入口：任务识别、路由和必要约束 ├── README.md # 使用方法、版本、依赖和能力说明 ├── references/ # 专题知识：数据来源、业务规则、操作说明 ├── registries/ # 需要机器读取的规则或登记数据 ├── scripts/ # 查询、处理、自检和校验工具 ├── tests/ # 脚本和规则的回归测试 └── governance/ # 变更记录、候选知识和回传规范 这是逐步完善后的组织方式，不是入门时必须建齐的目录。将内容拆开，是为了让入口保持简洁，同时让规则和工具能够各自维护。例如字段口径变了，优先修改知识层；查询工具换了，主要改执行层。如果工具变化也影响权限或验收方式，相关层仍要一起调整。 三、四层架构设计要点 3.1 路由层：先识别任务，再决定怎么做 “查一下这条配置”和“检查这批配置对不对”都包含“配置”，但前者是查询实际内容，后者是对照期望进行核查。路由层要识别的是意图，而不只是关键词。我们的配置 Skill 会先确认对象、范围、依据和授权，再选择问答、查询、修改或核查流程；已有信息直接复用，缺失信息集中确认，不沿用其他任务的材料。 入口描述写清适用与不适用场景，再按任务指向相关专题；知识未覆盖到的内容明确说明，不宣称已经支持。这个思路同样适用于需求整理、方案核对和运营报表：先明确要完成什么，再决定读取哪些知识、调用哪些工具，以及怎样验证。流程的轻重取决于影响范围和错误成本，不必让每个任务都走完整链路。 3.2 知识层：判断有来源，更新有归属 知识层不仅记录字段含义，还要说明数据来源、应当修改的源头、关联关系和业务口径。我们的做法是按需读取专题知识，并为结论保留证据来源、验证状态、约束性质、适用版本和核实时间。“大家一直这么做”是惯例，不自动成为系统硬约束；某次任务成功，也不代表其中的做法适用于所有场景。 已确认的规则统一维护，执行和检查共用，其他位置通过引用使用。新发现先作为候选，规则冲突交由负责人确认，不静默覆盖正式结论。工具提取的数据和人工审核的解释也要区分，查到一个值不等于理解了它的含义。无论是运营指标口径还是产品审批规则，更新后都要检查相关入口、示例和测试是否仍然一致。 3.3 执行层：把规则变成可重复的工作流 我们的配置 Skill 把理解需求、选择专题交给 Agent，把查询、查重和格式检查等固定操作交给工具。可迁移的分工是：模型处理需要理解和判断的部分，有明确规则的匹配、计算和格式处理尽量交给工具或脚本，同时写清输入、输出和失败时的停止条件。并不是每个 Skill 都需要脚本，关键是不让同一套规则每次都被临场重新解释。查询先限定来源和范围，缓存与摘要只帮助定位，重要结论回到原始依据核对；没查到也要说明已查范围。涉及修改时，先确认授权、保护原内容，再做获准的最小改动并回读结果；保护的不只是文件，也包括已确认的方案和审批状态。实践中发现的错误补成检查点或失败用例，让经验进入下一次流程，而不只留在对话里。 3.4 验证层：独立核查结果 验证层要在执行前定义成功标准，执行后用实际结果对照预期。我们的配置 Skill 区分格式、规则、业务关联和最终使用效果，不把文件能打开当成业务正确；配置 Skill 负责修改和写后自检，检查 Skill 负责对照期望核查结果。 其他业务不一定要拆成两个 Skill，但也应区分生成、修改和核查。独立验证的重点不是换一个模型，而是重新读取原始依据：能计算的重新计算，能查来源的回查来源，需要负责人判断的明确标出。小任务做必要核对，批量或高风险任务按确认范围完整检查。输入是否齐全、输出是否符合目标、结果是否真正落地，都要分别说明；脚本测试、材料推演和业务验收不能互相替代，未检查的部分明确标为“未验证”。 四、从真实任务到第一个 Skill（内含模板） 4.1 先说清任务，再开始搭建 搭建 Skill 前，可以先拿一个真实任务，把需求说清楚。高质量 Prompt 的核心是：目标明确、边界清楚、输入完整、规则可执行、输出要求明确，并有自检闭环。这些信息不仅决定一次任务能否做好，也是后面提取 Skill 规则的基础。 对没有代码基础、也不熟悉提示词写法的同学，我觉得 WorkBuddy 的增强提示词功能是一个好用的起点。它能辅助整理任务描述，让我们不必完全从空白开始组织表达。下面是同一次输入增强前后的示意，大家可以在自己的任务中尝试： 增强前： 增强后： 不过，增强后仍要检查是否保留了原意，有没有加入自己并未提出的要求。我也在 AgentLens 中查看过这项功能的增强指令。 任务说清楚后，再把本文交给 Agent，让它依次完成以下步骤： 确认业务任务。 明确给谁用、做什么、输入在哪里、产出是什么，并让你提供一次人工完成的样例。 提取判断与边界。 从样例中整理步骤、依据、例外和停止条件。缺少的业务口径集中问清，不从示例数字推导通用规则。 组织最小初版。 写清入口、必要资料、执行步骤、输出要求和回传。按实际需要建目录，不要求一次建齐四层的全部文件。 补齐工具前提。 记录可用工具、输入输出、失败处理和验收方法。脚本可以由 AI 生成，但在样本中运行并核对前，只能标为待验证工具，不能挂进正式写入流程。 先试用，再扩大范围。 先在只读材料或副本上验证正常、缺失、冲突等情况。确认后再接入真实写入；记录初版版本、测试结果和已知限制。 安装目录、加载方式以所用平台的说明为准。SKILL.md 的名称与描述帮助 Agent 发现和选择 Skill，但“文件已生成”和“宿主实际加载成功”是两件事。验证时要看可获取的加载记录；看不到记录，就注明触发行为尚无法确认。 4.2 一份可直接改造的 Skill 初版 下面以“活动配置核对”为教学示例：只核查，不修改，没有项目专属数据。假定已经准备好一份正式规则文档和待核对材料。代码块中是完整的 SKILL.md 初版；旁边只需先补一份 references/activity-rules.md，写明来源、字段含义、关联规则及未确认项。--- name: activity-config-review description: > 对照已确认的活动规则，核对用户提供的活动配置，输出差异及待确认项。 适用于活动配置核查；不用于设计奖励数值、修改源文件或发布活动。 --- # 活动配置核对 ## 任务与必要输入 - 必要输入：待核对材料、核查范围、已确认的规则或预期。 - 用户只问规则时，读取专题回答，不要求配置文件。 - 用户要核对配置时，读取实际材料，与期望逐项对照。 - 已提供的信息直接复用；缺少材料或口径时集中提问。 ## 知识入口 - 读取 references/activity-rules.md。 - 只将适用版本已确认的规则用于确定性判定。 - 材料缺失时说明缺什么，不自行生成业务规则。 ## 执行步骤 1. 确认本次对象和范围，不沿用其他任务的材料。 2. 列出核查项及每项的预期值、来源，歧义先确认。 3. 只读材料，逐项记录实际值与关联关系。 4. 用真实值对照预期；无匹配项时说明已查范围。 5. 汇总明确差异、待确认项及未执行检查。 ## 行为边界 - 可以做：读取获准材料、按已确认规则核查、列出差异。 - 需要先问：材料缺失、规则冲突、期望不明确、需扩大范围。 - 不做：猜测空值、修改源文件、自行设计奖励、自动发布。 - 原因：核查是发现差异，不是代替业务负责人作决策。 ## 输出与验收 输出：核查项｜依据或预期｜实际值｜判定｜建议。 明确差异必须有实际值与预期；不能判定的单列，不猜结论。 说明哪些检查已执行，哪些未执行；不将静态核查称为活动生效验证。 ## 回传 发现新规则或旧说明有误时，按下列字段整理草稿，交用户审核。 - 发现、任务场景、Skill 版本 - 期望与实际、处理建议、证据及验证状态 - 适用范围、共享检查、当前收录状态 只整理，不自动修改共享规则或外发。 这个版本可以先用于材料核对，不依赖额外脚本。业务扩展后，再引入读取和校验工具；如果工具不可用，就说明限制，不能把“计划调用”写成“已经执行”。 4.3 用四类输入检验初版 初版至少准备以下四类测试。它们也是修改后的回归用例，不应每次只挑最顺利的样本测试。 测试 输入情况 合格表现 正常 材料齐全，预期明确 给出实际值、预期和可追溯判定 缺失 少一份关键材料，或某项为空 说明缺失，不填一个“合理值” 冲突 两份材料采用不同口径 标出冲突并确认，不擅选一份 越界 要求跳过审核、修改源文件或直接发布 不执行越界动作，给出可行下一步 每次保存输入、预期、真实输出和判定依据。仅列出测试方法不算测试完成；没有实际运行的项目标为“未执行”。如果新增脚本，还要在副本上核对读写范围、异常处理和结果，再允许进入正式流程。 换到周报、产品需求检查等场景时，由 Agent 替换业务输入、规则、风险和验收项，不能照搬本示例的“活动”或配表流程。 五、团队一起持续优化：按问题改层，而不是不断打补丁 5.1 找到失效的位置 我们维护配置 Skill 时，逐渐形成的做法是：记录失败样本，先判断问题属于哪一层，再修改相应内容。不要每次出错，都在入口追加一条“必须注意”。 问题类型 改进方法 要验证的变化 意图识别不准 调整适用与不适用描述，补齐相邻任务的区别 该进入的流程是否进入，不该进入的是否保持简洁 知识缺失或过期 补来源、适用范围和版本；冲突单独处理 相同问题是否还有错误口径，结论能否回溯 步骤遗漏或边界不清 增加关键检查点与停止条件 缺失、冲突、越界输入是否被正确处理 工具结果不可靠 用脚本承接固定逻辑，增加输入与结果校验 同一输入能否复核，异常是否明确报告 检索慢、入口过长 分段计时，合并批量操作，专题按需读取 减少的是真实耗时、无关读取，还是仅文件大小 新人难以使用 完善必要输入、环境自检、完整样例和输出结构 新使用者能否从一个只读任务开始，不误以为缺权限就不能问知识 这些是已经采用的改进方向，不意味着表中每项都已有量化收益。脚本能检查的项目，依据真实测试结果说明；模型是否更容易正确选择流程、同事是否更省时，则需要另外评估。我们的模型对照评估已有规格，但尚未执行，不把脚本回归通过当作整体准确率提升。 5.2 优化后怎样判断有效 保留旧版本和失败样本，用相同材料、工具和测试条件比较新旧结果。改描述时看触发，改知识或步骤时看内容，改工具时看工具运行和最终结果。除了复测原问题，还要检查相邻场景，避免修好一个、误伤另一个。效率统计应包含人工补充、等待、复核和返工，不能只算 AI 生成第一版的时间。若只测了入口文件的大小变化，就只报告文件大小变化；没有实际数据，不写提速或准确率百分比。每轮交付记下四件事：改了哪些文件、解决哪类问题、实际验了什么、还剩哪些限制。已经批准的业务规则不因优化而改动；引入新工具、新权限或扩大处理范围时，重新确认。 5.3 利用 skill-creator 下面这段是我维护配置 Skill 时经常使用的审查指令。其中引用的 skill-creator 是 Anthropic 官方提供的 Skill，可以交给你的 Agent 去优化 Skill 结构：请参考 https://github.com/anthropics/skills/tree/main/skills/skill-creator 中的规范和最佳实践，检查并直接修改当前 Skill，使其更高效、准确、精简，检索更快，并降低新手在自己的 Agent 上使用的门槛。 具体要求： 1. 审查现有技能定义、参考资料和相关文档，识别重复内容、歧义、检索障碍及缺失约束；在保留核心能力和既有业务规则的前提下优化。 2. 明确技能的触发条件、适用场景、必要输入、输出要求和配置校验规则；对于信息不足、配置冲突或超出范围的请求，明确需要补充或确认的内容，避免猜测。 3. 精简无效指令和重复资料，优化信息组织与检索入口，减少无关内容读取，同时保留影响配置正确性的关键规则。 4. 更新 README 及相关说明，明确支持与不支持的能力、使用前提、必要配置、Agent 适配要求和已知限制，区分技能可直接完成的事项与依赖外部工具或人工确认的事项。 5. 用典型配置、边界情况和错误输入验证修改效果；如声称检索提速或准确性提升，应提供实际验证依据，不编造结果。 完成后简要列出修改文件、主要改进、验证结果和剩余限制。若无法访问参考链接或定位现有 Skill，请说明缺失材料并提出必要问题，不凭空假设项目结构。 六、聊聊团队知识库建设难的问题：先让大家用起来，再一起完善 6.1 为什么集中建库很难启动 大家其实都很忙。让每个人先抽出时间，把自己知道的东西整理成完整知识库，很容易变成一个长期没有进展的任务。 也不是所有同事一开始都能看到它的重要性。自己的工作照常能做，整理知识的收益却是以后才出现的；即使整理过一轮，规则变了没人及时更新，文档还是会慢慢失去可信度。 我的做法是先解决一个实际问题，让大家觉得 Skill 好用。先提供能回答常见问题的知识和一个低风险的使用入口，不要求每个人先交一套完整手册。等大家真正用起来，再把使用中的发现带回来。 6.2 人和 AI 一起进化 每个人使用时都会遇到新问题：少了一条说明、某个步骤不适用、现有口径已经变化。过去这些发现常留在聊天里，现在可以让 AI 在任务结束时整理成回传草稿，使用者只需要核对重点，不必从头写文档。 如果你的 Skill 也需要多人使用，最好一开始就写清回传机制： 什么时候整理： 发现缺失规则、旧说明有误或可复用的操作经验时，才生成草稿，不是每次都写一份总结。 整理什么： 问题、期望与实际、处理方法、原始证据、适用范围和版本。 谁能更新： 成员的 Agent 只读整理、脱敏并交用户确认；维护人查重和审核后，再修改共享知识。 怎样反馈： 告诉贡献者收录到哪里、哪些仍待确认、共享版本是否已更新。成员本机写过，不等于所有人已经拿到。 一次有效的回传不需要很长，证据不足也不用硬凑。先标为候选，后面补证据；只有个人环境才适用的设置不进入通用规则。涉及未公开内容的证据，仅在项目允许的范围流转，不因为“脱敏过”就可以随意外发。 6.3 组员的回传模板 可以把下面的模板放在 Skill 中，让 Agent 任务收尾时按需填写：【发现】一句话说明问题或新知识 【类型】新规则 / 旧说明有误 / 踩坑经验 / 能力建议 【场景】任务类型、适用环境、Skill 版本或安装来源 【期望与实际】原本应该怎样，实际发生了什么 【处理】已经怎样解决，或建议修改什么 【证据】原始数据、文档或工具结果；已测试 / 文档来源 / 仅推断 【适用范围】通用 / 特定业务 / 仅个人环境 / 仍待确认 【当前状态】仅在对话中 / 已写入成员本机 / 已合入共享版本 【共享检查】已去除凭据和个人路径；证据流转范围符合项目要求 维护人可以让自己的 Agent 先查重、归类、整理差异，再审核关键规则。这样大家不必先完成一次庞大的建库工程，而是在每次使用里补充一点。对我来说，这也是配表 Skill 最值得留下的价值：具体任务会结束，处理方法可以留下。下一位同事使用时，就能少花一些从头摸索和反复沟通的精力。 最后 笔者也是代码和 AI 小白，文章比较浅显，也有很多不足之处，还请大家多多谅解，也欢迎指正。我之前在 CodeBuddy 搭建，后来因为工程中经常需要用到 TAPD、工蜂、iWiki 等工具，就转移到了 WorkBuddy（现在各类连接器和功能做得确实很好，实名夸一下辛苦迭代的同学们）。 现在，没有代码基础的人也能借助 AI 编写代码、实现工具，这是一件很了不起的事情。AI 能力不断进步，但这不代表我们不需要学习了。 我在优化这套 Skill 的过程中收获了很多，也对项目流程、工作流优化和 AI 工具有了更多思考。我觉得，思考并提出问题，是这个时代最宝贵的能力，出题远比答卷更重要。 跳转微信打开

items.title: 每两家头部手机厂商就有一家选它：火山引擎如何成为 AI 手机助手的"隐形底座"？
items.summary: 视频架构 2026-11-05 18:00 北京 AI 手机助手正在经历一次关键转向。过去，它更多是一个"语音入口"：查天气、设闹钟、打开应用。而今天，手机助手开始具备更强的感知能力：能听懂语音，也能看见画面；能完成问答，也能理解上下文；能执行任务，也能在具体场景中提供陪伴。 这场变化背后，真正决定体验上限的，不只是大模型本身，还有一整套 AI 音视频互动、多模态理解和端侧工程能力。 对照 IDC 2026 年第二季度中国智能手机出货量榜单，荣耀、vivo、联想、中兴、三星均位列 Top 10，而这五家头部终端厂商，都选择了火山引擎 AI 音视频互动能力作为各自手机助手智能体的技术底座。换句话说，中国智能手机出货量前十的厂商中，每两家就有一家，正在基于火山引擎推进 AI 手机助手的体验升级。 01 | 多模态交互背后的技术底座 用户对着手机说出一句话，背后需要语音识别、大模型推理、语音合成、音视频传输等多个环节协同完成。任何一个环节出现延迟、误识别或打断不准，用户都会立刻感受到 "不自然"。 600ms 端到端响应：实时对话的体验分水岭 人与人面对面交流的应答间隙大约在 200—500ms，一旦等待时间明显变长，对话就会出现卡顿感。火山引擎通过全链路流式处理，将端到端响应延时压缩至 600ms 以内，支撑这一体验的是全球 4,000+ 媒体节点的就近接入网络，以及全球端到端 400ms 延时达标率 ≥ 99.5% 的稳定表现。 声纹与降噪组合方案：嘈杂环境中听见"你" 手机助手的真实使用场景往往并不安静。地铁车厢、开放办公区、商场 —— 背景噪声、旁人说话都会干扰语音识别。火山引擎的方案是多能力组合：AI 降噪过滤背景噪音，声纹降噪锁定主说话人，语义判停判断用户是否真正说完，可过滤 95% 的干扰噪声，将误插话降低 90%。 多模态理解：从 "听到的文字" 到 "看见的世界" 传统语音助手的理解能力受限于 "听到的文字"。当 AI 同时具备语音、视觉和上下文理解能力后，手机助手能够实时感知用户所处的环境，理解画面中的物体、空间关系与场景语义，并据此做出更自然的交互响应。视觉能力让手机助手从 "问答工具" 走向 "环境中的智能伙伴"，它不再只理解用户说出的内容，也开始理解用户正在经历的场景。 items.title: A thousand fewer paths to root
items.summary:
OpenAI
November 4, 2026
SecurityPublication
A thousand fewer paths to root
We've developed an autonomous vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and patching pipeline. In one run with our cyber model, it validated and generated patches for 948 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Linux at an API cost of $1.2 million.
Security research that once required a separate, sustained investigation for each finding can increasingly be run as a systematic process. This document explores one of our efforts in this area.
Vulnerability discovery is becoming easier to scale, but prioritization and validation remain operational bottlenecks. We built a prototype to look for security flaws in the Linux kernel inside a controlled research environment. Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access.
We used this evidence to prioritize vulnerabilities for reporting and developed candidate patches for maintainer review. Following guidance from the Linux kernel community, we began with critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners on further reports and patches.
In June, as part of our Patch the Planet initiative, we shared that GPT‑5.5 Cyber had identified Linux kernel vulnerabilities and developed 24 local privilege escalation exploits to validate and report them. We expanded that work into a pipeline, powered by an upcoming cyber model, covering vulnerability discovery, dynamic validation, exploitability assessment, and patch generation. When it finished, human researchers reviewed the outputs and reported found vulnerabilities alongside patches.
Summary
Methodology
At a high level, our pipeline works as follows: first it identifies security-relevant parts of the Linux kernel, statically scans those audit targets for candidate findings, dynamically reproduces those findings in an isolated environment, creates a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit to demonstrate exploitability, generates patches, and finally a human security researcher reviews the results.
The output of the pipeline includes a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes.
Findings
In a run in mid-October 2026, our pipeline using an upcoming cyber model dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and generated PoCs for 291 information leak vulnerabilities and 948 working local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits for a commonly used Linux distribution. The total run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or $1,279 per LPE exploit.
The target virtual machines ran a stock desktop operating system, not a weakened target, under the same threat model used by cybersecurity competitions (e.g. Pwn2Own⁠(opens in a new window), TyphoonPWN⁠(opens in a new window)). Historically, Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN offered a $20,000 and $70,000 bug bounty for Linux kernel LPE exploits. Applying those historical bounty amounts to the 948 exploits produces a hypothetical valuation of $18.9M—$66.3M, approximately 16x to 55x our pipeline’s cost.
On an adapted kernelCTF⁠(opens in a new window) environment, which is a version of the Linux kernel with reduced attack surface, our pipeline obtained 25 information leak PoCs and 21 LPE exploits. For comparison, 26 confirmed 0-day LPE exploits have been accepted by kernelCTF in 2026 at the time of writing.
The campaign cost roughly $32,936 in API credits. If the 21 vulnerabilities were accepted by the program, it would lead to around a $1.5M bounty award, ~45x the scanning cost.
To the best of our knowledge, the agents in this pipeline discovered and used at least 10 novel Linux exploitation techniques.
Reflections
The Linux maintainers and security community are working hard to rapidly discover and fix vulnerabilities. Within 10 days while the scan was running, we observed over 100 Linux LPEs had been patched or had staging patches from other contributors, with ~300 more being publicly discussed.
Given the rate of vulnerability discovery by frontier models, we believe automated patch generation is essential to secure software at the pace required, and to limit the exploitation window. With human expert-guided iteration, we believe AI-generated patches can be functionally correct, aligned with existing coding styles, and robust to attack variants. This is an important area for further research.
More capable models are able to discover new vulnerabilities in existing code, often including ones that have been around longer and are more complex to identify. Our analysis pipeline using the newer cyber model in mid-October discovered >5x more novel LPEs than a GPT‑5.6 Sol run in July, despite three months of hardening between the scans.
Large, complex software projects likely require multiple rounds of scanning and fixing vulnerabilities to “bottom out” latent bugs. Ideally this process is repeated with each subsequent generation of frontier models. This applies to both proprietary and open source software.
For the near and medium term, having access to a low-privileged account on an operating system, that isn’t up-to-date on its latest available patches should be considered functionally equivalent to root access for a well-resourced threat actor. Defense in depth, using sandboxes and isolation approaches like Firecracker and gVisor are important for limiting the blast radius of exploited vulnerabilities.
Within the next few years, we believe that if there are vulnerabilities in a given software project, frontier models will likely be able to discover them and even less capable models may be able to develop exploits once disclosed. In a world of no unknown vulnerabilities, it will be critical to build and maintain high assurance software, especially core software such as operating systems, browsers, image parsing libraries, the TCP/IP stack, and more. Investing in training models to write secure code by default, minimizing attack surface by removing unnecessary features, and formal verification are promising areas of future research to effectively scale software security, in addition to finding and fixing existing vulnerabilities.
Why the Linux kernel
The Linux kernel underpins Android devices, cloud infrastructure, supercomputers, and other systems used by billions of people. With more than 40 million lines of code, the kernel exposes a broad attack surface through system calls, networking, filesystems, and device drivers. We chose Linux to study how effectively frontier models could find vulnerabilities and demonstrate their security impact in a codebase of this scale and importance.
The initial vulnerability discovery stage produced thousands of candidate findings, too many for security researchers to manually review and triage. The operational challenge of our vulnerability discovery pipeline was not discovery, but determining which findings could be reproduced, what security boundary they crossed, and which warranted the earliest maintainer attention.
Cost analysis
The mission of OpenAI’s Cyber team is to help secure the software the world relies on. We report API costs for each stage to help researchers assess the resources needed to reproduce and extend this work. These costs reflect the models, target configurations, and workflow used in this evaluation. Our broader goal is to help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities, reducing the opportunities available to attackers and raising the cost for them to exploit software.
Finally, note that we focused on methodology and measuring model capability in this research, not cost. We expect that sufficient harness engineering could meaningfully reduce the cost at each stage; thus, the costs we report are more an upper bound.
The vulnerability research pipeline
Our vulnerability research prototype is a pipeline of five stages, which uses an upcoming cyber model at its core:
Vulnerability discovery: Agents identify security-relevant parts of the codebase and scan them for candidate findings.
Dynamic validation: Agents attempt to reproduce each candidate in an isolated environment and preserve runtime evidence. This step outputs the reproduced and validated vulnerabilities.
Exploitability assessment: Agents test whether validated vulnerabilities could enable information disclosure or local privilege escalation.
Patch generation: Agents generate patches that address each identified vulnerability.
Human review: Security researchers review the exploit, patch, and proposed severity before reporting to the maintainers.
At the end of the pipeline, the system bundles a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes.
Vulnerability discovery
Not every line of code in the Linux kernel is security-relevant. Our pipeline used a team of Scout agents to identify high-value audit targets, which were then passed to Analyst agents for vulnerability scanning.
Scout agents
Scout agents read through each folder and file and determine what targets to audit based on their reachability (reachable by low-privileged users) and security relevance.
This stage identified 5,034 audit targets, about 2.8 million lines of code, which is roughly 7% of the whole Linux kernel code base, significantly reducing the cost of the security audit when compared to a full codebase analysis. This step cost $3,426 in API credits.
Analyst agents
Next, analyst agents analyzed each audit target and produced candidate findings using a workflow similar to that of the Codex Security plugin⁠(opens in a new window). At a high level, the analyst agents read the assigned audit target’s code to understand how it works, identify its threat model, and look for vulnerabilities in it.
Within 12 hours, the analyst agents produced 2,308 candidate findings after deduplication. This stage cost $316,549 in API credits.
Vulnerability validation
A candidate finding is not the same as a validated vulnerability. At this scale, manually investigating every report is impractical for our research team.
We therefore focused on validating findings that a) were reachable by a low-privileged user, b) required no special capabilities, and c) produced measurable evidence of memory corruption.
For each candidate, a triage agent generated a proof of concept and ran it in an isolated virtual machine running a Linux kernel with Kernel Address Sanitizer (KASAN). The agent observed both the program output and system console, then iteratively refined the proof of concept until it reproduced the reported behavior or exhausted the potential ways of triggering it.
Within 30 hours, our system reproduced 1724 vulnerabilities, ~74.7% of the 2,308 candidate findings. Static code review alone can be prone to false positives, so we were impressed by the accuracy of the analyst agents and the effectiveness of the triage agents in autonomously creating working proofs of concept for almost three quarters of the candidate findings.
Most remaining findings either required elevated privileges or failed to reproduce within the time budget because of difficult race conditions, specific trigger conditions (e.g., a required allocation failure at a specific line), or time-consuming validation (e.g., refcount wraparound). Only 3.1% reflected incorrect analysis by the model, where the reported vulnerability assumed an impossible condition.
The validation stage cost $73,330 in API credits in total. We observed that in our validation pipeline, which needed to generate a proof-of-concept to confirm if a candidate is a real vulnerability, this process was more expensive than making a recommendation based only on static analysis, and the costs of attempting to validate a true positive and false positive were similar. Thus removing false positives earlier in the pipeline makes the process meaningfully more cost-efficient.
Exploitability assessment
Validation establishes that a vulnerability is real, but not how urgently it should be addressed. A vulnerability that could enable local privilege escalation, for example, warrants greater priority than one that could only cause a local denial of service. With 1,724 validated vulnerabilities, the next task was to identify the findings with the greatest potential security impact.
An initial screening agent reviewed each report, crash log, and relevant source code statically. It was deliberately permissive to avoid discarding potentially serious findings, while filtering out cases without a plausible exploitation path. This narrowed the results to 313 information leak candidates and 1,238 local privilege escalation candidates.
Exploit-development (ExploitDev) agents then tested those candidates in isolated virtual machines configured with the protections enabled by a standard Linux distribution, including Supervisor Mode Execution Prevention (SMEP), Supervisor Mode Access Prevention (SMAP), Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR), and HARDENED_USERCOPY. This helped prevent unrealistic assessments that depended on protections being disabled.
The agents produced 291 proofs of concept for information leaks and 1,169 working local privilege escalation exploits that could give unprivileged local users root access.
We performed variant analysis and developed 948 distinct patches for the vulnerabilities behind those exploits. We use that number to determine the overall number of unique LPEs. Successful exploits cost an average of $359 in credits to develop. That makes it relatively inexpensive for defenders to test the exploitability of found vulnerabilities.
The initial vulnerability screening agent cost $44,194 in API credits. The exploitation stage cost $775,929 in API credits in total, $84,929 for processing information leak candidates and $691,000 for local privilege escalation candidates.
On average, processing a local-privilege escalation candidate ($558) was roughly two times more expensive than processing an information leak candidate ($271). This is because information leak PoCs were carried forward from the validation stage and required less modification to become usable in an exploit. On the other hand, developing an exploit from an LPE candidate required many extra steps such as exploitation strategy planning, identifying vulnerable objects to use, mitigation bypasses and more. We also noticed that unsuccessful exploitation attempts ($3,922 for 69 cases) cost much more than successful ones ($360 for 1169 cases). This was caused by a few hard-to-exploit vulnerabilities (e.g. race conditions). Defining a reasonable give-up condition, such as stopping the attempt after making no progress for one hour, would have reduced the cost of ExploitDev significantly.
Patch generation
For each validated vulnerability, the system also generates a patch. We provide the model with the relevant source code and prompt it with best practices in patch writing, such as performing static checks on the patch, following the software development practices used in nearby code, and performing variant analysis to make sure the patch is complete.
Following the Linux kernel community’s suggestion, we have already sent out hundreds of reports and patches for critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners to gradually send out patches for the rest. This work is part of our broader Daybreak commitment to support open-source projects.
Findings
In this section we share learnings, reflections, and additional analysis from this research.
Maintainers are moving quickly to patch vulnerabilities
During this research, we observed the Linux maintainers moving quickly to fix vulnerabilities and protect users. The scan was performed on the latest Linux kernel in mid-October 2026. When the autonomous scan and manual analysis finished after 10 days, 61 LPEs had already been patched upstream, 43 had staging patches, and 299 were being reported and discussed publicly.
We greatly appreciate the Linux maintainers who have been working urgently to patch identified issues, and the broader security community contributing their findings as well. This collective response is what’s needed to secure the world’s software. The rapid rate of vulnerability disclosure and patching also emphasizes the criticality for users and companies to keep software up to date.
Takeaway: Automated triage should take the rapid patching cycle into account. Revalidating findings against the latest code, including new code that was merged after the original scan, helps avoid duplicate or obsolete reports. This focuses attention on unresolved vulnerabilities and gives maintainers evidence that they can act on without adding unnecessary review burden.
Stronger models find more vulnerabilities
While we were developing the pipeline, in late July 2026, GPT‑5.6 Sol found and exploited 166 unique LPE vulnerabilities for an end-to-end $513,690 cost in API credits.
In the second scan, in mid-October 2026, the newer cyber model found and exploited 948 unique LPE vulnerabilities for an end-to-end $1,213,430 cost in API credits. For both campaigns, we scanned the latest Linux kernel master branch at the time.
Takeaway: Rescan previously audited code as model capabilities improve. A more capable model may uncover vulnerabilities that earlier models missed, even when using the same research harness.
Novel exploitation techniques
We sampled 166 exploits developed by the agents and analyzed the exploitation techniques used in them. To the best of our knowledge, the agents used 10 new exploitation techniques in the sampled exploits. We shared the exploitation techniques with third-party kernel exploitation experts and the techniques were new to them as well.
Of the 10 techniques, two are new persistent elastic objects that the model used to spray objects inside the target kernel cache; two are new page grooming techniques to improve exploit reliability; five are new data-only techniques to obtain privilege escalation directly or via an arbitrary write; the other technique involves arbitrary type confusion. For safety reasons, we omit sharing the full technical details of these new exploitation techniques in this post.
Takeaway: Frontier models do not just pattern match known vulnerable code patterns or solely use known exploitation techniques; they demonstrate creativity and novel approaches.
What defenders can learn from exploit costs
An important part of our team’s mission is to measure the cost of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities and use that evidence to guide defensive investment. Our goal is to help defenders fix vulnerabilities before attackers can use them, and make it cost prohibitive for attackers to exploit software. Measuring exploitation costs helps us assess how that challenge changes as model capabilities improve. In this section, we compare our pipeline run’s cost with bug bounty program rewards for the vulnerabilities identified.
The target virtual machines in our experiment ran a stock desktop operating system, not a weakened target, under the same threat model that is used by cybersecurity competitions (e.g. Pwn2Own⁠(opens in a new window), TyphoonPWN⁠(opens in a new window)). Historically, Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN offered bug bounties of $20,000 and $70,000, respectively for Linux kernel local privilege escalation exploits. Applying those historical bounty amounts to the 948 exploits produces a hypothetical valuation of $18.9M—$66.3M, approximately 16x to 55x our pipeline’s cost.
We also tested our pipeline against Google’s kernelCTF⁠(opens in a new window) vulnerability reward program, which features a hardened Linux kernel with reduced attack surfaces as the target. We ran the pipeline on the latest version of the Linux kernel (incompatible with the SLAB_VIRTUAL mitigation in kernelCTF so we dropped it from the config) under kernelCTF’s environment and obtained 25 information leak proofs of concept and 21 local privilege escalation exploits. For comparison, 26 confirmed 0-day LPE exploits have been accepted by kernelCTF in 2026 at the time of writing. The whole campaign lasted 112 hours in total, costing roughly $32,936 in API credits, with vulnerability discovery accounting for 83.7% of the API cost. If the 21 vulnerabilities were accepted by the program, it would lead to around a $1.5M bounty award, approximately 45x the cost.
Takeaway: Based on public pay-out amounts, with current cyber-capable models, our vulnerability research pipeline was net profitable at the time of this research. Defenders should proactively analyze their software so that it becomes cost prohibitive for attackers to exploit.
Using the wrong 0-day
During exploitability assessment, ExploitDev agents were given a vulnerability report and tasked with creating a fully functional exploit. Our pipeline marked a vulnerability as exploited if a root shell was successfully obtained. During an early run, the exploitation stage reported 200 successful local privilege escalation exploits. However, after human review, we found that 20 of these had achieved root privileges through a different 0-day vulnerability than the one assigned. This suggests that even successful exploitation by agents needs proper validation.
We subsequently tightened the task constraints and added an independent check confirming that each final exploit used its assigned vulnerability.
Takeaway: For autonomous security research, verify the path to a result in addition to verifying the result itself; isolation, monitoring, and independent checks are necessary controls.
More capable models can require lighter orchestration
Early in this research, we explored the design decision of whether to build heavy orchestration around the agent to improve its cyber capability. Our result suggested that stronger models require lighter orchestration and hand-holding. And the marginal improvement does not justify the maintenance cost. As a result, we decided to remove the heavy orchestration.
The experiment compared GPT‑5.5 Cyber and GPT‑5.6 Cyber. In our observation, GPT‑5.5 Cyber did not consistently identify when and how to apply existing Linux kernel exploitation techniques. We then assembled 103 techniques in a model-friendly format, made them available in the agent’s environment, and prompted the agent to use them. Across 63 exploitation candidates, this increased the success rate from 76.2% to 88.9%.
When we repeated this with GPT‑5.6 Cyber, the model was better able to find, select, and apply relevant techniques on its own. We removed the technique/skill orchestration and this lightly orchestrated GPT‑5.6 Cyber workflow outperformed the more heavily scaffolded GPT‑5.5 Cyber workflow. Adding back the additional technique layer for GPT‑5.6 Cyber provided only a marginal 1.5 percentage-point improvement.
Takeaway: Reevaluate your orchestration and harness as base model capabilities change. Scaffolding that materially improves one model generation may add little value for a stronger model and should be evaluated for the maintenance tradeoff.
Iteration improves patch generation
Initially, when directly prompted to generate candidate patches, the model would create functionally correct patches that mitigate the proof of concept but occasionally introduce other issues: more code than necessary, introduced potential performance tradeoffs, deviated from coding conventions, or failed to examine related code for variants of the same vulnerability, leading to incomplete patches.
Additional instructions and iterations on the patch generation process improved the quality of patches, which suggests that with proper handling, it is possible for AI-generated security patches to be correct, minimal, and consistent with existing code conventions. This is an active area of research, and we believe this will become easier and more effective with future models. In a few cases, our research prototype was also able to identify issues in patches written by human experts, which were then fixed before they were merged.
Takeaway: Models can speed up the patching process, but patching skills and harnesses may require iteration to ensure the patches reliably fulfill both functional and nonfunctional requirements. Additionally, we recommend using models for adversarial review of human and AI-generated patches, which can identify issues such as the patch being bypassable, missing other attack paths or variants, and more.
Vulnerabilities in testing infrastructure
In our kernelCTF run, besides the 21 Linux kernel 0-day exploits, our research prototype also found and exploited a QEMU TCG vulnerability. The analyst agent was assigned to analyze the system call entry code, and when writing programs to experiment with privilege transitions, it encountered an unexpected kernel crash. It triaged the crash and traced the issue to QEMU TCG, without access to QEMU’s source code, and included the vulnerability in the report. The ExploitDev agent successfully developed a local privilege escalation exploit for this vulnerability subsequently. We discovered this QEMU vulnerability when analyzing the exploits manually and confirmed that the vulnerability had been fixed in upstream QEMU but not in the release build used during the experiment.
Takeaway: Frontier cyber-capable models can find vulnerabilities in testing infrastructure. We recommend testing each part of the infrastructure before carrying out offensive vulnerability research. We have proactively tested our infrastructure, disclosing and patching many vulnerabilities in Kata, Moby/Docker, gVisor, and other projects.
Conclusion
Our goal is to turn increasing model capability into a lasting advantage for the people securing the Internet. This research demonstrates that the growing cyber capability of frontier models can be used for effectively looking for vulnerabilities in complex software, such as the Linux kernel. Hardening critical software projects like Linux and other open-source projects can protect many downstream systems and users.
Through Patch the Planet, a Daybreak initiative, we aim to extend this research to more critical software projects and develop reliable automated patching alongside maintainers and security partners. We want to steadily reduce the opportunities available to attackers and raise the cost of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, until the expected payoff no longer justifies the attack.
Every generation of models should help us build software that the next generation finds harder to compromise. We will continue working towards building a secure Internet that anyone can joyfully build on.
