items.title: DevRev delivers autonomous self-service with GPT-6.1 Sol
items.summary:
OpenAI
November 4, 2026
Startup
DevRev delivers autonomous self-service with GPT‑6.1 Sol
DevRev uses GPT‑6.1 Sol to power Computer and Operator, balancing reasoning, speed, and cost for enterprise service.
Start building with OpenAICompany size: StartupRegion: North AmericaIndustry: TechnologyProducts: API, CodexShare
DevRev⁠(opens in a new window) built Computer and Operator to help service and operations teams carry even the hardest customer and employee requests through to completion. Computer and Operator are designed to reason across live data. Actions are reversible, and answers point back to their sources, explains Ahmed Bashir, DevRev’s chief technology officer.
DevRev combines OpenAI models, including GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol, with its harness for connecting company knowledge and giving teams control over the actions an agent can take. DevRev sees OpenAI models as providing reasoning and reliability with the speed and cost of serving customers and employees.
“It’s a combination of being able to have the right reasoning capabilities, being able to be trusted, highly aligned, and most importantly, it has to work from a latency perspective.”
—Ahmed Bashir, Chief Technology Officer, DevRev
Making AI work with company context
OpenAI models power the reasoning, planning, and tool selection behind both Computer and Operator. In DevRev’s Agent Studio, users can describe how they want a tool to behave in a conversation with AI and define parts of its behavior with fixed rules.
DevRev tests the models together with the software that supplies company context, enforces permissions, and controls actions. Its Enterprise-Bench benchmark evaluates how well they work when data has multiple versions, information sits in different systems, and access depends on a person’s role.
Ahmed says GPT‑6.1 Sol performs well in those evaluations. When a customer or employee is interacting with an AI agent, the model needs to understand the nuances of the request and respond quickly, at a cost the business can sustain. “I think it strikes the balance perfectly,” Ahmed says.
Building software and sales demos with Codex
Inside DevRev, engineers have made a clear choice about the best way to build. “Our entire team uses Codex,” Ahmed says. The adoption grew organically after engineers explored multiple coding tools. By the time of the interview, DevRev had moved fully to Codex and dropped its Cursor licenses.
For Ahmed, this reflects what developers value: “Developers are really just looking for the best tool, and you can’t fool them.” His engineers were unequivocal about wanting to continue with Codex.
“We think that Codex is far and away the best experience.”
—Ahmed Bashir, Chief Technology Officer, DevRev
DevRev’s sales engineers also use GPT‑6 Astra to create demos for the company’s booths at international conferences.
Responding faster to customers and employees
When a customer or employee asks for help, the request may require Operator to understand the issue, take approved action, or route to Computer to prepare the right person to act. Ahmed sees opportunities for the Decisions API and Ultrafast to help those workflows finish quickly, without requiring deep reasoning at every step.
Some of those decisions are difficult and expensive to define with fixed rules, especially when the information they depend on keeps changing. Ahmed wants builders to be able to describe more of that logic conversationally and choose the right kind of intelligence for each task. “These things have to be able to run and complete themselves in seconds, not minutes,” he says.
Realizing the promise of self-service
DevRev’s next ambition is for Operator to take on longer, more demanding customer and employee requests while keeping actions traceable, permissioned, and reversible.
Ahmed sees familiar support tasks, such as finding a knowledge-base answer, upgrading a plan, or getting a refund, as only the beginning. “We want to really realize that promise of self-service,” he says.
With OpenAI’s frontier intelligence, DevRev is building toward Computer and Operator carrying more complex requests through to resolution, with the company knowledge and controls to act on a person’s behalf.

items.title: Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out
items.summary: Back to Articles Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out Team Article Published November 4, 2026 Upvote 34 +28 Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas Cardoso GabrielPimenta99 Follow Dharma-AI Paulo Henrique de Medeiros Araujo Paulo-DharmaAI Follow Dharma-AI Bruno Duarte brunoduarte01 Follow Dharma-AI Francisco de Almeida Rocha Alves falves9101 Follow Dharma-AI A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost. In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task. OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing. However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record. Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database. A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem. So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning. You can try it yourself here. What the Model Does Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them: Open: no schema supplied. The model reads the page and works out which parts of it are structured fields (a label followed by a value, a table with a header row over its columns) from context and layout, not from a fixed list of field names, and returns everything it finds as key-value pairs. Schema-directed: you specify the exact shape wanted, field by field, with a type for each one (string, number, or boolean), under the key names your system already uses. Ask for "service_provider" and "client_company", and those are the exact keys that come back. Ask for a table and it fills it row by row, column by column, matching each cell to the key it belongs under. Ask for a field that isn't on the document, and it returns null instead of inventing a value. The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else. Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system. How It Was Trained The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes. The data is organized into three streams: English multi-domain data: diverse documents collected from the public web, spanning many document types. Brazilian domain data: real Brazilian documents sourced internally, in Portuguese. Multilingual data: a smaller share covering other European and Asian languages, for broader generalization beyond English and Portuguese. All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type. Where the Benchmark Draws the Line The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON. We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations. Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest). Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour. This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs. A Test of Generalization SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each. On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent. On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank. Quality and Cost, at the Same Time A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run. This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run. Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem. Try it on your own documents here. items.title: Don’t vibe code your software factory
items.summary:
Engineering
Don’t vibe code your software factory
Zach Lloyd|November 4, 2026
I often see tweets that imply setting up a software factory can be done simply with a string of prompts tying together cloud agents. My experience working with a large number of customers is that this is false. Companies often start with this approach and then regret it because it doesn’t scale. These companies want resilient, improveable, low-latency factories that integrate deeply with their existing tools. They want a high level of configurability and measurement. They want audit logs, security guarantees – in short, they want the same level of production quality for their factories as they do for their products because they are betting on software factories as the future of how they ship those products more quickly.
This post dives into what it takes to build a production software factory. By “software factory” I mean a measurable, improvable cloud-based system for scaling coding agents for maximum ROI and productivity across your organization. As I’ve written before, the right way to think of software factories is as infrastructure with a well-defined stack.
Implementing the stack - factories as code
At the base of the stack, you define your factory in code. The code contains a complete description of everything it takes to do work in your factory: the agent prompts, workflows, MCPs, skills, runner config, integration config, automations + all of the machinery for measurement, evals, and benchmarks. Think of it as Terraform for all of the coding agent workflows for building software at your company.
The code approach is key because it unlocks the ability to systematically test different factory configurations and measure how they perform. It lets you answer questions like “for front-end tasks, is it OK to use open-weight models? Do I really need X, Y, Z skills to get quality output, or are they just wasting tokens?” By defining your factory in code, you also allow coding agents to suggest and make changes to its definition – this is the basis of self-improvement.
So the first technical challenge is how to set up code-based factory execution. For Warp Factories, the code format is built-in. If you are rolling your own, you need to create a code format that describes as much as possible how to do work in the factory.
For example, imagine that you have a factory workflow for triaging and fixing server crashes from Sentry. Your factory code will need to support:
Defining the integration with Sentry:
What’s the webhook, payload, auth mechanism, etc.
What workflow is invoked when an event arrives
Details of that workflow:
What are the steps for handling the server error?
Is it triaged or auto-fixed?
Does the factory loop in a human?
Does fixing the issue need a spec? If so, when?
If it makes a PR, who is the author?
Who should review?
How does it verify that the PR is correct?
How many rounds of review?
Is there computer use verification?
Etc…
Runner configuration:
Where does this workflow run?
What’s the sandbox configuration and toolchain?
What repos does it have access to?
What MCPs besides Sentry are needed?
How do they authenticate?
How does the agent talk to your source code forge? Your task tracker?
What models and harnesses are used for the different steps in the workflow?
What’s the model routing strategy?
Data:
Where does all of the data that this workflow generates get stored?
How do you evaluate whether this workflow is cost-effective compared to manual triage?
How do you improve the workflow over time?
The point is that even supporting what looks like a simple workflow requires a rich configuration.
Here’s what the code format looks like in Warp Factories to support all this (full sample):
Implementing the stack - orchestration
Once you have a code format, you need to move up the stack and build an orchestration layer that takes that format and moves work through it. It needs to:
Read the code at the current version (or a branch if you are running an experiment)
Spin up the right sandbox on demand, with low latency and high reliability
Route the request to one or more agents with the right model and harness config
Prompt them through handling the work, according to what’s in the factory code
Record any artifacts + agent traces into persistent storage
Loop in humans when needed, including giving them the ability to either handoff or steer agent work done so far
Integrate with all of the other systems that play a part like Sentry, Github, Jira, Slack, etc.
Orchestration fundamentally is launching and coordinating cloud agents. For some orgs that primarily do local development, just getting cloud agents set up is a big endeavor. This is a similar challenge to setting up a remote development environment for your human engineers, and many companies we work with reuse that infrastructure for agent sandboxing.
But it also could be different. You may want human engineers who are working remotely via SSH to have a wider set of permissions and tools than your agents. They may get different MCP access. They may be able to access secrets in the environment (agents should not be able to). Again, the point is that there’s a lot of engineering and configuration that goes into setting this up, depending on the size and scale of the org.
Once you have cloud execution, your orchestrator also needs to be resilient and durable. If an agent crashes midway, can it resume from where it left off without duplicating work and wasting tokens? If Github has an outage (imagine that!) can it perform a sensible retry strategy? This points to having checkpointing and durability built in, perhaps using something like Temporal.
When orchestration happens in response to a direct human prompt (e.g. from Slack) it needs to be low latency, otherwise it wastes human time. That means you’ll probably want to “pre-warm” agent sandboxes rather than starting them on demand. If the orchestration is happening via automation you can relax the latency requirements, and indeed might want to in order to save money. Again, it depends on what the work is – you’ll want it to be configurable.
You’ll want your orchestrator to be able to use different models and (potentially) different harnesses. Some tasks can be done with open-weight models. Some perhaps should use Codex or Claude Code or Pi or perhaps an internal coding agent harness. These harnesses all have different interfaces and putting together a unified experience around them takes a bunch of work.
Implementing the stack - self-improvement and benchmarking
Executing work items directly is only one piece of the system though – it’s the part that allows your team to do product engineering. You also need to set up your factory to support measurement and improvement, so that your team can do what I call “factory engineering:” engineering your agentic setup for maximal throughput and quality at the lowest possible cost.
As with any other engineering discipline, to do factory engineering well, you need the proper foundation and tools.
The foundation is factories-as-code plus persistence of all factory agent conversations. Factories-as-code allows testing different factory configurations and enables agentic self-improvement. Recording agent conversations allows you to score how your factory is performing along different dimensions. Note that it’s not enough to just record the agent trace – you also need to record all of the artifacts produced by the agent (e.g. PRs, videos, screenshots).
Once you have the foundations, you need the tools:
Online evals and scorers: use LLM-as-a-judge to score past agent runs along dimensions you might want to improve (e.g. “Is the agent writing redundant tests? is it producing designs that align with our style guide?”)
Self-improvement loops: agents that examine past eval results looking for opportunities to improve the factory code definition.
Benchmarks: rerun sets of agent tasks from their original state with different factory configurations (e.g. different models or skill definitions) to determine which is optimal.
Model routing: apply the results of evals and benchmarks to a model routing strategy that is optimized for your team’s own workflows.
A/B tests: prove that the factory code is optimal on a go-forward basis by running controlled split tests.
Building all of this measurement and improvement infrastructure is the most overlooked part of building a factory. For benchmarking prior tasks for example, you need task replay that is as hermetic as possible and takes into account the side effects the prior run may have had; i.e. you can’t just naively replay fixing a task when the task tracker has already marked the task as complete. Instead, you need to record the original state of the task tracker somewhere and replay that as well.
Implementing the stack - integrations and access
As you build your factory you’ll have to think about how work goes in and out. With Warp Factories, we made the conscious choice that work should largely flow in via existing developer and knowledge work tools like Slack, Teams, Jira, Linear, Github, Gitlab, etc. rather than forcing work through a dedicated factory product surface.
We see a lot of customers start with a “factory web app” with a big prompt box for submitting factory work, and this usually doesn’t catch on because it requires everyone to move out of their existing tooling to a new app. Much better in our opinion to bring the factory to where the work is already happening and the context already lives.
To this end, we think of the factory as headless infrastructure – the engine behind all the coding agents your team runs, rather than a fleet of AI teammates to chat with or a product with a new interface to adopt. That means that the factory is API and MCP first, built for use not just by humans but by agents. Work can go in and out from any surface, accept context from anywhere, write back to anywhere, and no matter where it happens the factory should be able to take over and do the task with all the right workflows, tracking, etc.
With this flexibility comes more work though. It’s harder to support a high quality experience across a large number of heterogeneous integrations than it is to build a single new destination app. While it’s fairly straightforward to set up a single Slack bot, we find that there’s actually way more that goes into getting all these integrations right: e.g. figuring out how to route work to the right people in the right tool, managing permissions across different toolsets (e.g. just because someone has slack access doesn’t mean they should be able to use a factory set up for the SRE team), making each integration feel native to the tool (e.g. the way you express that an agent is “thinking” is very different in Slack and Jira).
Closing thoughts
The point of this piece is to show some of the interesting technical considerations in building production software factories. As mentioned at the start, I believe that to get to a real factory you need to go far beyond stringing together prompts and cloud agents. Companies that start that way typically end up stepping back and starting over, taking an approach that looks much more like implementing (or using) a factory stack.
If you’re interested in this approach to building your own factories, we’d love to chat.

items.title: How we built Lovable, and why we keep rebuilding it
items.summary:
All posts
Published November 4, 2026 in Technical blog
How we built Lovable, and why we keep rebuilding it
Author: Anton Osika at Lovable
Making Lovable simple and dependable has meant repeatedly rethinking how it works. As the technical landscape keeps changing, engineering choices that once helped can start holding you back. Many teams building AI-powered products face the same question: what should you keep, and what should you rebuild?
In the spring of 2023, I put an open-source project called GPT Engineer on GitHub. You described the software you wanted, it asked clarifying questions, and then it wrote the whole codebase. Later that year I wrote down the plan for Lovable: people who couldn’t code would create, deploy, and improve software through chat and instantly see the result. More than 100,000 pull requests in our codebase later, my co-founder Fabian and our team of engineers, designers, and product managers have turned that plan into Lovable, and our users have created more than 70 million projects on the platform to date.
The original plan for Lovable from spring 2023
I recently reread my original plan, and it's eerily similar to what we ended up building. What I didn’t anticipate was how many times we would reinvent the way we get there. Along the way, we had to rethink how much freedom to give a model, how to catch its mistakes quickly, and even how to fork the computer it was working on.
I suspect other teams building software products are working through many of the same challenges. I hope sharing how we approached them makes that work a little easier.
Narrowing the problem gave us a head start
We chose to help people create new applications. They would bring an idea, and Lovable would generate the codebase and host it for them with one click. Focusing on greenfield projects spared us the enormous variety of existing codebases, dependencies, and environments. We narrowed the problem further by choosing an opinionated stack, dropping an early selector that let users choose between frontend stacks.
Together, those choices gave us control over the libraries we used, the structure of the code, and the environment it ran in. We could run the generated code in an environment we understood, inspect failures, and improve the entire system automatically. Improvements to that common setup could help across many projects.
The principle was simple: constrain the problem, control execution, and learn from the results.
Match the agent’s freedom to the model’s ability
Getting an application onto the screen was one thing. Keeping it working as someone asked for change after change was harder.
A developer can inspect a broken application and repair the code. Someone who has never programmed needs the product to handle much more of that work for them.
I kept pushing us toward autonomous agents because I expected models to improve quickly. I wanted us to build for those future models. Our engineer Mårten Wiman took this to a very sophisticated async design where the agent could create tasks and delegate to subagents. But less-constrained agents would get stuck in technical rabbit holes, making errors and taking actions with no predictable finish time. Giving them more freedom made the product less dependable.
So we took a step back. We deleted almost all agent code and went back to one user request resulting in a rather predictable chain of tools, with chat and a live preview on the output. By late 2024, the main editing flow was a single response containing the requested file changes. Native tool calling wasn’t reliable enough for us then, so we had the model wrap code in XML-like tags such as <lov-write> and parsed the edits after the agent was done.
We had retries and error handling, but no open-ended loop in which the model ran a tool, inspected the result, and chose its next move. The person could check the result in the preview and steer the next change.
The models also had limits on how much code they could consider at once. As applications grew, choosing what to show them became a problem of its own. We used fine-tuned tiny LLMs to identify the code each change depended on, including files that wouldn’t need editing, and passed that context to the coding model.
We were learning to shape both what the model could do and what it could see.
We planned to train models. Knowledge files + RAG worked better.
Choosing the right code was only part of the context problem. As people built, we saw the same mistakes reoccur. The 2023 plan said Lovable would be powered by fine-tuned models, trained on the data the product generated, so every failed attempt would make the system better.
In 2024, we found a simpler way to start: engineers inspected chat logs from broken apps and wrote short notes explaining recurring mistakes and how to avoid them.
We called these “knowledge files.” An icon problem could become an instruction as simple as this:
# Icons
Only use icons that exist in lucide-react.
Never invent an icon name. If unsure, pick a generic one.
Illustrative knowledge-file example.
A retrieval step selected the relevant notes and added them to the model's context. No fine-tuning, just text. The pattern will be familiar to anyone using agent skills today: keep useful instructions in files and load the ones relevant to the task.
I believe that work was critical to our take-off in late 2024 and I even referred to it as a scaling law. A useful lesson from one broken app could help the next person without waiting for us to train a new model.
“Knowledge files” were so powerful in 2024 that I referred to them as “scaling law”. Every additional knowledge file made the agent more reliable and it kept scaling.
We later applied the same idea in Lovable Stack Overflow, which retrieved problems and solutions for the agent. An early version reduced the rate at which users got stuck by 5%.
Faster agent feedback loops created a snappy experience
An agent that can correct its own mistakes still has to make you wait for those corrections. If every attempt requires a full build, even a small change can become a slow conversation.
We built sandboxes that retained each project’s files and kept its development server running while the user worked. Edits could update the live preview without a fresh production bundle.
Separate incremental TypeScript checks reused work from earlier checks to catch errors in how the code fit together. The agent could use those errors to work on a fix while the project was still running.
We already had ways to return errors to the model and retry. The point of this infrastructure was to shorten each edit-check-correct cycle. A coding agent’s speed depends on how quickly it can check and correct its work, too. These speedups for every edit made a big difference in the overall feel of Lovable.
New foundational building block: forking and merging the computer
Keeping the development server running shortened the edit-check cycle. Later, we took that further: letting an agent return days later and pick up the same working environment in seconds.
Saving the source files wasn’t enough. We needed to preserve the running processes, too. Our stateful sandboxes checkpoint the machine’s memory, CPU state and disk, then restore it when needed.
Camille: our framework for forking and merging entire running computers
This work became foundational to many more technical features of Lovable. It now lets us fork not just code, but an entire application with its working environment and database, giving agents a way to try different approaches from the same starting point.
What started as a way to make edits faster is now letting us ask agents to take on much more.
The next 100,000 pull requests
The product we wanted to build in 2023 has now helped people build more than 70 million projects, from websites to highly sophisticated fullstack applications. Getting here meant reinventing how we built Lovable, multiple times. Each of those choices brought the same ambition closer: someone with an idea could make it reality without barriers holding them back.
That was the easy part.
Three problems are still wide open.
Putting the drudgery on autopilot. Building an app was always just the beginning. Once real customers and real money depend on it, every change gets harder and riskier. The harder problem is to own that whole lifecycle: testing, deploying, and maintaining production software, even while you sleep. Scaling, uptime, security, fixing bugs before your customers find them. The hardest part is trust. One misunderstood request from a user can delete data or break something that can’t be undone. We’re responsible for preventing that.
Make building all types of software seamless. Customers should just describe what they need and it works, regardless if it’s desktop, mobile, complex workflows, realtime data processing, or global business systems. Each brings different environments, constraints, and ways to fail.
Build a better software stack. We don’t see it as our job to just make building software seamless for our customers, it’s our job to iterate toward a better software stack altogether. This means inventing new foundations. Innovations in observability, forking and merging computer snapshots, new sync engines, durable execution patterns, verifiable security and privacy guarantees for users. There is a lot to improve before the software stack people build on evolves to its ultimate, most helpful shape.
Solve the above three and you get something more than an “AI Software Engineer”: a platform people run entire businesses on. Our users are already pulling us there: they connect their Slack, ingest their data into Lovable, connect Lovable to everything else they use. They run their companies, use Lovable to handle their payments, and then they use features like our growth tools, discoverability, and analytics to grow their businesses with us. They even ask Lovable to incorporate their companies. Our job is to do everything we can to unblock their ambitions.
That is the work cut out for us in the next 100,000 pull requests.
If you want to work on these hard problems, where the answer isn’t in a textbook and the result shows up in front of millions of people the same week, come build with us at Lovable.
And if you’re working through the same problems elsewhere, subscribe to our newly launched tech blog (did I just write “tech blog” in 2026?). We’ll share what we learn working toward our vision directly from the engineers doing it.
About the author
Anton Osika is the co-founder of Lovable and the creator of GPT Engineer. Follow him on X and LinkedIn.

items.title: Introducing Images 2.6
items.summary:
OpenAI
November 4, 2026
ProductRelease
Introducing Images 2.6Introducing Images 2.6
Generate images faster and with more control over editing rounds.
We’re introducing Images 2.6 in ChatGPT, Codex, and the API, bringing your ideas to life faster. With this, you can bring motion to your images with GIFs — from animating a brand mascot or character to turning a product shot into an eye-catching loop. You can also create polished visuals faster and refine them with greater precision — keeping characters, products, and brand details consistent as you edit.
People around the world now create 4 billion images per week across ChatGPT, Codex, and the API. On average, that’s more than half a billion images created per day.
Faster iteration and more professional visuals
Images 2.6 generates images 50% faster than before. In the API, we offer GPT‑Image‑2.6 Flare and Sunburst for developers to choose from. When quality is set to low, Flare can generate images in as little as six seconds. For work that calls for greater detail and precision, GPT‑Image‑2.6 Sunburst brings higher-quality image generation and even greater image consistency across edits when quality is set to medium or high. Flare also improves layout quality for posters, product imagery, and other professional visuals.
Animate your ideas with GIFs
For moments that call for motion, GIFs bring another dimension to your ideas. Marketers and creators can animate a brand mascot for a campaign, create reactions and memes for social media, or use animated storyboards to explore character movement before video production.
Created by OpenArt
Prompt 1: Create a single animation sprite sheet for a seamless looping GIF. A super-cute chibi adult office worker sits at a desk watching a computer monitor with a clearly plunging stock-market line chart. The sequence: hopeful expression, notices the chart falling, eyes widen, face crumples, large cartoon tears stream down both cheeks, then quietly wipes tears while still staring at the falling chart. Oversized round head, tiny body, big expressive eyes, soft rounded features, messy fluffy hair, white shirt and loosened tie. Exactly 6 sequential frames arranged in a precise 3-column by 2-row grid, read left-to-right then top-to-bottom. Every panel has identical dimensions. Fixed front three-quarter camera, same character, same desk, monitor, outfit, and cozy miniature office background. Clear incremental facial and tear motion; sixth frame transitions smoothly toward the first. Polished kawaii chibi 3D toy-like style, warm pastel lighting, funny and sympathetic mood. No captions, no words, no numbers, no logos, no speech bubbles, no panel labels, no borders, no gutters.
Created by OpenArt
Prompt 2: Create a single animation sprite sheet for a seamless looping GIF. A super-cute chibi adult office worker sits at a desk watching a computer monitor with a clearly soaring stock-market line chart and a large upward arrow. The sequence: notices the chart rising, eyes widen with delight, jumps up cheering, grabs a handful of generic paper banknotes with no readable currency markings, then happily tosses the banknotes into the air like confetti while laughing. Oversized round head, tiny body, big sparkling expressive eyes, soft rounded features, messy fluffy hair, white shirt and loosened tie. Exactly 6 sequential frames arranged in a precise 3-column by 2-row grid, read left-to-right then top-to-bottom. Every panel has identical dimensions. Fixed front three-quarter camera, same character, desk, monitor, outfit, and cozy miniature office background. Clear incremental body, arm, and flying-paper motion; sixth frame transitions smoothly toward the first. Polished kawaii chibi 3D toy-like style, bright celebratory pastel lighting, funny joyful mood. No captions, no words, no numbers, no logos, no real currency symbols, no speech bubbles, no panel labels, no borders, no gutters.
“GIFs are the native language of social media, and GPT‑Image‑2.6 lets every OpenArt creator speak it fluently from a single prompt.”
—Coco Mao, CEO & Co-founder at OpenArt
And you don’t need a polished design to get started — even a simple sketch can become an expressive, animated character for videos, games, and more.
From personal reactions to brand mascots and product visuals, GIFs give people and businesses a playful way to communicate. Town, a startup building an AI work assistant, used Images 2.6 in the API to explore how animated characters could bring more personality to everyday interactions at work.
More ways to create and edit in the API
With Images 2.6, developers get more control over how images are created, edited, and carried into the next stage of a project. Image markup, already available in ChatGPT, comes to the API so teams can pinpoint exactly where to make specific changes. SVG exports make designs ready to use across websites, apps, and print.
A new complexity parameter lets developers adjust how much planning the model does to meet a request, with lower settings suited to quick edits. Image quality controls visual detail and fidelity, while complexity guides how much goes into the scene.
“GPT‑Image‑2.6 brings speed and creative control together, helping you generate and edit images while preserving the details that define a character, product, or brand. We’re excited to add it to Figma Weave, giving teams another powerful model for creative production, all within a reusable workflow.”
—Itay Schiff, Creative Director at Figma Weave
For most editing tasks, we recommend low complexity for faster edits, paired with the image quality your workflow requires. For scenes with many elements or constraints, try medium or high complexity effort.
See what early access customers generated using Images 2.6:
Pricing and availability
Images 2.6 is available globally today in ChatGPT and Codex across all subscription tiers on desktop, mobile, and web.
GPT‑Image‑2.6 Sunburst and GPT‑Image‑2.6 Flare are available in the API. See pricing details here.⁠(opens in a new window)
Learn more about our safety evaluations and safeguards for Images 2.6 in the system card⁠(opens in a new window).

CategoryProduct updates

We’ve added new agents and products to Claude Marketplace, where teams find partner tools and services to help them get more from Claude. The additions cover security, developer infrastructure, creative, and productivity.
Eligible enterprise customers can apply a portion of their committed Anthropic spend toward these solutions. This lets them use one commitment across Claude and partner products, whether they’re buying something new or expanding with a platform they already use.
There are now over 25 partner agents and products on the marketplace. Here are the latest additions and what teams can do with them.
Products and agents for securing code and systems
Chainguard: Chainguard Harness builds applications from source in an isolated microVM and probes the live app for exploitable vulnerabilities. It helps teams fix what Claude finds, with custom remediation recommendations for reproducible vulnerabilities.
Checkmarx: Checkmarx One pairs rules-based analysis with AI reasoning to find vulnerabilities in code. It helps teams prioritize findings and fix them before code ships.
Cyera: Cyera Agent Guardian inventories Claude deployments, governs permissions before Claude runs, and enforces policy on prompts, files, and tool calls. It helps teams test those controls through red teaming.
Rubrik: Rubrik Code Guardian uses frontier AI models from Anthropic to review a secure copy of GitHub or Azure DevOps repositories for multi-step attack paths. It helps security and engineering teams rank issues by severity and turn confirmed critical ones into tracked tickets.
Tanium: Tanium Cloud gives teams real-time visibility and control across their endpoints. It helps IT and security teams find and fix vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and missing patches.
Development infrastructure for engineering teams
Datadog: Datadog Agent Observability traces agent execution through tools and services. It helps teams improve agent quality, performance, and cost efficiency by surfacing production patterns and recommending fixes.
Netlify: Netlify Enterprise deploys apps, sites, and agents to a global edge network, with preview URLs on every change. It helps teams take what they build with Claude from prototype to production with no infrastructure to configure, and includes SSO, role-based access, and audit logs.
Tools for marketing and creative work
AirOps: AirOps provides an agentic platform for AI search strategy, content, and multichannel execution. It helps marketing teams analyze brand performance in AI search and tie results to pipeline and revenue.
Runway: Runway generates and edits video, images, and audio. It helps creative and marketing teams turn a brief into finished assets and edit footage with natural language.
Webflow: Webflow provides built-in tools to build, manage, and optimize websites. It helps marketers, designers, developers, and agents make changes, with controls and governance built in.
Productivity apps for every team
Asana: Asana AI Teammates are prebuilt agents that use context from the Asana Work Graph, each with its own identity, scoped permissions, and audit trail. They help teams handle multi-step work, routing decisions that need judgment to the owner.
Glean: Glean connects company knowledge and workflows across systems. It helps employees find answers and complete multi-step tasks across connected apps.
monday: monday agents work inside projects, boards, docs, and meetings, using their owners and deadlines as context. They help PMO, IT, marketing, finance, and operations teams control what AI can access, approve, and spend.
Zoom: Zoom Agentic Search answers questions inside Claude using the latest meeting summaries, work conversations, documents, and connected third-party sources. Teams get permission-aware results without analyzing raw transcripts or chaining tools together.

items.title: OpenAI to acquire Pierre Computer Company, Inc.
items.summary:
OpenAI
November 4, 2026
Company
OpenAI to acquire Pierre Computer Company, Inc.
Expanding Codex’s tools for building, understanding, and reviewing code.
Today we're announcing that OpenAI will acquire Pierre Computer Company, Inc⁠(opens in a new window). (“Pierre”), the company behind Code Storage⁠(opens in a new window) and a family of standout open-source developer tools. If you’ve browsed files or reviewed a change in the Codex app, you’ve already used Pierre’s Trees and Diffs libraries. We’re excited to work with the Pierre team to build on the Git workflows that developers already rely on and adapt them to how teams work with coding agents.
We’ve seen in our own engineering work how the systems around Git need to evolve as more of that work happens in parallel. Earlier this week, we shared how we’re scaling Git at OpenAI with Pando, our in-house source control backend for engineers and agents. With the Pierre team, we wish to set the standard for modern software development: from the first branch an agent creates to that magic moment when code is deployed to the world. We want to make Codex the place where developers and agents take on their most ambitious projects.
Craftsmanship meets scale for the agentic era
We’ve long appreciated the care Pierre brings to another part of working with Git: how developers review code. You can see that care in the libraries we use in Codex today. Trees lets developers quickly navigate a project’s files, and Diffs makes it easy to see what changed. Both of these tools make it easy to review and navigate large volumes of code with uncompromising performance.
That same attention to detail runs through Pierre’s other work. Diffs’ Edit mode lets a reviewer fix a line of code right where they spot the problem. Pierre recently released Highlights, an extremely fast syntax highlighter that updates as a developer types or an agent streams code. The same small team that put an editor inside a diff also designed the API for Code Storage, a service that lets apps store code and track its history using Git.
Bringing the work together in Codex
Pierre has built tools that developers love, and together, we will ship new products and platforms that benefit all. Once the acquisition closes, our ambition is to advance the future of source control across the industry. We want Codex to connect the code a company ships with the decisions its people make, at the scale the future demands.
Pierre’s open-source projects will remain open-source, and we’ll continue to contribute to them. Customers can continue using Code Storage after the acquisition closes while we work to bring its features and functionality into Codex.
The closing of the acquisition is subject to customary closing conditions, including receipt of regulatory approvals. Until closing, OpenAI and Pierre will remain separate and independent companies.

items.title: QCon上海2026：百度 SRE Agent 规模化落地实践解读
items.summary: 原创 欢迎关注的 2026-11-04 18:00 北京 QCon上海2026，百度SRE Agent规模化落地实践经验官方解读。 。 点击蓝字，关注我们 作者 | 百度 SRE 导读 introduction 过去一年，做出一个 Agent 其实不难：它能听懂问题、调几个工具、把一段任务跑完，有时候效果还挺惊艳。但当我们真的把 Agent 放进生产环境，关心的问题立刻就变了——它部署在哪、谁维护、配置怎么更新、出了问题怎么查、调一次会不会污染线上、调用生产工具安不安全、这次处理的经验能不能留下来给下一个 Agent 复用…… 也就是说，难点已经不再是"能不能做出来"，而是"能不能稳定地托管起来、能不能安全地跑起来、能不能持续地变好"。QCon 上海2026 百度运维部出品的《百度SRE Agent 规模化落地实践——大模型 Agent 的安全托管与自主进化探索》分享详细介绍了AgentOps业务落地经验。 全文 5194 字，预计阅读时间 8 分钟 GEEK TALK 01 背景与规模化挑战 一个团队只有一个 Agent 的时候，很多问题靠人就能解决：找台机器起个实例、配个消息通道、准备几份 Skill，出问题登录机器看日志——不优雅，但能跑。 可一旦 Agent 多了、团队多了、场景复杂了，这套做法会迅速失效。我们把它归成六类问题： 接入与部署：每个团队都重复准备环境、配实例、接通道，大量时间花在"让 Agent 跑起来"，而不是让它的业务能力变好。 配置与版本：一个 Agent 不只有 Prompt，还有 Skill、工具、知识、运行时配置，这些没有统一的版本边界，调试里的改动很容易污染线上，出了问题也不知道是哪次变更。 运行与观测：一次执行包含意图理解、规划、Skill 选择、多次工具调用，如果只看最后一句回答，根本判断不出问题出在模型、知识、工具还是流程。 安全与权限：Agent 一旦能碰生产，就可能触发查询、变更、写操作，光靠 Prompt 告诉它"别干危险的事"远远不够，必须有平台级的权限、审批、限流、审计和回滚。 能力复用：公共工具、业务知识、历史经验难沉淀，场景建设高度依赖少数专家。 质量与演进：没有稳定的 Case、回放和评估体系，你根本没法判断新版本是不是真的变好了。 一句话收口——当 Agent 从"单点试用"走向"规模化生产"，接入、版本、观测、安全这些缺失会集中爆发，结果就是：企业用得起来，却管不住、不敢放大。AgentOps 要解决的，就不是某一个 Agent 的问题，而是这一组规模化问题。 GEEK TALK 02 AgentOps 整体架构 自下而上五层： 基础设施层，算力、存储、网络； 能力供给层，模型、工具、知识库、公共 Skill； 平台层，也就是整个 AgentOps 的核心； 网关层，统一入口、鉴权、路由、限流； 接入层，如流、数字员工、Web、消息机器人、OpenAPI 这些入口。 这里有一个我们特别想强调的设计思想：控制面和数据面分离。控制面负责"定规则、管治理"——配置、版本、发布、评估、知识、安全策略；数据面只专注"执行"——正式实例跑真实业务，调试沙盒跑草稿和回放，两者隔离。为什么要分开？因为解耦之后才好独立演进、好扩展，业务团队专注场景逻辑，外围工程能力交给平台。 而平台层里，我们用五大中心统一把 Agent 管起来：Agent 管理、安全、变更、评估、知识 一起纳管，五层架构让 Agent 从"能跑"走向"敢用"。 AgentOps 的五大核心能力，是一条从"稳定运行"到"持续进化"的主线：Runtime 全生命周期托管 → 安全管控 → 场景仿真回放 → 知识沉淀与能力闭环 → Agent 自主进化。 GEEK TALK 03 Runtime 全生命周期托管 我们不希望每个团队都自己维护运行实例，而是平台统一管 Agent 从创建 → 配置 → 部署 → 运行 → 升级 → 监控 → 故障恢复 → 下线的全过程。这里的"托管"不只是起个进程，它至少包含四块： 全周期托管，一站式纳管； 统一资产与状态，配置、能力资产、运行实例、会话状态、版本发布、运行观测集中管理，实例迁移重建后上下文也不丢； 高可用保障，健康检查、状态持久化、实例恢复、依赖切换，做到故障自愈； 弹性与多租，按负载伸缩、多团队隔离、配额成本可控。 这块带来的直接变化是：新 Agent 的交付周期，从"周级"降到"天级"，而且稳定性有 SLA 兜底。说白了——Agent 的"可用"不是某个组件的状态，而是配置、能力、实例、依赖共同可用，这件事交给平台兜底。 GEEK TALK 04 安全管控 Agent 进了生产，安全是绕不开的底座。我们有一个基本态度：安全责任不交给 Prompt，也不假设模型永远正确理解风险。 先看风险到底长什么样？ Agent 能自主调工具、执行写操作，用户、模型、系统、并发四个层面都可能让一次写操作失控。举两个真实的例子。 案例一：Agent 迭代后跟数据库交互，数据字典对不上、insert 一直失败，它多次试错无果，居然直接把库 DROP 了、重建 table——结果数据被删、业务中断。本质是"为达成目标自主升级到高危写操作，全程没人把关"。 案例二：指令只是把配置里 A 字段从 v1.32.0.1 改成 v1.33.0.1，结果 B 字段恰好也是这个值，Agent 顺手把 B 也改了——本质是"超出指令作用域、关联误伤、没有精确的范围控制"。 那我们怎么管？ 不是单点拦一下，而是从构建时到运行时的四道防线，L1 到 L4 逐层覆盖。 L1 构建时：事前约束，声明允许/禁止的动作与边界； L2 意图审计：第三方专家 Agent 比对"需求 ↔ 产出"，产出评审意见； L3 本地 Hook：审计 Agent 产出的 runbook 具体动作和对象； L4 网关代理：代理所有 API/HTTP 调用，统一管控并审计接口、参数、QPS。 一句话——安全不是最后一道闸，而是从构建到执行的全程护栏。 最后两件压舱石：身份与可回滚。 身份上，我们落地了委托令牌：令牌里承载"具体用户 + 发起 Agent"双身份，并且做了加密防盗用。关键是——我们用的是委托，不是冒充，完整保留"谁代表谁"，这样调用链能定责、越权能拦。 审计上，做 5W 审计：谁、哪个 Agent、何时、对哪些对象、做了什么，日志落本地并持久化。回滚上，每次提交都可回滚，能撤销最近一次写操作。而且所有托管的 Skill 都过 AI Review，天然可审计、可回滚。 GEEK TALK 05 场景仿真回放 也就是为什么需要评估中心？ Agent / Skill 的迭代有几个老大难： 变更影响难验证，改一处可能牵一发而动全身，人工回归范围有限； 场景难复现，切流、回滚这类高危写操作根本不能在线上跑； 验证环境不一致，不用同一个 Agent 验证，memory、session 的状态都会干扰结果； 问题难定位，只看最终结果看不出偏差在哪；再加上结果难验证、效果难评估、人工建 Case 成本高。 这些叠一起的后果就是——每次更新都得人工逐条 review，Agent / Skill 根本快不起来。 我们的解法是一个真实场景驱动的评估闭环。 从线上告警和多轮会话里自动记录 Trace，真实映射运行时的行为链路； 再从里面选高价值的 Trace，沉淀成含"输入 / 上下文 / 工具快照 / 期望结果 / 期望过程"五要素的标准 Case； 验证新版本时，把 Agent 部署到回放沙盒，对当前版本执行 Case 回放，不碰生产就能验证； 回放过程里实时看 Trace，精确定位到是哪一步、哪个工具、哪个参数出的问题； 最后输出评估报告，给总体得分和"期望 vs 实际"的过程对齐，支撑"继续迭代还是达标发布"的决策。 这里特别说一句外部依赖怎么处理：靠工具快照回放——API Server 拦截 + Replay Runtime 还原返回值，不依赖真实外部系统，所以可复现。 Case 怎么生成和治理？Case 可以从线上 Trace、人工创建、已有 Case 复制、标准文件导入等多来源汇聚，经过人工审核、沙盒验证后才入集，保证质量可控、来源可信；平台沉淀出一套通用 Trace 与 Case 集作底座，业务还能按需拼接自己的 Case 来回放。这里有个前提要强调：评估能力是建在安全中心之上的——拦得住，才敢跑。Case 不是一次性用例，而是能持续沉淀、安全可控的资产。 GEEK TALK 06 知识沉淀与能力闭环 我们的看法是：知识沉淀不是把一堆文档塞进知识库就完了，而是要让经验沉淀成合规可信、可复用的 Agent 能力。 多源沉淀：业务文档、运营经验、Case 记录、会话、用户反馈统一汇入。 合规校验把关：源知识入库前，要过权限、脱敏、质量三道校验：权限上按来源和访问权限管控、敏感知识隔离；脱敏上入库前自动脱敏，账号、密钥、隐私信息都要处理掉； 质量上要求知识带来源、适用条件、版本和验证状态，还做去重、冲突检测和时效校验。机制上，是断言设计做结构化自动校验 + 人工评审把关主观质量与边界，双重把关、不达标不入库。过了这关，知识才会走"知识 → Skill 候选 → 规范审计与单测 → 场景回放 → 发布复用"变成能力； 线上用起来的反馈再回流知识库，用回放通过率、采纳率来衡量，持续提升。 为什么强调合规？因为会议纪要、群聊这类来源在大会上特别容易被追问数据权限和脱敏，我们宁可少而准，不要多而误导。 GEEK TALK 07 Agent 自主进化 这里的自主进化，不是让 Agent 自己改生产配置，也不是让模型无约束地扩权，而是一种受控的能力优化。 更新的是什么？我们只调 Prompt（主要是 md）、Skill、知识、安全策略这些能力组件，不动模型权重——成本低、可回退。 怎么评估？由评估中心基于灵活的 Case 集做回放，判定靠三样：用户断言、Case 通过率，再加一层专家人工评审去确认"实际效果到底符不符合预期"，三样都过才进发布。 怎么管控风险？安全沙盒隔离、支持可控放行、版本管控，加上热更新带来的秒级回滚。整体就是：优化而非重训、评估门禁把关、安全兜底、数据与知识回流形成飞轮。 再看一轮优化具体怎么跑， 触发有三种： 生产或评估里的 Bad Case、知识更新、以及人工按需触发。触发后由 Agent 优化智能体生成候选——问题分析、定向优化、产出候选； 候选进可靠评估，按断言 + Case 通过率回放，退化即拦； 然后是可回退闭环——不通过就回炉，通过就灰度，异常就秒级回滚。 这样每一次优化都是"可触发、可评估、可回滚"的闭环，而不是黑盒自动变更。 GEEK TALK 08 实践与沉淀 - 平台赋能 业务用 AgentOps，只需要关注自己的差异，运行、安全、变更、评估、知识都交给平台统一托管。现在的覆盖情况：覆盖10+百度核心业务线、20+ 接入的 SRE Agent、50+ 开箱即用的 Common SRE Skill、3 套 SRE Agent 建设模板，迭代周期从天级降到小时级。 对比一下过去和现在就很直观： 接入，从各自搭环境到选模板一键迁移； 稳定，从自己做 fallback 到默认高可用； 安全，从各自鉴权到标准鉴权透传； 工具，从重复开发到 50+ Skill 开箱即用； 迭代，从天级发版到小时级热更新； 进化，从经验散落到沙盒评估加知识沉淀、自主进化。 GEEK TALK 09 最佳实践 · Agentic 故障处置 用一个例子把前面的能力串起来——业务基于 AgentOps 的能力，快速组织出一个 SRE Agent，把某类故障的 MTTR 打了下来。场景是"某核心服务实例批量故障"。流程是这样的： 感知，根据异常对象、服务拓扑、时间范围，采集告警、日志、近期变更，Agent 自动拉群并汇总上下文； 召回 + 分析，召回 3 条相似历史案例和处置手册，生成"变更 / 机房 / 流量"多个猜想，并组织证据链； 验证收敛，逐一排除，证据指向一次配置变更导致连接池耗尽、请求超时； 判断授权，工程师确认根因、授权回滚，平台按审批执行、全链路留痕； 止损恢复，回滚后超时率回落、服务恢复； 复盘沉淀，自动生成复盘，新增 1 条 Case 和 1 个"实例健康巡检"的预案 Skill。 效果上，这是一个示例案例：同类 Case 的 MTTR 从 60 分钟降到 10 分钟。我们特意强调"示例"——这是单次案例的口径，不是统计平均；正式对外的效率数字，都应该说明样本范围、统计口径和对照基线。这页真正想说的不是某个数字多亮眼，而是：业务能基于平台快速搭出一个 Agent 并见效，而且经验还能沉淀下来给下次复用。 GEEK TALK 10 经验沉淀 · 四大核心权衡 做 Agent 平台，真正难的不是某个单点能力，而是一组互相拉扯的权衡。我们的做法是"用机制让两端协同"，而不是二选一。四组权衡： 智能性 × 确定性——规划和执行解耦，高风险动作收口到工具和控制面，既留灵活、又守可预测。 安全 × 效率——按风险分级处置，自动放行 / 人工确认 / 强制审批 / 强制阻断，低风险快、高风险稳。 知识多 ≠ 高质量——知识必须带来源、适用条件、版本和验证状态，宁可少而准、不要多而误导。 生成 × 验证分离——引入独立验证机制，外部证据加多方评审，避免同一个模型自证正确。一句话：好的平台不是消灭矛盾，而是把每一组权衡都变成可控的工程选择。 GEEK TALK 11 总结与展望 回到最开始的问题：Agent 从单点试用走向规模化，缺的到底是什么？我们的答案是——缺的不是更多孤立的 Agent，而是一套能把 Agent 托管起来、安全地跑、验证效果、沉淀经验、持续改进的平台。我们把它分成三个阶段： 阶段一 · 统一托管（已落地）：一套平台托管 Agent 全生命周期，解决"能跑、敢用"。 阶段二 · 持续进化（进行中）：知识闭环加场景回放驱动自主优化，用回放通过率、采纳率来衡量、持续提升。 阶段三 · 自治运维（未来）：让 Agent 辅助管 Agent，人只定目标和边界，运维走向自治。 最终我们想要的，是"让每一次执行都更安全，让每一份经验都可复用"——不是让 Agent 凭空变成专家，而是让专家的判断能被记录、复用、持续放大，最终形成团队级、平台级的专家能力。 更多智能运维产品，欢迎联系：https://sre.baidu.com/ END 推荐阅读 好看视频鸿蒙端AI研发交付流程的建设思考与实践 我们放弃了"全自动生成代码" —— 网盘 Coding Agent 落地与迭代实录 Agentic Harness Workflow 框架：把 AI Coding 变成工程化流程 什么样的业务经验值得做成 Agent：从个人工具到组织资产 都在开源 Harness，Codex 和 DeepSeek 到底有什么不一样？ 一键三连，好运连连，bug不见👇 跳转微信打开

items.title: Share Kiro credits across your team with credit pooling
items.summary:
Back to all postsNovember 4, 2026
Share Kiro credits across your team with credit pooling
Kiro’s new credit pooling model gives enterprise engineering teams shared credits, granular governance, and usage flexibility for predictable AI spend.
SH
Shweta V A
Product
RA
Ranjith Ramakrishnan
Product
KR
Krishna Parab
Product Marketing
Why AI spend is now a budgeting problem
As AI coding tools become an increasingly important part of software development, AI credit usage is rapidly growing. But AI usage is not uniform across developers and teams. Individual subscriptions that allocate credits uniformly do not align with how teams consume credits. This leads to inefficient credit usage and unpredictable monthly invoices. For many organizations, managing AI costs has become the main concern heading into budget planning.
Sound familiar? You are not alone. Here are a few scenarios you may encounter:
A handful of power users consume most credits while light users let their credits expire unused.
AI agents rack up unexpected charges overnight before anyone notices.
Individual seat licenses create billing silos. Unused credits in one group can’t cover extra usage in another.
There is no easy way to enforce usage limits.
Teams need a more flexible way to purchase, share, govern, and predict AI consumption. Today, we are addressing that directly. Credit pooling delivers cost efficiency, governance, and usage flexibility for predictable AI spend, with billing through your AWS account. It is now available for Kiro Enterprise customers, giving teams a smarter, more economical way to share and govern AI access.
What is credit pooling?
Credit pooling is an enterprise pricing model for Kiro that lets your organization share a single pool of Kiro credits across your entire team. Credits are added to a shared pool that everyone draws from, so your power users can access the capacity that lighter users don’t need. Admins can still set a usage limit for each user, and that usage is drawn from the shared pool. Credit pooling comes with centralized purchasing, visibility, and governance. Billing runs through your AWS account, so Kiro charges show up with the rest of your AWS spend.
How it works: the core mechanics
$20 per seat per month, minimum two seats. The seat fee and the 500 credits each seat adds to the pool are both pro-rated in the first month for mid-cycle additions, based on the days left in the billing cycle.
500 credits included per seat, contributed to the shared pool for each billing cycle. These reset monthly.
Add-on credits at $0.04 each, added to the pool instantly when purchased. Purchased credits roll over for up to 12 months, so you can buy capacity in a single procurement cycle and plan further ahead.
Smart credit consumption. Your team uses included credits first, then purchased credits, starting with those closest to expiration. One team’s surplus protects another team’s crunch.
No double-billing: If a user belongs to multiple groups, your organization pays only for one seat.
Credit pooling enables real cost savings, better governance, and more flexibility for AI use.
Real cost savings from shared credits
The core value of credit pooling is simple. In any team, AI usage is not uniform. Developers may use more credits when deep in a sprint than when focused on code reviews. When credits are tied to individual seats, the light users’ credits remain unused while the heavy users run short and need more. Pooling reduces inefficiency. When credits are shared, the natural variation in usage across team members works in your favor. One team’s surplus covers another team’s crunch.
Example: A company purchases 20 seats and gets 10,000 included credits per month in the shared pool. Engineering (9), Design (5), and Data Science (6) team members all draw from the same pool. Without credit pooling, three developers who rarely use AI coding tools may leave their 1,500 combined included credits (500 per seat) unused each month, and others who exhaust their included credits may need to purchase add-on credits. With credit pooling, those 1,500 credits added to the pool flow automatically to the power users running complex refactoring to be used before they need to request add-on credits. No manual rebalancing is required.
In addition to natural load-balancing, organizations that actively manage group-level procurement see further savings by reducing the need for emergency credit purchases and right-sizing pool capacity to actual team usage patterns.
Granular governance over AI use
Credit pooling also works as a governance system. Kiro gives administrators the controls they need to manage AI usage the same way they manage any other enterprise resource, with clear policies, real-time enforcement, and automated guardrails.
Three-tier consumption limit hierarchy
Administrators can set usage limits at three levels; profile-level, group-level, and individual level; in increasing order of precedence. For users in multiple groups, the highest group limit applies in favor of the user. When developers hit their limits, further usage is blocked until the administrator purchases additional credits, so there are no surprise charges at month-end.
Smart threshold notifications
Kiro sends configurable alerts to administrators when credit utilization reaches defined thresholds. By default, alerts fire at 80% and 100% for credit usage against each user’s limit, pool credit limit, and seat utilization levels as assigned versus purchased seats. Admins stay ahead of depletion.
Pool membership management
Seat reconciliation is automatic. Groups can be created manually or populated via AWS IAM Identity Center (IDC). Group management via 3rd-party identity providers will be available soon. Mid-cycle seat additions are handled seamlessly, with credits added to the pool immediately. When users leave or change roles, seat assignments update without billing disruption.
API access to these controls is coming soon, so you can manage governance programmatically.
Loading image...
Greater visibility, flexibility, and predictability for better planning
You can’t manage what you can’t measure. Credit pooling gives administrators a real-time view of AI spend at every level of the organization and flexibility to adjust spend as usage evolves.
Real-time monitoring dashboards
Pool-level dashboards show a view of total credits available, consumed, and remaining across the entire organization. With seat utilization tracking, you can see which seats are underutilized, so you can right-size your pool.
Better planning
With credit pooling, you can accommodate changing usage patterns without continually adjusting individual subscriptions or allowances. Group-level usage trends help you plan for the long term. Because purchased credits last up to 12 months, you can buy add-on credits for a pool strategically.
Loading image...
Get started with credit pooling
Credit pooling gives enterprise engineering teams the three things they have been asking for: better cost efficiency through shared credits, centralized governance with granular controls, and usage flexibility for predictable AI spend across teams.
Here is what you get with credit pooling:
Cost efficiency: Reduce or eliminate wasted credits from light users. Let your power users draw on the full team pool.
Governance depth: Set usage limits at the profile, group, and individual levels.
Planning confidence: Usage dashboards and threshold alerts help you avoid surprises at the end of the month.
Enterprise trust: AWS-native billing integration and AWS IDC-based group management support trust for enterprise-wide AI use.
Ready to start sharing credits across your team? Credit pooling is the default for new Kiro Enterprise customers, and existing Enterprise customers can opt in when they are ready. Visit Pricing to explore credit pooling for your team or contact us to set up a pilot. For detailed setup instructions, see the docs.

items.title: Updated GPG Signing key for Warp Linux Releases
items.summary:
Company
Updated GPG Signing key for Warp Linux Releases
Warp|November 4, 2026
Due to precautionary measures from a security incident last week, we recently rotated our GPG signing subkey which we use to sign some of our Warp Linux artifacts.
We have no evidence of misuse by unauthorized parties but we’re doing this out of an abundance of caution.
Follow the instructions below to get our updated public key.
Ubuntu / Debian (if using our package repo)
Shwget -qO- https://releases.warp.dev/linux/keys/warp.asc | sudo gpg --dearmor --yes -o /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/warpdotdev.gpg
sudo apt update
If you configured our apt repository manually (following our docs) instead of installing the .deb, the key is at /etc/apt/keyrings/warpdotdev.gpg; use that path instead.
Arch
Shsudo pacman-key -r "linux-maintainers@warp.dev"
sudo pacman -Syu
Fedora 43 and newer
Import the updated key, then upgrade. Fedora 43's rpm updates the existing key in place, so there is nothing to remove first:
Shsudo rpm --import https://releases.warp.dev/linux/keys/warp.asc
sudo dnf upgrade warp-terminal
Fedora 42 and older, RHEL, CentOS, Rocky, AlmaLinux
Remove the old key before importing the new one. Importing while the old key is still installed can appear to succeed without changing anything.
Shsudo rpm -e --allmatches gpg-pubkey-d60f803f-65c9382c
sudo rpm --import https://releases.warp.dev/linux/keys/warp.asc
sudo dnf upgrade --refresh warp-terminal
openSUSE / SLE
Remove the old key before importing the new one. Importing while the old key is still installed can appear to succeed without changing anything. Then refresh zypper and update:
Shsudo rpm -e --allmatches gpg-pubkey-d60f803f-65c9382c
sudo rpm --import https://releases.warp.dev/linux/keys/warp.asc
sudo zypper refresh && sudo zypper update warp-terminal
Verify the key
Our public key is published at https://releases.warp.dev/linux/keys/warp.asc. To check its fingerprints:
Shwget -qO- https://releases.warp.dev/linux/keys/warp.asc | gpg --show-keys --with-subkey-fingerprints

items.title: Why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
items.summary:
Deep AgentsConceptual Guide
Why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
Gowri HarishSineha ManivannanNovember 3, 20268minGo back to blogCreate agentsCreate agentsShare
Key Takeaways
Human expertise defines what good looks like. Domain experts bring the judgment needed to identify quality, explain why an interaction succeeds or fails, and uncover gaps in automated evaluations.
Context is essential to evaluating agents. Reviewing the full conversation, including earlier messages and tool calls, helps teams understand not just what an agent answered, but how and why it got there.
Human feedback becomes the foundation for better evals. Structured scores and reviewer comments can be used to calibrate LLM judges, improve online evaluators, and build golden datasets for continuous testing.
As agents take on longer, more complex tasks, evaluating their performance means looking beyond the final AI-generated answer. Human review plays an important role in agent development: it helps teams define what good looks like, evaluate performance in context, and turn expert judgment into data that drives improvement.
In this blog, we explore three principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows: defining quality through expert judgment, evaluating agents in context, and turning human feedback into reusable evaluation data that drives continuous improvement.
What is an agent trace?
An agent trace is a record of everything an agent did in a single attempt: user messages, model responses, tool calls, and intermediate steps. Teams use traces to debug behavior, score quality, and decide what to fix.
Often an engineer or an online evaluator flags a trace when something looks off. The flag is a signal, not an explanation. It usually is not enough to know how to change the agent.
The flagged trace goes into an annotation queue. A human reviewer opens the interaction and leaves feedback: did the agent do the right thing, and why or why not? Automation chooses what to review. The human supplies the judgment that builders act on.
In LangSmith, a queue item can be one run (a single step or span) or a thread (the full multi-turn session). With a thread, the reviewer sees the conversation the user had, instead of one step cut out of it.
Principle 1: Human perspective defines what good looks like
Each reviewer brings domain judgment the trace does not contain on its own: what “good” means in that job, what the user was trying to do, and what the agent should have done instead. This expert judgment is often highly specific to the company, role, or individual's expertise, and is a key part of building differentiated agents. Or as Snoop Dogg put in his commencement speech at CSU Long Beach: “Nobody can do you, like you do.”
When a domain expert reviews a trace, one of the most valuable parts of the review is their reason. An expert can say why an output was right or wrong, and how a high-quality agent should behave.
While reviewers can catch what automated evals miss, they also surface problems that sit beside the agent’s answer. For example, they might discover that an eval is scoring the wrong behavior, or that there is a gap in the rubric. One note in a queue can reveal a broader pattern worth fixing in the evaluator itself.
This expert feedback changes the evaluations, and ultimately how the agent is built. In an annotation queue, that perspective is stored on the run or thread as a score plus the reviewer’s reasoning, so builders can turn a single expert review into a clearer definition of quality for the next iteration.
Principle 2: Context is what makes the judgment hold up
A reviewer’s perspective is only as good as the interaction in front of them. If they only see one step from a multi-turn session, they can miss earlier messages, tool calls, and decisions that explain the final answer. That's why comprehensive HITL workflows involve reviewing the full thread.
Threads in annotation queues put the whole session in front of the reviewer. They can see what the user was trying to do, how the agent arrived at its answer, and whether that answer holds up. Editing one sentence is not the same as editing the essay that sentence belongs to.
A reply can look right on its own and still be wrong for something the user said earlier. The mistake may have happened several turns back, but only in the final message did it became obvious. As agents run longer and take more steps, that missing history gets harder to diagnose by hand.
For multi-turn agents, the unit of review should be the conversation. A thread in an annotation queue is that session as one review item, so the reviewer reads the interaction instead of assembling it.
Principle 3: Turn expert judgment into high-quality evaluation data
Building better agents depends on data that reflects what good performance actually looks like. Subject matter experts (SMEs) bring that standard, as builders usually cannot get it from automated metrics alone.
Human review is how that standard gets written down in a form the system can reuse. In practice it looks like this:
A reviewer opens a run or thread in an annotation queue and scores it against a rubric (pass/fail, 1–5, “empathy,” “correct tool,” etc.), often with a short note on why.
That labeled example becomes ground truth for that interaction: not just “bad,” but which dimension failed and what “good” would have been.
Builders use those labels in a few concrete ways:
Align an LLM judge: compare the judge’s score to the human score on the same traces. Where they disagree, update the judge prompt or rubric until they match more often.
Update online evaluators: if humans keep catching the same miss, change the evaluator that should have caught it, then re-run it on new traffic.
Build a golden dataset: promote strong human-labeled examples into a dataset and run offline experiments against them when the agent or prompt changes.
Next time an eval runs, it is scoring against criteria that came from expert review.
When that data is connected to the runs and threads it describes, builders can use it to identify failure modes, improve evaluators, refine rubrics, and build datasets for ongoing testing. The result is a feedback loop where expert knowledge becomes a reusable asset for agent development, not just a score in a review queue
Over time, this creates a reusable foundation for evaluation: expert judgment on a specific thread → structured scores and notes → better evaluators and datasets → scored evals that track the same definition of quality. The annotation is the raw material for evals that the team can run again without asking the expert every time.
Why we built threads in annotation queues
A reviewer does better work with their own expertise, the full interaction in front of them, and a way to leave feedback that a builder can use. Once an agent works across many turns and tools, one trace leaves out the context that judgment depends on.
A trajectory is another view of the conversation. It shows messages and tool calls in the order they happened, with the nested run tree and other duplicate information removed, in a readable view. The queue item is still the thread, because the thing being judged is the conversation. Reviewers read the trajectory as they annotate the thread.
Threads in annotation queues keep the review next to the interaction a person actually had. Domain experts can focus on the content of the conversation without first learning how to read a trace tree. Try out this feature yourself in LangSmith today.
Case Study: Fetch Rewards
Fetch Rewards uses annotation queues to turn human judgment into a reference point for its automated judges. Reviewers assess individual turns of the AI Rewards Assistant - an input and an output - but the transcript is only the starting point. To determine whether a response is good, they often need to investigate further. A fluent answer can still be wrong if it isn’t grounded in real data, so reviewers inspect trace metadata to see which tools the assistant called and whether its answer matches the results.
When a user asks about an offer, for example, they confirm that the assistant searched for offers and that its response accurately reflects the offer returned. They also check product-card images against the products they represent: for example, making sure a card for a 20 oz Coca-Cola doesn’t show a 2 liter bottle. Since a recommendation is useful only if the recipient can actually use it, reviewers look up the user’s offers to confirm that the suggestions were available to them.
Some cases are ambiguous: an image may be almost right, an offer technically valid but unhelpful, or an accurate response may miss the user’s intent. Reviewers weigh the evidence and document what they checked, what remained unclear, and why they assigned each score in an annotation-queue comment. Engineers then use that reasoning to identify where an automated judge’s logic differs from the human review and tune it accordingly.
Make Human Review Part of Your Agent Development Lifecycle
We believe human review is an important part of building better agents, and we've been investing in making it easier to bring that into your workflow with LangSmith.
Try reviewing your agent traces with a human reviewer. You might be surprised by the insights and useful data points you uncover! We'd love to hear what you find. Reach out to us on LinkedIn to share your discoveries.
