items.title: Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language
Enterprise Article Published
November 3, 2026 Upvote 23
+17
Praveen Venkateswaran praveenv Follow ibm-research Anupama Murthi anupamamurthi Follow ibm-research Hamid Adebayo harmedox Follow ibm-research
Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.
Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.
Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.
Why decks are hard for small models
A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.
It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.
It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.
There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.
Build it like a human: a designer and a coder
Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:
The designer reads the plan and writes a structured JSON brief: the palette, the type system, and for each slide its layout, its exact content and a short design rationale.
The coder takes one slide's spec from the brief and writes the pptxgenjs JavaScript that draws it, preceded by its reasoning.
Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.
We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.
Synthesizing decks and their reasoning
There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.
Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:
"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."
The coder reasons about geometry:
"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."
The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.
The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.
What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.
Steering a deck in plain English
Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:
## Rollout plan
- March: pilot with two teams
- May: security review complete
- July: rollout to all of engineering
- September: company-wide launch
- November: first adoption review
[[make this a timeline]]
The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.
The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.
Category
Example directive
Layout
[[make this a timeline]]
Tone
[[be candid, no spin]]
Audience
[[this is for the board]]
Order
[[lead with the ask]]
Leaving out
[[no pricing]]
Emphasis
[[highlight the headline number]]
Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.
Building a check-and-repair harness
Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.
Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.
First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.
The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.
Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).
To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.
Evaluation
We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.
Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.
Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.
PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.
What's next
The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.
We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.
What we learned
Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:
Put the reasoning in the data. Training on why a choice was made, including what was rejected, teaches more than the choice alone.
Fix the examples before adding a rule. When the teacher got something wrong, our first instinct was to add a rule to its prompt, and that rarely helped. The teacher copied its reference decks far more than it followed instructions, so fixing the reference was what actually changed its output.
Make repairs safe by default. A fix that's kept only when it measurably helps can run on every output.
Build the checker first. It's what makes the data trustworthy and the outputs safe to ship.

items.title: Service Accounts
items.summary: Amp now has Service Accounts. A service account is a workspace-owned account that's not tied to a single user. Service accounts are created by workspace admins. They have their own API keys and third-party credentials. Each thread created under a service account can be viewed by other members of the workspace. These threads are multiplayer too, so workspace members can send messages in them. Since anyone in the workspace can drive a service account's threads, make sure to only assign credentials to it that you would be happy bestowing on all workspace members. When to Use Service Accounts Service accounts fit any work that belongs to the team rather than to one person. For example, threads with automations that workspace members want to have access to, even if the person who set them up is on vacation. We've found two patterns where service accounts work especially well. Codebase Review and Maintenance Reviewing every pull request or keeping docs accurate is work that belongs to the team, not to a single user. When a service account owns that work, anyone on the team can step into its threads and steer them. Here are some example prompts for setting that up via Puck: Trigger a Workspace-Scoped Orb for New GitHub PRs Hey Puck, let's set up a listener so that any new PR that lands triggers a new orb and reviews the changes. **The orbs should be owned by the whole team, not just me.** Amp knows how to set up github PR listeners like this. Because the user asked for the threads to be owned by the workspace and not by the user, Amp will use a service account for these threads. A Recurring Review of Public Docs Hey Puck, **start a workspace-owned thread** which scans our public documentation every 24hr and checks it's up to date. If you find an issue, @ mention the person responsible for the change. Service accounts are useful for continuous clean up and maintenance tasks like this, which are shared by a team rather than an individual. Programmatic Work There's work that starts from a script, like a CI job that spawns a thread via amp -ox every time a build fails. By using a service account's API key for that amp invocation, the thread it starts belongs to the service account instead of whoever set up the pipeline. Here's an example: A Review Bot Running in CI run_tests if tests_failed; then AMP_API_KEY=<SERVICE_ACCOUNT_API_KEY> \ amp -ox "Tests failed. Is this a real regression or a flaky test?" fi CI and programmatic invocation of Amp is another useful use case for service-accounts, which should not be tied to any individual user.

items.title: Transformers Model Integration Contracts
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Transformers Model Integration Contracts
Published
November 3, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 18
+12
Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow
On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention
(SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens.
During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict.
Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.
When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged
it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built
around it.
Why bugs reach main
Transformers supports over 750
model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus
200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also
test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention
kernels.
The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on
real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs
busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a
regression, it may already be in main.
Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small
model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower
layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files
unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests"
against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our
CPU study,
the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint
is 1,227 MB.
This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU
runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.
Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-*
checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and
checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5
bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.
Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a
chance to catch bugs before they reach main.
Introducing Model Integration Contracts
transformers-mic is a proposed
standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has
three parts:
a fixture: the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned
a usage path: a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the
model, such as generating text or running a training step
baselines: the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a
human
The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the
baselines.
A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint:
compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected
results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.
For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital
of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading
the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:
inputs = tokenizer("The capital of France is", return_tensors="pt")
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=4, do_sample=False)
new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:]
print(tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens=True))
It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies
that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full
usage.md.
A fleet dataset
on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions
used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it
used, so we can reproduce it later.
On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.
The UMT5 regression
We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small
UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026
until its fix on September 28.
Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training
loss by about 0.20.
One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path.
Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only
helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.
We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check
failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step
took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.
The replay results
and the CI demo
have the measurements and reproduction details.
How models are shrunk
The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer
layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no
use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.
The recipe now has four steps:
Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce
hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds,
including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers.
Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible.
We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the ModelTester in
test_modeling_<model>.py already picks a small config by hand, so we
take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name.
Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and
input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte.
Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test.
Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change
the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training
it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and
check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds.
Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable
outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each
supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses
it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR.
We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the
conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint.
The full recipe
has more detail.
The Llama 4 Scout shrink report
shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7
million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from
48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.
Building MICs with agents
Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new
model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure
the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed
expectations require human review.
To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:
pip install "transformers-mic[runtime]" "hf-doc-builder @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/doc-builder.git"
hf auth login
tmic run org/model --local-only --fixtures-only --no-history --bill-to ''
It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your
machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything.
For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed
to your own account (--bill-to ''). The
CLI docs
cover the individual steps.
We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge
case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from
model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the
coverage space.
Random vs Overfit
With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in
the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.
So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green".
We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible
in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study,
the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit
fixtures caught all 24.
That gives us two ways to build the weights:
Start with random weights and a fixed seed.
Overfit on a few examples, like "The capital of France is" => "Paris".
The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic
faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit
version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper
checkpoint exposed.
So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need
better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one
more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison
has the results for both.
Open questions
As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI
reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on
things we haven't measured yet:
How many real bugs does it catch on PRs, not just in replays?
How often does it send us chasing false alarms?
How much work do baseline reviews take?
We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only
show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.
Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use.
When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay
it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their
coverage is accounted for.
Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a
developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on
that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.
Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the
coverage space, try
the tmic workflow,
and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

items.title: 让改进有迹可循：Storage Agent Family Eval 工程实践
items.summary: 原创 火山引擎存储 2026-11-03 18:00 北京 我们在上一篇文章《Storage Agent Family: Agent 时代，重构云存储的“人机交互”》中，介绍了云存储智能助手家族 Storage Agent Family ——一组部署在云端的智能助手，可以帮助用户查询云存储资源配置、估算扩容成本、排查访问故障等。实际生产环境中，用户需要它们准确理解意图、查清真实资源状态、调用合适工具，并在安全边界内完成任务。 但问题也随之而来。为让 Agent 更好用，团队会不断修改提示词（Prompt）、技能（Skill）、命令行工具（CLI）和底层执行框架（Harness）。这些模块环环相扣，改一处往往牵动全局：今天修好 A 场景，明天可能就破坏原本正常的 B 场景。如果上线前只靠人工随意测试几句，或只看最终回答是否通顺，既难以判断改动是否产生副作用，又难以在出现问题时定位卡在哪一步。 为此，我们围绕 Storage Agent Family 建立了一套持续评测与改进机制：通过离线回归实验检验每次改动后的回答与工具调用过程，结合调用链（Trace）定位具体模块的问题，再将线上真实对话中暴露的典型问题持续沉淀至评测集。这样，每次版本改动的效果都清晰可量化，既能在发版前及时拦截场景退化，也能推动多款存储 Agent 的任务完成率与回答准确率持续提升。 01 | 如何构建覆盖任务、行为和安全的评测体系 先看一个日常高频场景。用户给出目标云盘 ID，向块存储智能助手（EBS Agent）提问：“我想给指定云盘在原有大小的基础上再扩容 100 GiB 可以吗？扩容后我每个月要多花多少钱？” 要给出可靠答案，Agent 需先调用只读工具查清该云盘现有的容量、类型和计费方式，再核对扩容上限规则，并调用询价接口计算差价。 除此之外，遇到异常或高风险情况还需严格把关：例如用户未提供云盘 ID 时会先追问；工具未查到数据时不能编造价格；涉及修改配置的操作需先识别风险并请用户确认（只读场景下仅提供操作指引）；删除资源、越权访问这类高危请求则直接拒绝。 可以看到，即使是一句简单的日常提问，背后也同时考验意图理解、工具调用与安全边界。因此在准备评测集时，业务团队会先理清 Agent 的能力边界，再从两个维度设计测试题：既关注用户通常如何提问（用户意图），也关注底层会调用哪些技能和工具（Skill 链路），以覆盖完整的执行路径。 举个例子，针对“访问失败排查”这类常见问题，评测集里不仅有查网络、查权限、查流控这些正常排障流程，还会专门放进一批“难题”——如故意不提供资源 ID、模拟工具报错，或要求直接修改线上配置、越权删除资源。 这样，评测集既检查任务能否完成，也检查遇到异常或越界请求时，Agent 的响应是否符合预期。 存储 Agent 评测集结构：按用户意图、Skill 链路与边界条件组织 当评测集同时考察“任务完成”“数据真实”与“操作安全”时，只看回答是否通顺，或只给出一个笼统的总分远远不够。例如，在上述扩容询价场景中，如果 Agent 回答流畅，却忽略已知的云盘 ID、也没有查询真实云盘规格，表面看回答不错，实际上却并没有完成任务。 为此，评测采用 LLM 评估器与 Code 评估器相结合的方式：前者围绕任务理解与回应聚焦、事实依据与可信度、任务完成度、能力边界与操作安全、表达清晰度与可行动性五个维度，评估语义与过程质量（涉及报表生成任务时，额外评估报告质量）；后者通过代码与正则规则，直接检查空回答、运行报错、工具调用约束等可程序化验证的行为。 当然，由大模型评估也可能出现误判。因此，团队会定期使用人工标注样本校对评估器的打分结果，对存在争议的评分进行人工复核，持续提升自动打分与实际业务判断的一致性。 存储 Agent 评估器职责分工：LLM 评估器与 Code 评估器 评测集与评估器就绪后，每当研发团队为优化某类场景修改提示词、技能、工具或执行框架时，需让待测版本跑一遍这些任务，来检验这次改动是带来正向提升，还是引发退化。 02 | 如何让每次 Agent 改动都有据可查 日常迭代中，团队依托自研评测工作台开展离线回归实验，持续验证每次改动的效果。 整体架构上，回归实验由三个角色协同完成：评测工作台负责版本与基线管理、实验分片调度、Code 评估器规则校验、红线判定与版本对比；云端隔离沙箱负责并发运行完整的待测 Agent，产出真实回答、报表与结构化调用记录；火山引擎日志服务 TLS AgentLoop 负责 Trace 调用链与 Session 会话分析、LLM 多维评估打分及线上会话质量分析，并将得分与调用链证据回传至评测工作台。 评测工作台、云端隔离沙箱与 TLS AgentLoop 协同关系 2.1 准备可追溯实验并在隔离沙箱中运行 团队先将代码、提示词、技能和工具打包为一个待测版本，再选择评测集与运行环境。任务会自动保留对应的评测集快照、评估器版本和评分配置，使实验结果可追溯到具体条件。 评测集与运行环境确定后，评测工作台将核心任务与边界用例分配到云端隔离沙箱，并发运行完整的 Agent 流程——让它实际走完“理解问题、选择技能、调用 CLI 工具、处理返回结果并生成回答或报告”的全过程。 如需对比新旧两个版本，平台会自动核对双方的题库版本、评估器版本、评分配置和运行环境，确保二者在同一基准下进行对比。 2.2 采集运行轨迹并结合双层规则评分 沙箱运行结束后，系统收集每道题的实际回答、原始 Trace 和生成的报告；同时，将问题、预期结果与行为约束、实际回答，以及从 Trace 中提取的结构化工具调用记录写入 TLS AgentLoop 评测集进行打分。完整的原始 Trace 则单独归档保存，供后续排查细节时随时调取。由于“沙箱运行”与“评估打分”相互独立，后续调整评分规则时，直接基于已保存的运行结果重评即可，无需重跑沙箱。 评分时，许多云存储任务依赖实时的云资源状态，因此评估器会结合测试环境当时的真实资源数据、工具调用记录与最终结论来综合评分。 不同业务可按需配置 LLM 评估器与 Code 评估器的权重及通过门槛；其中安全红线与核心完成度均实行一票否决制，任意一项不达标即直接判为“未通过”。 TLS AgentLoop 评测集数据项（上）与 LLM 评估器按维度打分（下） 2.3 查看评测报告与版本对比 以块存储 EBS Agent 的一轮版本迭代为例，在包含 124 道用例的回归实验中，综合得分由 88.7 分提升至 95.1 分（+6.4），通过用例数由 104 道增加到 122 道。 与综合得分变化相比，更值得关注的是任务完成度，由 55.4 分提升至 92.2 分。逐题对比显示，多道此前未通过的题目，在新版中都能主动调用工具查清配置并给出完整结论。 版本对比总览：综合得分由 88.7 提升至 95.1，任务完成度由 55.4 提升至 92.2 03 | 如何从一次失分定位到具体的 Skill 问题 评测报告和对比总览能够直观指出哪些任务表现不足、哪些维度发生变化。但要将分数差异转化为有效的研发改进，团队还需沿着未通过的题目回溯实际执行过程：当时 Agent 在沙箱中执行了什么？问题究竟来自知识库、Skill、CLI 工具，还是执行框架？ 3.1 下钻到单题评分、版本对比与 Trace 调用链 回到前文提到的 EBS Agent 云盘扩容与计费咨询题（“我想给指定云盘在原有大小的基础上再扩容 100 GiB 可以吗？扩容后我每个月要多花多少钱？”）。在该测试场景中，用户已在上下文中提供目标云盘 ID，且 Agent 具备查询云盘配置和调用询价接口的只读权限。 但在旧版本的回归实验中，此题被判为“未通过”，任务完成度为 0 分。查看单题评分详情与 Trace调用链发现：旧版 Agent 忽略已有的云盘 ID，未主动调用工具查询目标云盘的现有配置，而是直接把问题抛回用户，要求用户手动提供本可通过只读工具查到的云盘容量、类型和计费方式。 通过对该题 Bad Case 的评分理由与 Trace 记录进行归因分析，团队定位到问题是源于 Skill 拆解指引缺失，随即在对应 Skill 中补齐调用链路要求：先通过只读工具核查目标云盘现有配置，再结合扩容规则与询价接口测算费用。 修改完成后重新发起回归实验，通过单题并排对比视图与“查看 Trace”中可以清晰看到变化：新版 Agent 依次完成边界判断、提交执行计划、激活技能、读取目标云盘对应的扩容规则并核验容量上限，随后在沙箱中通过 ebs-cli 实查该云盘的现有配置（1024 GiB ESSD_FlexPL），再根据该云盘的按量计费模式调用 CalculatePriceV2 获取扩容前后的小时单价并估算月度费用差额，在不触发任何写操作的前提下给出完整结论。 该题由此从“未通过”转为“通过”，任务完成度由 0 分提升至 100 分（任务理解 95 分、事实依据 95 分、能力边界 100 分、表达清晰度 95 分，Code 评估器各项检查全部通过），并与同批修复的其他题目一起使整轮实验的任务完成度由 55.4 分提升至 92.2 分。 EBS 云盘扩容题前后版本变化摘要、任务完成度对比与关联 Trace 调用链详情 3.2 用可观测链路定位知识、Skill、CLI 与 Harness 问题 无论是在回归实验中排查失分原因，还是在日常运行中分析异常会话，TLS AgentLoop 的观测看板、会话分析（Session）和调用链视图（Trace & Span，用于记录一次请求中各次模型推理与工具调用的层级、参数与耗时）都提供完整的执行记录。研发人员可逐层核对输入消息、检索结果、工具调用参数及返回信息，定位具体原因后，再针对性修复对应模块： 知识或检索问题：知识文档缺失或未检索到产品规格、错误码与排障步骤，导致回答缺依据 → 由业务团队补充知识文档或调整检索策略。 Skill 或 CLI 工具问题：任务拆解指引不清，或 CLI 工具返回信息不完整、报错提示难定位 → 调整 Skill 提示词或优化 CLI 工具的参数与返回格式。 执行框架（Harness）问题：上下文管理、会话状态传递或安全围栏拦截异常 → 在公共执行底座统一修复。 另外，如果只盯着固定的测试题修改代码，很容易变成“背题应试”。因此团队修复 Bad Case 时有一条硬性要求：必须修改通用的 Skill 逻辑、工具接口或补充知识库，不能专门针对某道题写死提示词，同时还会用不同问法的变体题和线上真实对话进行交叉验证。 04 | 如何让真实用户问题持续推动 Agent 进化 离线回归评测能帮助团队在上线前守住基本盘，但固定的评测集很难穷尽千变万化的真实提问。Agent 进入实际使用后，还需结合真实用户会话持续评估任务质量。 围绕线上真实数据，评估重点覆盖四个方面：用户的任务是否完成、结论是否有依据、多轮交互是否有效、是否出现不必要的拒答或越界行为。运行耗时和工具报错提供基础监控信息，人工抽检与自动评估则进一步判断任务质量。 在线上评估中，我们采用“人工标注校准、LLM 评估扩面”的方式推进：先由业务与 QA 抽样复核真实会话、校准评估器标准，再通过 LLM 评估器扩大线上质量检查的覆盖范围。 线上评估不仅直接检验真实使用场景的质量，也让团队能够持续积累日常暴露的真实问题。结合当前实践与持续建设机制，经确认的线上异常会话与典型运维工单，在指导知识、Skill、CLI 和 Harness 修复的同时，再经筛选、去重、隐私脱敏和业务复核（补充预期结果与测试条件）后，作为新增样本回流至评测集，进入下一轮回归实验。 Storage Agent Family 质量演进闭环：从线上真实会话与工单回流至下一轮回归 衡量一个云存储 Agent 的质量，关键看它能否基于真实资源状态做出判断、选对工具与执行路径，并严格遵守权限和安全边界。 围绕这一目标，Storage Agent Family 将业务要求沉淀为可重复执行的评测用例、可回溯的运行轨迹和可对比的版本实验，在持续的验证与反馈中稳步提升任务表现。 跳转微信打开

items.title: Artifacts
items.summary: Agents in Amp can now collaborate with you in Artifacts. These are documents that belong to a single thread and that the agent, you, and your teammates can all edit. Here are two examples from our real threads. This one is from Nicolay's thread, where he asked whether Amp wastes model calls while it waits on a long shell command. The agent went through 60 of our threads and wrote up what it found: how much the waiting costs, why, and a plan to fix it in two steps. Reading it gets you up to speed on the problem before you decide what to build: Artifacts also work well for pulling together what several threads found. In Beyang's thread, a user had asked for a rendered preview of Markdown files in the Changes pane. Beyang had the agent build two versions at once, each in its own orb. When both reported back, the agent put them side by side in one artifact, with what each costs and which one to ship first: You don't have to ask for one. When the agent has something for you to read, like a plan, a report, or notes from a call, it writes an artifact instead of a long reply. The artifact opens next to the thread. Edit it like any document: tick off a checklist, fix a table, rewrite a paragraph. When the agent comes back to it, it reads your edits first and works them in instead of writing over them. Open Views → Artifacts in any thread, or just ask Amp to write one. More in the docs.

items.title: Hierarchical budgets: manage AI spend the way your company is organized
items.summary:
Today we’re introducing a new way for enterprises to manage AI spend: hierarchical budgets. Enterprise administrators can allocate ACU budgets to department leaders, who can then distribute and approve usage limits for sub-teams. Now, teams can align Devin usage with the way your company is organized: one centralized account limit, group budgets for business units, dedicated budgets for projects, and per-user limits inside each budget.
Hierarchical budgets build on our work developing efficiency-based cost controls, to keep your most productive engineers unblocked while giving your team more visibility and granular control over AI spend.
How it works: a tree of shared ACU pools
Every enterprise has one Account budget at the root. Child budgets sit under it, up to three levels deep. A budget can hold one org or several, and each org belongs to exactly one budget.
Each budget has:
a limit: the ACUs that the budget and everything under it can use in a monthly window
an optional temporary limit: a bump that lasts until the end of the current window
a parent budget: the limit is controlled by the parent administrator
its own user limits: tiers and per-user overrides that apply inside that budget
its own people: who can draw from it, adjust child limits, and share permissions with more people
Here are two ways enterprises use them today.
1. Departments with delegated administration
Admins of large accounts get overwhelmed trying to micromanage individual user limits. Permissions on a budget let its owner delegate one layer down.
Consider Acme Corp, an enterprise software team with 10 departments. Alice in Central IT sets each department’s total, while each department head manages the limits of their own orgs. This means department managers can make their own child budgets, set budget limits, and manage the tiers and limits of their users.
Bob runs Engineering and can set limits on any budget under Engineering. Limit increase requests within Bob’s organization route to Bob. For a busy launch week, Bob might grant the Payments team a temporary limit increase of 5,000 ACUs, from 10,000 to 15,000 ACUs for the current window. Meanwhile, the engineering orgs underneath Bob are still bound by the combined limit of 30,000 ACUs, because Bob’s administration grant is granular. This means that each department head does not have visibility into other department budgets, so if Engineering needs more ACUs this month, Bob can file a request with Alice for a bump.
Bob's Budgets page: only Engineering and its children. Payments shows 15,000 ACUs this window with its temporary allocation.
Bob gives Payments a temporary 5,000-ACU bump for this monthly window.
Manage access on the Engineering budget.
2. A dedicated bucket for a sprint
Every Acme developer gets a monthly ACU allowance. For a security hardening initiative, Acme sets aside a dedicated pool of ACUs, in which a small group of security engineers runs a swarm of Devin sessions to find and fix vulnerabilities across the codebase in parallel.
Alice keeps the everyday orgs in a Developer tools budget with a 200-ACU default tier. She creates a Security hardening budget with a 5,000-ACU limit and gives it a more generous default tier with efficiency-based approvals.
Carol is a developer with access to both budgets. She can use up to 1,000 ACUs in the Security hardening org, and up to 200 ACUs in the Developer tools orgs.
The hardening project has a budget ceiling. The whole initiative is limited to 5,000 ACUs.
Trackable spend. Carol has access to separate pools of spend, but to spend ACUs in the Security hardening budget, she has to actually be working on security hardening.
Carol's My Analytics page across all her budgets.
Budgets let you set limits at the right level. Carol has 200 ACUs in her discretionary budget. This limit is intended to help accelerate her day-to-day work. She starts with 1,000 ACUs in the dedicated project budget, where the ACUs she spends can be directly attributed to project delivery, and her usage can be audited and graded based on efficiency.
Get started
We believe budgets are the best way to cap and understand total spend. For customers on a Devin Enterprise plan, you can use hierarchical budgets today: just read the Budgets docs and open Enterprise Settings > Usage Policies > Budgets.
If your team is interested in getting started with hierarchical budgets in Devin, please contact us.

items.title: Introducing the Grid Protectors Program
items.summary:
OpenAI
November 2, 2026
Global AffairsCompany
Introducing the Grid Protectors Program
Launching a national program to help our future compute campuses support reliable, affordable electricity.
Today we’re launching the Grid Protectors Program, a national effort to support affordable, reliable electricity for families and businesses in the communities where we build. Working with utilities, regulators and policymakers, we’ll develop arrangements for our future campuses to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain.
Whether it’s heating homes during a northern cold snap or running air conditioning through a southern heat wave, families need reliable electricity. Our goal is to make campus flexibility a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most.
With U.S. data center capacity projected to exceed 100 gigawatts by 2030⁠(opens in a new window), we have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to strengthen the electric grid by building campuses that can adjust their power use when communities need it most.
Through Grid Protectors, our ambition is to make this kind of flexibility a core part of how we build and operate future campuses. That means designing facilities to reduce electricity use when needed and working with utilities to agree on how much demand can be reduced, how quickly and for how long. The arrangements will differ by location, and we will share additional commitments as they are finalized.
Depending on local needs and the equipment available, we will also work with grid operators to supply power from on-site generation or storage, and use batteries and power controls to smooth changes in demand.
Power lines, substations and other grid infrastructure builds are a fixed cost whether demand is low or high. By using more electricity when the grid has room and reducing our use when it is under strain, we can help pay for that infrastructure while limiting the need for costly upgrades to meet peak demand. That can help keep costs down for other customers.
America needs more electricity to support economic growth, and AI is becoming a significant part of that demand. Families and small businesses should not be asked to subsidize a compute campus’s electricity needs. We’ve always been committed to paying our own energy costs, including the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve our campuses. Large computing facilities should pay their costs and help utilities manage the systems they depend on.
A model in Georgia
For our planned Effingham County campus, we have committed to pay the full infrastructure and electric-service costs required to serve the project. Once the campus is operating, we can reduce the power we draw during times of need, helping preserve electricity for other customers.
Our agreement with Georgia Power also includes⁠(opens in a new window) up to 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response, freeing up power to help keep air conditioning running in hundreds of thousands of homes during extreme heat. For scale, that is equivalent to the average electricity demand of roughly 700,000 households. That’s more households than Washington, D.C., and Boston combined.
These compute facilities are much different than data centers built even a few years ago, allowing us to be flexible in our power demand.
This means we can turn down our demand so that families, small businesses, and other ratepayers will continue to have power. Building grid assets is expensive and Georgia Power says this flexibility can reduce the amount of new generation it needs to build to serve future growth. Although the campus is still in development, we intend for Effingham to serve as a pilot for Grid Protectors, building on an agreement that already provides a model for future campuses.
Imagine a restaurant in a vacation town. It needs enough tables and kitchen space for the busy season, but it has to pay for that capacity year-round. Regular customers help keep it in use and cover the bills when tourism slows. We are proposing to be that regular customer.
Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times. Our compute campuses need power year-round. With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest. We still need to pay the costs our campuses create; the goal is for other customers to benefit, too.
Our agreement also contributes to Georgia Power’s broader plan to lower costs for customers. The utility projects approximately $950 million in annual customer savings beginning in 2029⁠(opens in a new window) from its portfolio of large-load agreements and expected growth, including Project Camellia. It estimates a benefit of at least $15 a month for a typical residential customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours.
Looking forward
The Georgia agreement is a starting point. At OpenAI, through our Grid Protectors program, we see an opportunity to help communities keep the lights on even in times of emergency and high demand. We will work with utilities, regulators and policymakers to develop practical arrangements for the campuses we build in the future—arrangements that reflect local grid needs, help campuses support the grid when it is under pressure, and pay the costs we create. Long-term contracts and financial assurances can protect other customers if a project is delayed, reduced or canceled.
Flexibility cannot replace investment in new energy supply and transmission. Alongside those investments, our Grid Protectors program can help make the grid more reliable and protect families and small businesses from bearing the costs of AI infrastructure. That is the standard we want our compute campuses to meet.

items.title: Kimi 发布游戏开发与创意工作解决方案
items.summary: 原创 K3.1 Pro 2026-11-02 17:21 天津 从创意落地到持续迭代 今天，Kimi 发布「游戏开发与创意工作解决方案」。 基于 Kimi K3.1 Pro 模型、Kimi Code 与 Kimi Work 系列 Agent 产品，以及 Unity、Unreal Engine、Blender 等专业工具插件，我们希望帮助游戏团队更快验证玩法创意、推进工程和美术制作，并将发行与运营中的玩家反馈带回下一轮迭代。 游戏创意的价值，往往要到玩家真正操作时才能判断：策划文档能说明规则，却难以回答操作是否顺手、奖励是否明确、节奏是否吸引人。若这些问题在关卡、代码和资产大量完成后才暴露，调整就会牵动更多人和预算。 Kimi 希望帮助团队尽早做出范围明确的可玩版本，再根据真实体验决定如何投入。 左右滑动，查看全部 → 游戏行业的业务挑战 游戏开发的第一道门槛，是创意验证的成本。 一个玩法是否有趣，需要真正玩起来才能判断。但制作原型需要投入时间和人力，团队往往只能优先验证少数想法。如何降低单次尝试的成本，在有限时间内验证更多创意？ Unity《2026 Game Development Report》显示，52% 的受访开发者优先选择小规模项目来降低风险，67% 将原型阶段控制在三个月以内。更审慎的研发投入、更紧凑的验证周期，让原型制作效率变得更加重要。 Kimi 游戏解决方案，可以帮助游戏团队高效制作项目原型，在有限时间内探索和比较更多玩法方向，从而做出更准确的业务判断。 第二道门槛，来自跨岗位和跨工具的协作。策划需求，需要变成工程任务；美术资产，也需要符合引擎规范。AI 若只生成一段文字或一张图，仍需要团队花大量时间进行适配和创作，才能搬进原有流程。 Kimi 解决方案可以直接衔接团队现有的工作流，操作专业工具与编辑器、修改现有工程，并交付可继续编辑的文件和清晰的操作记录，方便团队审阅、协作和推进后续工作。 Kimi 游戏开发与创意工作解决方案 Kimi 可以从团队的实际目标出发，推动创意从设想走向实践。 例如，策划想验证「在三消玩法中加入可自由组合的规则卡」是否有趣，但仅凭玩法说明，很难感受规则叠加后带来的策略变化。Kimi 会围绕这一目标，梳理规则卡的组合方式及其对消除策略、得分与反馈的影响，再将其拆解为交互、数值、界面和视听等具体制作任务，制作可试玩的原型。 这样，策划、开发和美术就能围绕同一个原型，边玩边讨论，减少创意在沟通与交接中的理解偏差。 结合模型能力与专业工具，Kimi 还可以将这种工作方式的变化，延伸到游戏开发、制作等更多环节。 ➊ 模型能力与插件支持 一个游戏项目往往横跨多个团队，涉及策划文档、截图、代码、3D 资产等多种项目文件。 Kimi 可以为这一复杂流程提供支持：模型负责理解输入、规划并执行任务；Kimi Code 侧重代码开发与修改，Kimi Work 则可承接跨文件、多步骤的制作任务。生成的成果可供团队继续编辑和完善，衔接后续制作。 针对不同团队的需求，我们也提供了覆盖日常办公、代码开发与 API 集成的系列产品，供大家选择： Kimi 可以为这一复杂流程提供支持：模型负责理解输入、规划并执行任务；Kimi Code 侧重代码开发与修改，Kimi Work 则可承接跨文件、多步骤的制作任务。生成的成果可供团队继续编辑和完善，衔接后续制作。 此外，Kimi 还可通过插件与工具调用连接 Blender、Unity、Unreal Engine 等专业软件，直接操作现有工程，协助完成游戏开发与 3D 创作等任务。 ➋ 正式立项前：用 Godot 把想法做成可试玩原型 游戏立项前，团队往往需要快速验证新玩法，但开发资源未必充足。借助 Kimi，缺少编程经验的策划或创意团队也能在 1–2 天内做出可试玩原型。先验证玩法，再决定是否投入。 比如，团队想制作一款 2.5D 动作游戏的原型，可以提供参考图和视频，说明预期的场景氛围与玩法机制。Kimi 通过多模态能力理解参考素材中的关键视觉元素，再使用 Godot 游戏引擎搭建可试玩 Demo，呈现雨夜光影、地面积水和灯笼等场景细节，并实现挥剑、闪避和格挡等核心玩法。 制作过程中，Kimi 还可以实际运行游戏，结合渲染画面和试玩录像，检查视觉效果与功能是否达到要求。发现问题后，自主修改并重新验证，在交付前完成多轮迭代，让团队拿到的首个版本更接近预期。 有了可试玩原型，团队就能围绕实际体验展开评审：雨夜中的战斗辨识度、挥剑打击感，以及闪避与格挡的攻防体验。团队可以据此不断调整和复测，验证核心玩法是否成立，再决定是否扩展关卡与敌人类型。 ➌ 美术资产适配：让 Blender 资产从概念走向游戏场景 美术资产进入游戏场景，要经过比概念呈现更严格的检查：角色多视角是否一致，模型有无穿插，纹理和隐藏文字是否有缺陷，资源规格能否满足引擎预算。 Kimi 可以协助完成上述检查与初步调整：模型通过多模态理解，结合多视角视频与截图判断空间关系，发现并定位比例、穿插和材质问题；再将调整方案转化为脚本，借助本地 Agent 操作专业软件，完成初步修改。 通过 Blender 插件，Kimi 可以直接操作软件，协助美术团队搭建、预览和修改场景。团队既可以提供现有工程与资产，让它完成摆放、组合和布局调整；也可以提供参考图片或视频，附上制作要求，让它从零建模、组装资产并搭建场景，还原参考中的整体形态与空间布局。 以建筑场景为例，根据美术团队提供的资产或参考图片及制作要求，Kimi 会在软件里先确定建筑的整体形态与空间布局，再逐步完善结构、材质和灯光；复杂建筑则拆分为不同构件，分步搭建与细化。搭建过程中，通过多视角预览检查模型比例、穿插与材质表现，及时发现并修正问题，提升首版交付的完成度与质量。美术团队可在此基础上继续打磨，把握最终风格与质量，将更多精力投入设计判断与细节表现，减少基础搭建和反复排查的工作量。 ▲Kimi K3.1 Pro 使用 Blender 构建了一座机场室内雨林山谷场景，并制作了一段 17.5 秒、1920×1080 分辨率、60 fps 的 3D 建模展示视频。使用工具：Blender、Python、Geometry Nodes（几何节点）、Cycles（渲染引擎）、Pillow、NumPy 和 FFmpeg。使用的外部素材：来自 Poly Haven 的 4K HDRI 环境贴图 "Kloofendal 48d Partly Cloudy (Pure Sky)"，由 Greg Zaal 和 Jarod Guest 创作，采用 CC0 许可协议，用于天空照明和环境反射。 ▲Kimi K3.1 Pro 在 Blender 中构建了一个可交互的、基于浏览器的 3D 体验，打造了一座大教堂的内部场景。该场景约包含 330 万个三角面，并为 8,368 个组件制作了动画效果，呈现出肋拱穹顶、石雕塑像，以及色彩鲜明的彩绘玻璃光影。使用的外部素材：来自 Poly Haven 的石材纹理（CC0 许可） ；Mylius 拍摄的彩绘玻璃照片（CC BY-SA 3.0 许可）。 ➍ 游戏开发：把 Agent 带入 Unity 与 Unreal Engine 的现有工程 进入正式开发后，团队面对的是已有工程、既定架构和不断变化的需求。 一个看似简单的功能，可能同时影响角色状态、界面、存档和关卡逻辑；一个完整的 3D 场景，也要兼顾空间关系、视觉效果、物理交互与运行性能。工程越复杂，模块之间的依赖越多，问题就越难定位和解决。 面对这类牵一发而动全身的工程问题，Kimi 可以在获得工程文件和必要权限后，先梳理代码结构、场景层级和模块依赖，找到真正需要修改的位置，再借助插件在 Unity、Unreal Engine 等编辑器中完成具体操作。 改动完成后，Kimi 会结合问题复现、日志和运行数据验证效果，并根据结果继续调整。交付时保留代码差异和验证记录，方便工程师检查功能、性能与兼容性。 围绕这套工作流程，我们在内部探索了几类用法： Kimi + Unity：从网页试玩走向专业开发。可玩 Demo 只是开始，要走向正式上线，还需进一步完善工程，以支撑后续的调试、打磨与持续迭代。Kimi 模型与 Unity 中国推出的游戏开发智能体 Tuanjie Codely Agent 及团结引擎协同，将需求理解、工程实现与测试迭代串联起来：Kimi 模型负责理解开发者的创作意图与游戏设计、生成实现代码，并根据录屏与测试结果分析问题、制定修改方案；Tuanjie Codely Agent 则依托与团结引擎的原生整合，通过 Editor / Runtime Script 等方式直接在引擎中执行操作，完成场景搭建、玩法实现、工程修改与运行验证。 开发流程由此从「人提需求—模型写代码—人来操作」，延伸为「模型理解与生成—Agent 操作引擎—模型分析反馈—Agent 修改工程并验证」的完整闭环，减少了开发者在工具间切换与手动操作的成本。在一次演示中，Kimi 在没有人工干预的情况下连续工作 20 小时，不仅复现了原作，还产出了一份可持续开发的原生工程，为后续玩法扩展、画面打磨及多端适配打下基础。 Kimi + Unreal Engine：跨模块的玩法开发与联调。游戏玩法的新增或调整，往往会同时牵动角色行为、动画、物理效果和界面反馈。开发者提供相关脚本、组件配置与预期效果后，Kimi 可以梳理各模块之间的调用关系，协助修改代码、补充日志与测试，并结合 Unreal Engine 中的实际表现进行联调。以古风武侠游戏中的"处决"玩法为例，玩家靠近敌人后，角色需要连贯完成拔剑、攻击和收剑动作，并触发后续剧情。Kimi 可以协助完成人物动作绑定、模拟处决后的物理效果、衔接战斗与剧情逻辑，排查动作错位、倒地异常或剧情未触发等问题，让开发者将更多精力投入动作节奏、打击感与叙事体验的打磨。 Kimi K3.1 Pro 使用 Unreal Engine 5.8 构建了一座充满东方神话气息的天宫场景，其中包括一组半径达 1,750 米、由 36 间柱廊组成的宏伟建筑，以及一条在 Blender 中通过程序化方式建模的巨龙。主角角色使用 MetaHuman 创建，整个场景包含 3,600 万个原始三角面，并采用 Nanite 进行渲染、Lumen 进行光照处理。 使用的外部素材：Cloud Forge 的 VDB 云层、来自 Poly Haven 和 ambientCG 的 8K 材质，以及 NASA LRO/LOLA 的月球数据。 Kimi + Unreal Engine：协助搭建复杂场景。大型 3D 场景的搭建，通常涉及建筑、地形、植被等多种元素的组合，需要反复调整布局与细节，确保构图协调、光照自然、物理表现合理。以武侠游戏中的大型场景为例，云海、浮岛、古城与巨型佛像不仅需要各自成形，还要在尺度、位置与层次上形成合理的关系。在获得本地项目访问与命令执行权限后，Kimi 可以调用 Unreal Engine 里的相关工具，根据开发者的描述，先完成主要元素的放置、尺度设定与空间布局，搭出场景初稿，并提供不同视角的截图供开发者预览，为后续的细节调整与效果打磨提供基础。 Kimi K3.1 Pro 使用 Unreal Engine 5.8 制作了一支东方古风题材的 3D RPG 预告视频，画面呈现一位剑客穿越云海、掠过漂浮岛屿，最终进入云端之上的古典城池。概念设计及部分资产灵感来自小红书创作者 @-Duduu-。使用的外部素材：犍陀罗佛像与水月观音的 3D 扫描数据（明尼阿波利斯艺术博物馆，CC0 许可）。 ➎从发行到长线运营：把玩家反馈带回制作 游戏发布后，创意验证仍在继续。 发行团队要找到吸引目标玩家的玩法卖点，运营团队要从社区和客服反馈中识别真实问题，内容团队要持续处理本地化、UGC 与审核。素材量和反馈量不断增加，仅靠人工整理与分类，难以及时响应。 Kimi 可以成为各个环节的助推器，比如：快速验证各渠道的创意策略，协助起草发行内容；整理社区讨论，提炼带来源的反馈摘要；对 UGC 进行初步筛查，识别潜在风险。这些工作还可以设为定时任务，自动批量执行，让团队从重复劳动中抽身，专注打磨创意，探索游戏成长的更多可能。 从吸引新玩家到持续服务玩家，Kimi 都可以参与其中，为团队提供支持： 获客玩法开发：缩短从创意到验证的距离。投放创意的竞争，也在于落地速度。好的玩法需要尽快成为可玩版本，才能验证其潜力。Kimi 可以从一条参考视频出发，分析并还原核心玩法、编写游戏代码，再借助插件，使用 Blender 完成建模，调用 Godot 等引擎搭建场景。同时，它还可以持续调整数值、打磨动效，让原型逐步接近预期体验。整个过程可以沉淀为可复用的工作流，帮助团队降低试错成本，更快探索有潜力的玩法。 获客素材制作：通过批量测试，寻找有效创意。 Kimi 可以协助批量制作素材，让团队在同一周期内测试更多创意。有了创意参考后，Kimi 可以操控游戏引擎录制实机画面，再调用开源的动效与剪辑工具，尝试不同的开场、节奏和卖点组合。围绕这些版本，它还可以配套制作音乐、字幕和广告文案，适配不同平台与语言。素材进入投放后，Kimi 可以汇总数据、比较各版本表现，为下一轮素材调整和创意筛选提供依据。 游戏内助手：以个性化互动提升玩家体验。随着游戏交互日益智能化，玩家也期待更懂偏好、更贴合情境的回应。通过 API 将 Kimi 接入游戏或平台后，模型就能结合游戏知识与对话上下文，为玩家提供更有针对性的推荐、问答和玩法指导。例如，玩家用口语描述"想找一款能和朋友一起玩的建造游戏"，助手便可检索游戏库，返回附有推荐理由的卡片。在具体游戏中，Kimi 还可以结合游戏设定与当前情境，支持 NPC 问答、阵容建议和赛后战报，让互动更贴近玩家的实际需求。 社区与玩家反馈：及时看见玩家诉求。玩家反馈经常分散在论坛、社群和评论区等多个渠道内，数量多、内容杂。Kimi 可以协助梳理讨论，按故障、平衡性、付费体验和内容需求分类，保留原帖来源、游戏版本与反馈渠道。面对复杂争议，还可以结合帖子、截图和评论核实信息，起草带来源的答复。运营与研发据此安排热修或版本更新，让反馈更快得到回应、推动改进。 内容本地化：让翻译、校对更省心。从游戏字幕，到商店介绍、社区公告，本地化既要准确传达玩法，也要保留角色风格，符合当地玩家的表达习惯。Kimi 可以依据术语表、角色设定和长度限制生成初稿，标出需要人工判断的文化表达，帮助本地化负责人集中处理关键细节。人工复核后，还可借助 Kimi 进行抽样回译，检查术语与语义是否一致，减少疏漏。 内容审核：早一步发现风险。玩家自产内容一直是游戏生态的重要一环。从自建地图、内容文本，到游戏内聊天和图片，都需要依据规则与地区要求进行审核。Kimi 可以成为审核员的初筛助手，辅助识别违规内容及谐音、缩写等规避表达，并标出命中位置与判断理由，帮助审核员更快定位问题，将更多精力投入规则完善和复杂案例复核。 从一个可衡量的任务开始 团队可以先从现有流程中选择一项边界明确、结果容易检查的任务开始，比如制作一个核心玩法原型、修改代码库中的某项功能、检查部分游戏截图，或归类一批社区反馈。 团队可以根据任务需要，选择 Kimi Work、Kimi Code，并搭配相应的软件插件。开始前，准备好所需素材，明确操作权限和需要人工确认的环节；完成后，由对应岗位的成员检查成果，判断是否达到预期要求。 items.title: Kiro proves properties of its own harness in Lean
items.summary: We built an automated way for Kiro to model parts of its own code in Lean, prove theorems about those models, and check each model against TypeScript / Rust / Python code. We ran it first on Kiro itself. We analyzed 96 candidate properties and observations across models of 26 functions. Lean proved 70 of them, two received finite bounded checks, 18 were falsified in the model and reproduced against the analyzed code, and six produced partial results or observations. This is a demonstration of how Lean-driven verification workflows can be used in a real production setting to verify properties of the agentic harness and to catch hidden bugs.

items.title: LifeVal
items.summary:
OpenAI
November 2, 2026
ResearchPublication
LifeVal
Measuring AI progress on the tasks that matter in everyday life.
Read the paper(opens in a new window)Share
OpenAI’s mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. For the more than one billion people who currently use ChatGPT every week, we want to build AI that can help with the practical challenges of everyday life, like finding childcare, accessing government services, creating a budget, preparing for school, modifying recipes, ordering groceries, designing workout plans, and more.
When someone is looking for help making their life easier, they need more than advice or a chat response. To be a truly helpful personal assistant, ChatGPT should be able to take actions that actually get things done.
To measure model performance over time on everyday tasks, we built an evaluation of tasks covering areas where users wanted the most help from AI and personal agents. We used this evaluation to track and drive improvement in model performance on everyday tasks over the past year.
Background
To identify the tasks people value most, we started with two large studies that track how people spend time in both the U.S. and internationally: the American Time Use Survey⁠(opens in a new window) and the Multinational Time Use Study⁠(opens in a new window). Together, these datasets provide a detailed catalog of everyday life tasks that people do across different demographics, times of day, and seasons. To understand where people would most value AI assistance, we expanded on these existing surveys with a new demographically representative survey of 3,995 respondents. For each task, we asked a variety of questions to identify the areas where everyday people most wanted help from a personal assistant. The resulting tasks span the most important areas that people want help with, including caregiving, health, education, household administration, personal finances, shopping, and accessing government services.
Individual task examples
Below are some examples of how our current models perform on practical workflows from everyday life.
Enroll in the right kindergarten after moving
93.1%
Compare kindergartens near our new home and shortlist the best fits.
I’ve narrowed it to three kindergartens and organized the enrollment details. Two preferences still need your call. Want to review the shortlist?
Manage volunteers ahead of a flood
98.0%
Help me organize our community’s flood preparation volunteer force for four neighbors needing floodproofing assistance.
I’ve prepared a simple action plan to help volunteers assess the sites mentioned and help them prepare for upcoming severe weather.
Find a new home for my family
100%
Find a home in Luzerne County that fits my budget, has a separate living unit, and keeps my commute short after school drop-off. Add the deed to my cart so I can review it.
I found one home that meets your requirements. I’ve calculated the transfer tax and added the deed to your country records cart to review.
Watch a game with grandma from far away
96.3%
Set up an easy way for grandma and me to watch the game together remotely.
The easiest watch setup is ready, with a backup if the stream fails. Want me to walk you through it with grandma?
Meal prep for a parent adjusting to a new diabetes diagnosis
90.4%
Help my parent adjust to a new diabetes diagnosis with a practical care and meal plan.
The first-week plan is ready, including meals, reminders, and questions for the care team. Want to review it together before you share it with your parent?
Our latest models score very highly on many LifeVal tasks. See more
Over the past year, we’ve trained our models to become much faster, more capable, and more aligned on browser use, computer use, and connectors tasks. Enabling these capabilities in ChatGPT also expands the types of tasks the model can help with, helping move ChatGPT beyond a chat tool and towards a truly agentic personal assistant.
Why this matters
To ensure AGI benefits all of humanity, we need to measure and improve model progress on what matters in the lives of everyday people. That means going beyond academic assessments of model knowledge and actually measuring how well AI models can help people navigate decisions, manage everyday responsibilities, and get meaningful things done. We are hopeful that LifeVal represents a step towards that goal.

items.title: Make long-running agents faster with message threads
items.summary:
Make long-running agents faster with message threads
New in the Messages API, send your conversation once, and the API receives only what’s new with every turn.
CategoryProduct updates
ProductClaude Platform
DateNovember 2, 2026
Reading time3 min
ShareCopy link
Message threads is now available in public beta on the Claude Platform. With message threads, agents no longer need to resend the full conversation history on every turn, reducing latency for long-running sessions.
How message threads works
A coding agent might make hundreds of requests in one session, and each request resends every earlier message and tool result. Once a conversation reaches hundreds of thousands of tokens, resending all of it adds time before Claude starts responding. With message threads, agents send only what’s new since the last turn, which reduces time to first token (TTFT).
With message threads on by default for most Claude Code users, requests with 500k to 1M tokens see median TTFT drop by about 35%.
To use message threads, add the thread parameter to Messages API requests. The first request includes the full conversation and starts a thread. Each request after that includes only the new messages and the ID of the previous response. Between turns, we hold each thread in memory, where it’s encrypted and not written to disk. A thread expires 5 minutes after its last request and your client then resends the full conversation to start a new one. While each request is smaller with message threads, Claude still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage stays the same.
Message threads is best for active sessions where latency matters, including:
Long-running coding agents, where each tool result or file edit adds to the conversation.
Computer use agents, where screenshots stay with the thread instead of being re-uploaded on every turn.
Document and image-heavy workflows, where requests are made smaller.
The more context an agent carries, the more message threads can reduce time to first token.
Getting started
Message threads is available now in public beta on the native Claude Platform, and on Claude Platform on AWS, Claude in Microsoft Foundry, and on Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed). Standard Claude token rates and existing rate limits apply. See the documentation to get started.

items.title: Managed Deep Agents: the fastest way to ship a production deep agent
items.summary:
Deep Agents
Introducing Managed Deep Agents
Victor MoreiraMay 13, 20266minGo back to blogCreate agentsCreate agentsShare
Key Takeaways
Managed Deep Agents runs the open-source Deep Agents harness on LangSmith. You write what the agent does, and LangSmith runs it in production.
An agent is a project folder. You test it locally with mda dev and ship it with mda deploy.
Production capabilities like durable memory, sandboxes and schedules are files you add to the project rather than services you build and run yourself.
‍
Introducing Managed Deep Agents
Updated November 2, 2026. Managed Deep Agents is in public beta on LangSmith Cloud, and this post now describes how it works today. It first ran on May 13, 2026, when we opened a private beta.
Managed Deep Agents lets you build a deep agent as a folder of files and deploy it to LangSmith with one command. You write the agent's instructions and tools and pick the model, and LangSmith runs the Deep Agents harness and the production runtime around it. There are no servers to run and no infrastructure to wire together.
A support agent, for example, can answer questions in a Slack channel and sweep stale tickets every night, with each of those declared as a file in its project. Managed Deep Agents is in public beta on LangSmith Cloud, and the quickstart takes you from an empty directory to a deployed agent.
Why we built it
Building a capable agent keeps getting easier. The open-source Deep Agents harness already gives an agent a filesystem and lets it plan its work and hand parts of it off to subagents.
Running that agent in production is still a lot of work, and it's impossible for an agent to be proactive or multiplayer unless it's running in production. It needs threads that survive restarts and a safe place to run the code it writes. It also needs memory that lasts between conversations and a record of what it did, and teams end up building and operating all of it before the agent reaches a single user. It needs a cron server to manage scheduled runs.
Managed Deep Agents takes that layer off your plate. Every deployment runs on LangSmith Agent Server, which gives you durable threads and streaming runs without operating a server.
We build our own agents this way. GTM Agent, Open SWE and Content Studio all run on Managed Deep Agents, and Content Studio's code shrank by about 80% when we moved it over.
An agent is a folder of files
A Managed Deep Agent is a normal Python project. The only required file is agent.py, which defines the agent with define_deep_agent. This is the research assistant from the quickstart:‍
from managed_deepagents import define_deep_agent
agent = define_deep_agent(
name="research-assistant",
model="openai:gpt-5.5",
tools=[{"type": "web_search"}],
)
‍The system prompt lives next to it in instructions.md, and each folder under skills/ holds a playbook the agent loads when a task calls for it. Tools are ordinary Python functions under tools/ that you import into agent.py, and tools/mcp.py adds tools from remote MCP servers.
A few commands take the project from an empty directory to a deployment.‍
uvx --from managed-deepagents mda init research-assistant
cd research-assistant
uv sync
uv run mda dev
uv run mda deploy
mda dev starts a local Agent Server and opens the agent in LangSmith Studio, where you can chat with it and inspect its traces. mda deploy ships the project to LangSmith and adds your model provider's key to the deployment. If you'd rather have a coding agent do the setup, the managed-deep-agents skill walks it through the same steps.
Add what the agent needs
Each managed capability is a file or folder in the project, and mda deploy sets up whatever it finds. This lets you start with agent.py alone and add pieces as the agent grows.
Memory. By default an agent remembers only the current thread. Add memory.py and it keeps knowledge across threads, in a layer shared by every caller, a private layer for each user, or both.
Schedules. A file under schedules/ runs the agent on a cron schedule, and mda deploy provisions it once the deployment is live.
Channels. With channels/slack.py, people start runs from Slack and get the agent's answers in the same conversation. Any service that can send a webhook can start runs over HTTP.
Sandbox. sandbox/ gives the agent an isolated filesystem and shell for running the code it writes.
Identity and connections. identity.py authenticates callers, so each person gets private threads, memory and credentials. Connections store API keys and run OAuth, so end users authorize their own accounts instead of you provisioning credentials for each one.
Subagents. You declare subagents in the agent definition. An async subagent runs in the background while the agent keeps talking to the user.
Evals. mda evals init -i sets up a Harbor eval workspace under evals/ and hands off to a coding agent to write the tasks.
A schedule, for example, is a few lines in schedules/daily_digest.py.
from managed_deepagents import define_schedule
schedule = define_schedule(
cron="0 8 * * 1-5",
timezone="America/Los_Angeles",
prompt="Write the daily digest.",
)
Some capabilities need no file at all. The agent can use built-in web search powered by Parallel without a separate account or API key, and it can work in a browser, handing control to you when a site needs a login. To pause for human approval before selected tool calls, set interrupt_on in the agent definition.
Call it from your app or an MCP client
Every deployment serves the Agent Server API, so your own application can create threads and stream runs, or you can build a custom frontend on top of it. Deployments also serve an MCP endpoint at /mcp, which lets MCP clients like Claude Code call the agent as a tool.
What teams are building
Teams in the public beta run a wide range of agents on Managed Deep Agents, and a few patterns come up repeatedly:
Incident triage. An agent picks up monitoring alerts posted to a Slack channel, investigates them in its sandbox, and reports what it found in the thread. Some teams have it open a pull request with the fix.
Engineering workflows. A webhook from the team's issue tracker starts a run, and the agent works through a build-and-verify loop on the task. Other teams have an agent test fixes in preview environments with a browser before a person reviews them.
Internal assistants in Slack. Teams deploy one agent per job, such as an HR policy assistant or a finance assistant that manages the team's tasks in its project tool.
Agents inside a product. A customer-facing agent runs behind the company's own frontend through the Agent Server API, with per-user memory so each customer's context stays separate.
Long-running project agents. One agent per project keeps that project's memory and handles tasks for its project managers as the work goes on.
Scheduled work. Agents modeled on company functions, like sales or product, run on schedules and produce competitive reviews and marketing assets without anyone prompting them.
Improve the agent from real usage
Managed Deep Agents keeps the agent's instructions and skills in LangSmith Context Hub. Each mda deploy syncs instructions.md and skills/ from your project, and you can edit them in Context Hub for a quick change without redeploying. If someone changed the Hub copy since your last deploy, the CLI asks which version to keep.
Durable memory lives in Context Hub too, and the agent writes to it as it works. A support agent that learns your team's escalation path keeps it for every conversation that follows.
Runs are traced in LangSmith, so you can read every tool call and intermediate step. LangSmith Engine works from those traces to surface recurring issues and diagnose their cause. When you connect it to the agent's Context Hub repository, it can propose fixes to the instructions and skills.
Built on open-source Deep Agents
Managed Deep Agents runs the same open-source harness, with the same agent loop, filesystem tools, subagents and skills. In code, the difference is who compiles the agent. create_deep_agent returns a compiled agent that you run, and you own the backend, store, checkpointer and server around it. define_deep_agent takes the same parameters, minus the ones the runtime manages, and returns a definition that the managed runtime compiles for you.
If you've already built an agent with create_deep_agent, Move from Deep Agents walks through converting it. If you want full control over hosting, the Deep Agents SDK runs the same harness on your own infrastructure.
Get started
Follow the quickstart to deploy a research assistant. The tutorial then adds a custom search tool, durable memory and a daily schedule to the same project.
We would love to hear what you build, where the defaults work, and where you need more control.

OpenAI

Security
Preparing our next security sprint to harden OpenAI
We’re planning our next internal security sprint at OpenAI, bringing new researchers and security partners together with our own teams to use our models to test and strengthen our systems. We’re partnering with Cathedral, whose researchers will use OpenAI’s models alongside our teams to challenge our defenses, bringing differentiated expertise and approaches to finding weaknesses and helping us protect our platforms.
“OpenAI is setting an important example by partnering with outside security firms and using its own models to continuously test and strengthen its defenses. Every company should be thinking about how to put these capabilities to work. We’re excited to collaborate with OpenAI’s teams, combining their models and security expertise with our research to find weaknesses, test fixes and strengthen this approach to continuous defense.”
Gavin Kliger, CEO & Co-founder, Cathedral
We’re also making improvements to our Security Bug Bounty program including more than quadrupling our rewards for critical findings. We want researchers to challenge our assumptions and help strengthen both our systems and the methods we use to defend them.
This is part of our ongoing effort to use AI to continuously find and fix weaknesses in our systems. Our last sprint showed what this approach can deliver. We dedicated 25% of our product engineers to finding and fixing weaknesses in our systems. Using Codex, engineers investigated findings, reproduced vulnerabilities in isolated environments and prepared patches for review.
We’re building on that work because traditional cyber defenses alone are no longer sufficient. Recent incidents across the industry show how quickly threats can emerge and how important it is to build continuous defensive loops to find and fix weaknesses before attackers do.
Keeping the defender’s window open requires organizations to use frontier cyber capabilities to harden their systems. We’re using our most capable models to strengthen our own defenses and making them available to Daybreak customers. We’ve committed $1 billion in subsidized access over six months for frontline defenders protecting essential services and digital infrastructure. We’re also sharing our architecture and lessons⁠ from the last sprint, alongside our blueprint for empowering cyber defenders across industry and government.
We’ll keep advancing our models, using them to strengthen our own systems, and expanding access for trusted defenders. Keeping the defender’s window open will take action across the industry, and that work needs to start now.

items.title: Qodo builds context into AI code review with Codex
items.summary:
OpenAI
November 2, 2026
Startup
Qodo builds context into AI code review with Codex
Qodo brings organizational context and codebase standards into Codex, helping developers catch P0 issues across repositories.
Start building(opens in a new window)Company size: StartupRegion: North AmericaIndustry: TechnologyProducts: API, CodexShare
Qodo⁠(opens in a new window) builds AI tools for code review and software quality, giving coding agents the organizational knowledge they need to understand the code they change. Co-founder and CEO Itamar Friedman calls it “the coding agent’s best friend.”
Qodo uses OpenAI models including GPT‑6 Astra to gather engineering knowledge, review code, and monitor software quality. Its Codex plugin brings that context and review into developers’ coding sessions.
“We love OpenAI models. We want the frontier, the best reasoning models, but also those that are really fast.”
—Itamar Friedman, Co-founder and CEO, Qodo
Finding P0 bugs across repositories with Codex
Itamar describes customer environments that can span 10,000 or more repositories, where a local code change can break a downstream service, even if it looks correct on its own. Qodo built a plugin in the Codex marketplace to address this.
“Codex is really good at taking a local task and completing it in an efficient way,” Itamar says. Qodo’s plugin gives Codex access to codebase knowledge, organizational rules, and independent review through Qodo’s Agentic Toolbox.
With context, Codex can account for dependencies across repositories, including those hosted by different Git providers or services connected through Kafka. “Qodo will make that connection and will help Codex look at the software as a whole and not miss those P0 bugs,” Itamar says.
Automating review while keeping human judgment
Before Codex starts writing code, it can use Qodo’s plugin to retrieve the relevant codebase rules and pull request history and patterns. After Codex makes the changes, Qodo reviews them and returns its findings directly to Codex in the same session, before the developer opens a pull request.
Nnenna Ndukwe, Qodo’s AI Developer Relations Lead, sees developers using this workflow to build features and tackle technical debt with GPT‑6 models in Codex. They are automating the handoff between Codex’s coding work and Qodo’s independent review. “That’s what I’ve been seeing developers do, which is really exciting because GPT‑6 is extremely capable,” Nnenna says.
Itamar describes coding and review agents as “yin and yang”: one creates code, the other challenges it. Each role needs its own setup and context and may involve multiple agents. His vision is for agents to discuss findings and “surface only what they don’t accept” for human review. Developers would become planners and reviewers, able to inspect unresolved issues alongside the agents’ discussion, context, and prior developer decisions.
“That’s how you create trust,” Itamar says. “I think it makes the whole process overall more efficient,” Nnenna adds. “We get to leverage the best parts of our expertise.”
Putting Codex to work every day
Internally at Qodo, Nnenna has been using GPT‑6 Astra’s Extra High and Ultra effort settings in her own automated development workflows as well as knowledge work.
“What does Codex not do? I love everything that Codex does. I love the idea of combining AI and automation.”
—Nnenna Ndukwe, AI Developer Relations Lead, Qodo
Nnenna schedules Codex to report on what she accomplished during the week and where she could focus or improve next. She also uses it to research conversations about agentic engineering on social platforms and suggest ideas for developer content. When it comes to her own code changes, she schedules Codex to analyze her work and suggest agent skills to create or refine.
Choosing which coding rules apply with the Decisions API
Itamar sees an opportunity to use OpenAI’s recently launched Decisions API to choose which rules and agent skills apply at each stage of development, rather than rely on language models for every decision.
He cites an example where the Decisions API could select which of 200 rules need checking before a language model reasons through the relevant ones, helping to make selection faster and cheaper while improving the quality of the review. “The Decisions API is an immense opportunity for us to bring more trust to the process,” Itamar says.
Building software factories customers can own
Qodo’s approach combines “the best aspects of artificial intelligence and the best aspects of traditional software engineering and scripting,” Nnenna says. Company knowledge guides coding agents, independent review checks their work, and human expertise resolves the questions that remain.
This creates the foundation of what Itamar describes as a software factory: a system customers could assemble and own, bringing coding and review agents together with an understanding of how software changes in production.
With OpenAI, Qodo is building a future where coding agents put more of a company’s experience to work and developers can focus their judgment where it matters most.

items.title: Rewarding defenders with bigger bug bounties
items.summary:
OpenAI
November 2, 2026
Security
Rewarding defenders with bigger bug bounties
Security Bug Bounty program(opens in a new window)Share
We’re raising rewards in OpenAI’s Security Bug Bounty program to further encourage independent researchers to pursue vulnerabilities in OpenAI software that our testing may have missed. We’re also introducing new incentives for researchers to earn more for higher quality vulnerability reports.
Independent security researchers play an essential role in protecting technology across the industry. At OpenAI, incentivizing responsible disclosure is a core part of our security model, complementing our Defense Factory⁠ work, where our engineers use our models to find weaknesses, reproduce them, and test fixes.
Today’s updates are designed to encourage and empower researchers, and to continue building a collaborative, community-first security environment.
Serious vulnerabilities get serious rewards
We’re more than quadrupling the midpoint of our reward ranges for medium, high, and critical findings on average. A critical vulnerability in a core product such as ChatGPT, Codex, or the API Platform will now earn up to $30,000. Exceptional critical findings on those targets remain eligible for up to $100,000, and now up to $172,000 with bonuses. The full details are available in our security bug bounty program⁠(opens in a new window).
High quality report bonus multipliers
High-quality reports will be eligible to earn a bonus multiplier on the base bounty. A reliable proof of concept that isolates the bug, shows when it can be exploited, and demonstrates its impact gives us a head start on a fix. The quality multiplier recognizes the extra work that makes a finding especially useful.
Loyalty program bonuses
To build long-term relationships and continuously empower our security community, we are introducing a tiered loyalty bonus program. This 5-tier system provides scaling bonuses to recognize, support, and celebrate researchers who consistently partner with us in making AI technology safer for everyone.
Priority campaign multipliers
To support community engagement as technology evolves, priority campaigns will feature dedicated bonus pools for newly launched features. These short-term campaigns give researchers early, high-reward opportunities to test new developments and be recognized for their early contributions.
