items.title: Sliding window beats linear attention, but only on short answers
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Sliding window beats linear attention, but only on short answers
Community Article Published
November 2, 2026 Upvote 6
Lukas sirluk Follow
TL;DR
A recent paper, Sliding-window beats linear attention, shows that sliding window attention (SWA) with attention sinks matches or beats most linearized models.
Based on our work on attention linearization, we ran a clean ablation to test this. For short answers, our results agree.
We distilled Qwen3-4B-Instruct into four students with the same memory requirements per attention layer: two SWA students, one with learned sinks and one with sink tokens, and two students with our Bifocal layer, which spends part of the memory on a linear mixer next to a smaller sliding window.
On math problems that need long answers (from AIME and HMMT), Bifocal solves almost twice as many as SWA. The sliding window still matters, though. When Bifocal gives almost all of its memory to the linear mixer, the math scores collapse.
The Bifocal layer is cheap to run. In a Qwen3.5-4B-sized model where Bifocal replaces all attention and GDN layers, our fused kernels keep decoding at about 195 tokens/s for prompts up to 128K tokens, as fast as SWA in the same place and at the same memory.
The KV cache bottleneck
A transformer stores a key and a value for every token it has seen, in every attention layer. This KV cache grows with every token the model generates. For Qwen3-4B each token uses about 144 KiB, so one 10,000-token answer needs about 1.4 GiB. In a realistic serving setting, where multiple requests are processed at once, this can quickly exceed the available GPU memory. Reasoning models write answers this long all the time, so the KV cache becomes the bottleneck.
There are two ways to keep memory fixed: you can forget old tokens and only keep the last W tokens, which is what sliding window attention does. Or you can compress them into a fixed-size state, as in linear attention and its gated successors (Mamba, Gated DeltaNet (GDN), mLSTM).
Forget or compress
A sliding window is exact over the last W tokens and sees older tokens only indirectly through earlier layers. When retrofitting a pretrained model, SWA collapses as soon as the initial tokens leave the window, because attention heads use them to park spare probability mass. The fix is an attention sink, as proposed by StreamingLLM, which pins the first four tokens in the cache. Keeping those initial tokens around, however, complicates cache management and rules out standard sliding-window kernels. Instead, we use a learned sink as in gpt-oss, which is a learned bias in each head's softmax denominator that absorbs unused attention without storing extra tokens in the cache. This idea goes back to Evan Miller's Attention Is Off By One.
A linear mixer compresses all past tokens into a fixed-size state. In linearization, where a pretrained transformer is converted into a cheaper student, a linear mixer alone does not work well. The teacher's attention leans heavily on the last few hundred tokens and needs them at full resolution. In our distillation paper, pairing the mLSTM with a sliding window uniformly lowered cross-entropy loss by restoring exact short-range recall. LoLCATs and other linearization methods add a window for the same reason.
We run both, sliding window and linear mixer, side by side in place of every attention layer. LoLCATs already distilled into a similar layer structure, and we change two things:
Our linear mixer is an mLSTM. The argument should hold for other modern linear mixers too, such as Mamba or GDN.
We combine the two outputs using a data-dependent gate per head: a linear projection of the layer input to one sigmoid-activated scalar o per head, which mixes the two as o · mLSTM + (1 − o) · SWA.
We call this layer Bifocal: like bifocal glasses, it sees what is near sharply and what is far at lower resolution. But is this added complexity actually necessary? Isn't it better to just spend the linear mixer's memory on a larger sliding window?
The case for sliding windows
Sliding-window beats linear attention argues that a sliding window with sinks is enough on its own. Without any training, a 64-token window with four sink tokens recovers 99% of the teacher's score on six standard benchmarks. With a 512-token window, it has the best average on GSM8K and HumanEval among the training-free and linearized methods tested, and it beats retrofitted linear models by a wide margin on needle-in-a-haystack and BABILong.
We agree that SWA with sinks is a strong, cheap baseline, and every linearization paper should report it. Three things in the setup, though, limit how far the conclusion reaches:
Most linear models in the generative and long-context comparisons were retrofitted on small budgets, 20 to 600 million tokens.
"Long context" there means long inputs with short answers. None of the benchmarks require the model to write a long answer.
Much of the comparison runs on log-likelihood benchmarks.
The last point is a problem for the whole field. Many linearization papers report only HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA, ARC and MMLU. These benchmarks score a few fixed answer options in a single forward pass, and the model never reads anything it wrote itself. If a 64-token window recovers 99% on them, they cannot tell you whether a model remembers anything far back.
To address all three points, and follow up on the SWA paper's own suggestion to compare post-trained SWA against linear retrofitting at equal training budgets, we distill both architectures on the same 4B-token budget, match their inference memory, and evaluate them on benchmarks that require generating both short and long answers.
A memory-matched comparison
We initialize all students from Qwen3-4B-Instruct, replacing all 36 of its attention layers. The model uses grouped-query attention with 32 query heads sharing 8 key-value heads.
To match memory across students, we express the linear mixer's state in equivalent BF16 KV cache tokens. Without softmax, linear attention can be trained in a fast parallel form (like a transformer) and unrolled at inference into a recurrent state that accumulates outer key-value products. Because this recurrent state sums over thousands of steps, it must be kept in FP32 to avoid numerical drift from the parallel training form. So one 128 × 128 mLSTM state takes as much memory as 128 cached tokens of a BF16 key-value head. Because there are four query heads for every key-value head, it also matters where the states live: keeping one state per key-value head costs 128 tokens of window per layer, whereas keeping one per query head costs 512.
That lets us give four students exactly the same budget, the memory of 576 cached tokens per layer:
SWA, learned sink: a 576-token window with the same learned sinks as Bifocal.
SWA + sink tokens: a 572-token window plus the 4 sink tokens of StreamingLLM, as in the SWA paper.
Bifocal: a 448-token window plus one state per key-value head, worth 128 tokens, and learned sinks, which take no cache.
Bifocal, window 64: a 64-token window plus one state per query head, worth 512 tokens.
All four students are distilled with the same data, recipe, and 4.1-billion-token budget on sequences up to 40K tokens. This makes the SWA students much stronger baselines than training-free SWA, with every chance to learn to pass information across their 36 stacked windows (more on how far stacked windows actually reach below).
Our main comparison is SWA with a learned sink against Bifocal: since a learned scalar sink per head takes negligible memory, both use the exact same cache budget and differ only in how they spend it. We also trained an SWA student with pinned sink tokens to check whether the sink type matters—on the math benchmarks (AIME and HMMT), it doesn't, with both SWA variants scoring around 14%.
Sliding window alone is enough for short answers
On short answers, a larger window is as good as a state, or slightly better. The SWA student is ahead on all three short benchmarks, by 0.7 to 1.5 points. When answers are only a few hundred tokens long, the prompt and response mostly fit inside the window anyway, so the model rarely needs to fall back on a compressed state. SWA also has a head start in distillation as it keeps the teacher's architecture and only changes the attention mask and adds a sink, while Bifocal has to learn a new linear mixer and gate. So in this regime, our results agree with the SWA paper.
The linear mixer helps on long answers
Hard math is different. On AIME and HMMT, our students write about 7,600 tokens per answer. At any step, the window only covers about 8% of that. After a few hundred tokens of reasoning, the question itself has left the window, and as the answer grows, intermediate results from earlier steps leave it too. The linear mixer's state still holds a summary of all of it.
Bifocal is ahead on all four math benchmarks, but by small margins: 15.5% against 13.8% on average. With only 120 problems, this gap is right at the edge of statistical significance. The picture gets much clearer when we group the problems by how long their answers are.
On problems with short answers, both solve about 59%. On the 96 with long answers, Bifocal solves 1.8 times as many, and the SWA student with sink tokens does no better. Looking across all individual rollouts, Bifocal produces 66 correct answers longer than 4,000 tokens, compared to just 26 for the SWA student. Long answers are where the sliding window struggles and where the state helps.
Can't stacked sliding window layers see further?
A common argument for pure sliding window attention is that each layer passes information on to the next, so L stacked windows of W tokens can reach L × W tokens back, like stacked convolutions. This was introduced by Longformer in 2020 and popularized by Mistral 7B, which noted that 32 layers with 4,096-token windows give "a theoretical attention span of approximately 131K tokens".
For our SWA student, that theoretical reach is 36 × 576 = 20,736 tokens—longer than 88% of its answers. On paper, it can still see the question from almost anywhere in its answer, but in practice, it solves long-answer problems far less often than Bifocal.
The reason is the same as for CNNs, whose effective receptive field is a small fraction of the theoretical one (Luo et al., 2016). In a transformer, most of each token's signal stays on the residual path, and only a fraction moves through attention into the next window. Guangxuan Xiao shows that this makes the influence of a distant token decay roughly exponentially with the number of windows in between, leaving an effective range of about 1.5 windows, regardless of depth. A linear mixer does not need this cross-layer relay: each layer's recurrent state carries earlier tokens forward directly.
A linear mixer alone is not enough either
If the linear state helps on long answers, it is tempting to spend almost the whole budget on it. Our fourth student, Bifocal with window 64, tests this by keeping a state per query head (512 tokens worth of memory) alongside a tiny 64-token window. Rather than improving long-range reasoning, the model collapses, scoring just 4.2% on math (vs. 15.5% for Bifocal) and falling sharply on the short-answer benchmarks as well. Exact recall over the recent past is still essential, and a compressed state blurs that information.
This also highlights a practical lesson for grouped-query attention: because there are four query heads per key-value head, putting states on query heads costs four times as much memory, directly starving the sliding window (64 tokens instead of 448).
What does the linear mixer cost?
With memory matched by design, what about speed? We benchmarked decoding in vLLM on the Qwen3.5-4B architecture, replacing all of its attention and GDN layers with either SWA or Bifocal at a 576-token budget per layer. (Qwen3.5's key-value heads are wider, so a state costs more and Bifocal gets a 320-token window.) For comparison, we also ran full attention and Qwen3.5's native hybrid layout (GDN + attention, which pairs three GDN layers with each full-attention layer).
During decoding, Bifocal is just as fast as pure SWA. With all attention and GDN layers replaced, both hold steady at about 195 tokens/s from 1K all the way to 128K prompt tokens, staying within about 2% of each other at every length. Meanwhile, GDN + attention slows to 146 tokens/s at 128K as its full-attention caches grow with the context, and full attention drops to 92 tokens/s.
Where the linear mixer does cost time is prompt processing (prefill): Bifocal ingests prompts at 63% to 83% of SWA's speed, needing 1.8 s instead of 1.5 s before the first token of a 128K prompt. For long-form reasoning, though, where generating a 10,000-token answer takes almost a minute, that extra 0.3 s on the prompt is negligible.
Takeaways
SWA with sinks is a strong, cheap baseline, and worth reporting. On short answers, nothing in our runs beats it at equal memory.
Compare at equal memory. A linear mixer's state takes memory too: count it in equivalent KV cache tokens, and keep grouped-query attention in mind when deciding whether states are shared across query heads.
Evaluate on long generations, and look at them by length. Log-likelihood benchmarks and short answers cannot tell these architectures apart, and an average over all problems hides where the state helps.
Use both. A window alone runs out on long answers; a linear mixer alone blurs the recent past. Bifocal combines them at the same memory and decoding speed.
More on the distillation recipe in our paper, Effective Distillation to Hybrid xLSTM Architectures.
Details
Models. Teacher: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. All four students replace every attention layer (36 layers). SWA, learned sink: a 576-token sliding window with a learned scalar sink per head. SWA + sink tokens: a 572-token sliding window plus the first 4 tokens of the sequence. Bifocal: a 448-token window with a learned scalar sink per head, plus an mLSTM with one state per key-value head (8 states of 128 × 128 per layer, FP32), blended by a per-head, data-dependent gate. Bifocal, window 64: the same, with a 64-token window and one state per query head (32 states per layer).
Memory accounting. Per layer, one cached token takes 8 key-value heads × 128 dims × key and value × 2 bytes = 4 KiB. One FP32 state takes 64 KiB, so 8 states are worth 128 tokens and 32 states 512. The mLSTM's normalizer vectors add under 1% and are not counted.
Distillation. Layer-wise hidden-state alignment (2,500 steps, 819M tokens), then logit distillation with a KL-only loss (10,000 steps, 3.28B tokens), on sequences of up to 40,960 tokens. The same for all four students.
Data. Nemotron generalist mix: 40% chat and instruction, 20% code, 20% math, 15% science, 5% safety.
Evaluation. AIME 2024 and 2025, HMMT February and November 2025: 30 problems each, 16 samples per problem, up to 31,744 new tokens, temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, pass@1 averaged over samples. On the math benchmarks, 24% of Bifocal's rollouts and 12% of the SWA student's hit this limit, mostly by repeating a final answer they had already written. These answers are almost always wrong: crediting the few that contain the right answer would add 0.4 and 0.1 points. GSM8K: 5-shot, exact match, greedy decoding. IFEval: strict prompt accuracy, greedy decoding. HumanEval (instruct): pass@1, greedy decoding. Answer lengths are re-tokenized from the saved text with the teacher's tokenizer.
Statistics. Confidence intervals come from a paired bootstrap over problems with 20,000 resamples. For Bifocal's gain on the math average, the 95% interval runs from 0.0 to 3.4 points. On the 96 long-answer problems, it runs from 0.7 to 3.3 points. For the grouping by answer length, each problem's typical length is the median over all 32 answers of the two main students. The per-answer counts grade each answer by exact match with the reference answer, which agrees with the evaluation's per-problem scores on 472 of 480 problem–student pairs.
What we left out. For the SWA student with sink tokens, we report only math. Our evaluation code for sink tokens mishandles prompts longer than the cache: on GSM8K, whose 5-shot prompts are 700 to 870 tokens long, this student answered one of the example questions instead of the test question in 14% of problems, against 1% to 2% for the other students. The math prompts are under 200 tokens. GPQA Diamond's 3,072-token limit cut off 37% to 53% of the answers, so it mostly measures who finishes in time.
Speed. vLLM 0.28 on one H100 80 GB, batch size 1, synthetic weights with the Qwen3.5-4B shape: 32 layers, 16 query heads and 4 key-value heads with head dimension 256. SWA and Bifocal replace all 32 attention and GDN layers; the MLPs are unchanged. Each request reads a prompt of 1K to 128K tokens and then generates 256 tokens; we report the median of five requests. SWA: a 576-token window with a learned scalar sink per head (FlashAttention-3). Bifocal: a 320-token window with the same sinks, plus one 256 × 256 FP32 mLSTM state per key-value head, with fused Triton kernels for decode and prefill. Per layer, a cached token takes 4 KiB and a state 256 KiB, so both hold 2.25 MiB, 576 tokens' worth, or 72 MiB per model. GDN + attention and the full-attention model ran earlier on another H100 with the same software versions; a recent run of GDN + attention on the same GPU as SWA and Bifocal matched it within 0.2 tokens/s at 8K and 128K. Parameters: 3.74B (SWA), 3.78B (Bifocal), 4.21B (GDN + attention).

items.title: Bring Your Own Schema: How We Built kniv v7
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Bring Your Own Schema: How We Built kniv v7
Community Article Published
November 2, 2026 Upvote 5
Rohit Rai milliondreams Follow dragonscale-ai
A family of open encoders, from 55M to 538M parameters, that read across sentences, parse every sentence, and extract the entities, relations and fact attributes you name at run time, with no LLM call and no retraining.
An LLM can extract anything you ask for, at one API call per message. A tagger is cheap and runs locally, but it only finds what it was trained to find.
Agent memory needs the first one's flexibility at the second one's cost.
In May we released kniv v5, a cascade that gives the linguistic layer in a single pass: part of speech, named entities, dependencies, semantic roles and dialogue acts. It did that job well. But the memory systems we built on it kept asking for the next thing, and the next thing was facts. Who lives where. Who works for whom. What someone plans, as opposed to what they did. They wanted those facts in their own schema, not ours, and they needed to know whether each one is asserted, negated, hoped for or just reported.
So today we're releasing kniv v7, a family of six models with the same outputs and the same runtime, from a 55M-parameter model for small devices to the two 500M-parameter models that set its quality:

what it's for

All are Apache-2.0, with ONNX in three precisions included. Each pairs a fixed linguistic layer with a knowledge layer whose entity types and relations are inputs. You describe what you want in plain English, and the model reads for it.
This post follows the engineering behind that change: how we taught a shared encoder to read a schema, trained it on incomplete supervision, distilled it into smaller models, and made the resulting pipeline practical to run locally.
What v7 Does
One call returns two layers.
The linguistic layer is fixed. It covers part of speech, morphology, lemmas, named entities, dependency trees, semantic roles, dialogue acts and sentiment per sentence, and coreference.
The knowledge layer follows your schema:
entities typed with your type names;
facts for the relations you name;
for each fact:
its polarity (positive or negated);
its modality (asserted, hypothetical, planned, desired, questioned or reported);
its holder (who says so);
its time (when it applies).
Think of it as a form whose blanks you write yourself. kniv fills them in from the text, and notes who said it and whether it holds.
Conversations are first-class: each speaker is an entity. So "I live in Berlin" becomes (user, lives in, Berlin), attributed to the user.
import sys
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download
path = snapshot_download("dragonscale-ai/kniv-v7-xlarge-u-en")
sys.path.insert(0, path)
from kniv_v7 import Kniv
kniv = Kniv(path) # ONNX on CPU; Kniv(path, int8=True) is about 2x faster
out = kniv.extract(
turns=[("user", "I live in Berlin and work for Siemens."),
("assistant", "Nice, how long have you been there?")],
relations=[{"name": "lives in", "description": "the place where the head resides"},
{"name": "employer", "description": "the organization the head works for"}],
entity_types=[{"name": "location"}, {"name": "organization"}, {"name": "person"}])
for w in out:
for f in w["facts"]:
print(w["entities"][f["head"]]["text"], f["relation"],
w["entities"][f["tail"]]["text"], f["polarity"], f["modality"])
user lives in Berlin positive asserted
user employer Siemens positive asserted
Change the relations list and you've changed what the model looks for. No training and no labelled examples are needed. The only dependencies are onnxruntime, tokenizers and numpy. Every model in the family takes the same call, and returns these two facts; only the repository name changes.
Documents, Not Sentences
Most open extraction models work one sentence, or one entity pair, at a time. Real text doesn't keep its facts in one sentence. In Re-DocRED, about half of the gold facts span sentences: the entity is named in one, and the fact about it arrives in the next, often through a pronoun.
kniv reads a whole window, up to a page of text, as one unit:
coreference links mentions across the page;
the marker pass sees every mention of every entity at once, and pools context from wherever it is in the window, so a pair can be related by evidence two sentences away;
the evidence pass in training teaches the relation head which sentences support each fact.
The result is that the distance between two entities costs surprisingly little. Re-DocRED test, gold entities, by where the two entities are mentioned:
entities mentioned
UltraBERT
DeBERTa
in the same sentence
0.761
0.749
in adjacent sentences
0.694
0.701
two or more sentences apart
0.702
0.732
For DeBERTa, a fact whose entities are two or more sentences apart is extracted almost as well as one inside a single sentence. Given "Ada Lovelace was born in London in 1815. She later worked with Charles Babbage on his Analytical Engine.", it returns (Ada Lovelace, worked with, Charles Babbage), read through "She" in the second sentence.
Longer documents are split into windows automatically. Each window is read as a unit, and facts are not linked across windows (see "Where It Breaks").
Why a Fixed Schema Was a Dead End
Our previous research line (v6) reached 0.764 F1 on Re-DocRED, a document-level relation benchmark, given the gold entities. It got there by porting ATLOP's marker pass: mentions are wrapped in markers, and context is pooled locally around each entity pair. That number held for exactly one schema, Re-DocRED's 96 Wikipedia relations and 6 entity types. For a support desk, a CRM, a codebase or a personal memory, it was useless.
The first attempt was surgery. We transplanted the fixed relation head into a head that reads relation names. At step 0 the transplant was exact, reproducing the old logits, and then we trained on. It never regained parity: 0.755 against 0.764, and only 0.204 on unseen FewRel relations (8-way). The architecture could read labels. It just hadn't learned to.
The finding that changed the plan was that label variety beats architecture. Our own teacher-annotated data, however large, narrowed zero-shot behaviour to our own labelling style. Pretraining on thousands of knowledge-base relations, each worded in several ways, took unseen FewRel from 0.204 to 0.480. No architectural change we tried came close to that.
The second finding was that the encoder had to move. Keeping the encoder frozen and adding adapters left the linguistic layer bit-identical. But it capped relations at about 0.76: the representation simply didn't carry what document-level relations need. So v7 does it in two stages. Stage A pretrains the encoder itself for relations and entity types. Stage B then trains every head on that encoder, with the linguistic scores gated at every evaluation.
what v6 taught
what v7 does about it
A frozen encoder with adapters capped relations at about 0.76
Pretrain the encoder for knowledge first, then train every head on it
The marker pass was the largest single relation gain (+5.9)
Keep it as the relation pass
Label variety broadened zero-shot far more than any head change
Pretrain on thousands of relation and entity types, worded in several ways
Distant labels hurt in fine-tuning but help as pretraining
Use distant data in stage A only
Teacher labels are precise but incomplete
Positive-unlabelled training throughout
Thresholded zero-shot F1 was 0 before calibration
Ship per-model calibration with the weights
Two Teachers, Because No One Won
We ran a bake-off before committing compute: DeBERTa-v3-large, Ettin-400M and UltraBERT-380M. Each got the same budget, data and recipe, a short knowledge pretraining followed by a short linguistic stage. The selection rule was written down before any run started.
No single encoder won.
DeBERTa led the linguistic tasks and the fixed-schema relations.
UltraBERT led the zero-shot knowledge tasks by 4.2 points, and handles longer windows.
Ettin-400M was behind both on knowledge and 2 points behind on parsing, so we dropped it.
So we trained both, each tuned for its own best result rather than for a matched comparison. They are the two xlarge models, xlarge-u (UltraBERT) and xlarge-d (DeBERTa), and the teachers the smaller models learn from:
UltraBERT-380M
DeBERTa-v3-large
choose it for
open schemas, new relation and entity types, agent memory, long inputs
the most accurate parsing and fixed-schema relations
window
1,024 subwords
512 subwords
stronger at
10-way zero-shot relations, entity types, coreference, memory
SRL, NER, LAS, Re-DocRED, 15-way zero-shot relations (the two tie at 5-way)
One detail cost us a week. UltraBERT's tokenizer splits more words into pieces than DeBERTa's, and splits them with less of the word in the first piece (re|authorized). So reading each word from its first subword, as v6 did, cost UltraBERT SRL recall on long words: 0.652 against DeBERTa's 0.780. Pooling over all of a word's subwords fixed it.
The Architecture: Three Passes, One Encoder
kniv runs one encoder up to three times per window:
Plain pass. The window as text. Every linguistic head reads it, along with coreference and the entity typer.
Label pass. Your relation and type names, with their descriptions, are encoded into vectors. This happens once per schema, and the result is cached.
Marker pass. The window again, with every entity mention marked and a speaker tag before each turn. Every entity pair is scored against every relation, then each kept fact gets its attributes.
Why passes instead of separate models? Small LoRA adapters give the label and marker passes their own capacity on one shared encoder. The plain pass uses the trained encoder itself.
Relations. We kept ATLOP's mention log-sum-exp and localised context pooling. On top sit head and tail extractors, a compact pair representation, cross-attention from labels to the document, and a learned threshold column. A relation is predicted when its score clears that pair's own threshold.
Entity types. Candidate spans are up to 12 words within a sentence. Each is scored against type vectors from the same label encoder that reads relations, so types and relations share one way of reading a schema.
Fact attributes. For every extracted (head, relation, tail), a small head reads the marker pass and predicts:
polarity and modality, as fixed classes;
the holder and the time, as pointers to entities in the window.
Training on Labels We Know Are Incomplete
Much of our relation supervision came from our own LLM annotation of a varied corpus: prose, conversations, technical and business text. We measured those teacher labels against gold. They were precise but incomplete: 0.71 precision, 0.31 recall with gold entities.
Train on that naively and you teach the model that every missing fact is false. Two-thirds of the true facts would become negative examples.
So v7 trains positive-unlabelled throughout:
Every training item carries its own schema.
Relation and type columns outside an item's schema are masked. They are never treated as negatives.
Unlabelled pairs and spans are down-weighted rather than counted as "no relation".
Holdouts were fixed before any training. The 15 standard FewRel zero-shot relations were removed from every training source, so the zero-shot numbers below are real zero-shot.
Training then ran in stages, each gated on the linguistic scores:
knowledge pretraining;
every head jointly;
gold linguistic data added to the mix;
head fine-tunes with the encoder frozen: a predicate-aware SRL role head and a BiLSTM NER head;
a knowledge-only pass;
a coreference pass;
an evidence pass that teaches the relation head which sentences support a fact.
Each stage ran on a single A100 40GB in bf16.
Calibration Was Worth More Than Architecture
The most surprising number of the project was zero. Early on, thresholded zero-shot F1 was 0. Yet the ranking was already right: the correct relation was usually the top-scoring one. The model knew the answer. Its scores were just on the wrong scale for an unseen relation to clear the threshold.
One offset, chosen on held-out data, fixed it. That pattern repeated so often that calibration is now part of the model: calibration.json ships with the weights and holds
per-relation thresholds, chosen on dev;
an offset for relations the model never trained on;
an entity-span offset;
the coreference link bias;
the rule for grouping mentions into entities.
You can change every one of them at run time.
The span offset is the clearest case. Unseen entity types need a lower bar than trained ones. Moving the offset from 0 to about -2 was worth up to 8 points per CrossNER domain, with no retraining.
Calibration also told us where it can't help. On Re-DocRED, a threshold tuned per relation on the test set itself (a cheat, used only as an upper bound) adds at most 1 point. The gold relation is ranked first for 72-73% of facts and is in the top four for 98%. So what remains is choosing pairs and ranking, not thresholds.
What Mattered More Than a Bigger Head
The experiments that moved the numbers changed the supervision. The ones that changed the head, on the same supervision, mostly didn't:
A learned entity linker. Grouping mentions into entities with a trained linker did not beat exact name matching plus coreference. The rule stays.
Distilling one model's relations into the other. Averaging the two teachers' relation decisions is worth +2.7 F1, so we tried to teach UltraBERT DeBERTa's half. It gained 0.35 on Re-DocRED and lost 2 to 3 points of zero-shot. With the encoder frozen, a relation head can't reproduce decisions that come from another encoder's reading of the text. If you need the best relations, run both models and average them.
Type descriptions. We rewrote entity-type descriptions in four styles. No style helped reliably: UltraBERT moved by at most a point, and DeBERTa swung from +7 to -11 depending on the domain.
Bigger typing heads. An MLP span head and hierarchical type schemas changed CrossNER by under a point and cost 3 points on Few-NERD.
Supervised heads on frozen vectors. Probes show that the information for entity typing is in the representations. But no head trained on frozen vectors beat the jointly trained one.
The lesson that runs through the whole project: the limit was usually the data, not the head. Broader, more varied supervision (thousands of relation types, many wordings, incomplete labels handled as incomplete) is what built the knowledge layer. A cleverer head on the same supervision rarely did.
Distilling the Family
The two xlarge models are accurate but large. The smaller models are students: each learns from both teachers at once, on 117,000 windows of varied text the teachers labelled with everything they produce, plus the gold linguistic data.
Two teachers are better than one. We mixed the teachers' outputs per task, with weights chosen on dev, before distilling anything. The mixture beats either teacher on every head: +2.2 points on SRL, +2.7 on relations and 1.3 to 2.2 on entity types. That mixture, not either teacher, is what the students learn to imitate.
What the students learn from. Copying the teachers' final decisions isn't enough for an open schema. The students also learn how the teachers rank every relation for each entity pair and every type for each span, and the vectors the teachers give to relation and type names. That is what lets a student handle a relation it never saw in training. Adding cross-attention layers to the student's relation head on top of that changed nothing.
Attributes have to be distilled too. Trained only on the teacher corpus's hard labels, where 1.7% of facts are negated, the first students never predicted negation at all: negation F1 0.00 for the smallest, 0.30 for large. Distilling the teachers' attribute predictions, and repeating the windows that contain a negated fact, brought large to 0.72, level with the teachers.
What longer training buys. Training the small students three times as long (30,000 steps instead of 10,000) improved relations and zero-shot clearly: tiny gained 4.7 points on Re-DocRED with gold entities and 6.8 on 10-way FewRel. It didn't move NER, SRL or coreference. Those are limited by how much a small encoder can hold, not by how long it trains.
Coreference is where size shows most. On tiny we tried teaching coreference from the teachers' antecedent choices, and then gave the coreference head an adapter of its own on the encoder. Neither moved LitBank (0.610, then 0.608 and 0.606). Below about 70M parameters, coreference is the clearest cost of the smaller size.
Calibration matters even more for students. A student's raw relation scores sit lower than its teacher's. With thresholds chosen on dev, tiny's end-to-end Re-DocRED went from 0.38 to 0.54, with no retraining.
Making It Small Enough to Ship
Each repository ships ONNX graphs and kniv_v7, a small host runtime that turns text into the full analysis with numpy, onnxruntime and tokenizers. No PyTorch is needed. The fp32 graphs decode identically to PyTorch on every check text.
Compression was the hardest engineering of the release.
Plain INT8 destroyed UltraBERT: Re-DocRED went from 0.754 to 0.168. The cause is massive activations. In UltraBERT's layer 14, the inputs to the MLP down-projection reach about 8,000, against a typical value near 4. With one INT8 scale per tensor, the outliers take all the range, and every ordinary value lands in the same few buckets. DeBERTa has the same pattern, milder, in its feed-forward outputs.
FP16 had its own trap. Converting the exported graphs to half precision produced graphs that wouldn't load. Exporting the encoders from PyTorch in half precision, with normalisation kept in fp32, matched fp32 within 0.001 on every task.
SmoothQuant fixed INT8. Per input channel of every feed-forward down-projection, we divide the activations by a scale and multiply the weights by the same scale. That is exact in fp32, and it moves the outliers into the weights, where per-channel INT8 handles them. DeBERTa's relation pass proved the most fragile, so it keeps per-channel INT8 with its down-projections in fp32.

Small models put their weight elsewhere. In tiny, the transformer layers hold only 3.9M parameters. The word-embedding table holds 12.9M and the heads about 38M, and our INT8 recipe, built for the large encoders, had left both in fp32. Quantising the embedding table row by row and the head graphs weight-only took tiny's linguistic graph from 66 MB to 28 MB and halved its INT8 download, at a cost of at most 0.4 points on every task.
Agreement with fp32 is the wrong check. INT8 changes about 15% of the semantic-role arguments the model outputs, a number that looks alarming. Scored against gold, the cost is 0.2 points: the changes are borderline arguments, wrong about as often in either precision. The INT8 gate now scores NER, SRL and coreference against gold, not against fp32.

FP16: a smaller download, and for GPUs.
INT8: CPU speed, within 0.7 points of fp32 on every task, for every model.

The results table above reports the harder setting, every predicate found end to end (0.810). The relations row supplies the reference entities to both systems; kniv's fully end-to-end score is 0.627.

Coreference: level.
The linguistic layer: kniv's reported scores are higher on every task, by up to 4 points.
Document-level relations: kniv is 26 points ahead. Even handed every candidate entity pair explicitly, at 5.4 times the calls, GPT-6 reached only 0.545.
The relation gap has a clear cause. 75% of GPT-6's misses were pairs it never proposed, and 81% of its false facts were on pairs that hold no relation. Reading a whole document and deciding which pairs are related is exactly what the marker pass is built for.
Speed and cost. We timed both on the same job:

On this workload, kniv's median is about 90 times faster than the hosted call, on a laptop CPU, with no per-message API fees and nothing leaving the machine.
How the comparison was made: GPT-6's scores come from our v6 annotator bake-off, with zero-shot prompts. Its linguistic rows (POS, lemma, parsing, NER, SRL) were scored on 300-item samples of each test set, and coreference and relations on the full test sets. kniv's scores are on the full test sets throughout, taking the better of the two xlarge models per task. kniv's relation scores use thresholds tuned on dev. The metrics are task-specific: accuracy for POS and lemma, attachment scores for parsing, F1 elsewhere.
Where It Breaks
The guide in each repository covers these in detail, with workarounds.
Document-level relations trail specialist systems. About 29% of gold facts are missed, mostly borderline decisions just under the threshold. Lowering the relation offsets trades precision for recall: you'll find more of the missed facts, and more false ones with them. It doesn't fix the underlying limit. As the calibration section showed, even thresholds tuned on the test set add at most a point of F1, because the remaining errors are in which pairs get related and how relations rank.
Near-synonym relations get confused ("located in" against "headquarters location"). Don't put both in one schema. Merge them downstream if you need both.
Facts are per window, up to a page of text. Nothing is linked across windows or documents; that's your memory layer's job.
Conversation attribution isn't perfect. A relative's location can be attributed to the speaker as well ("my sister lives in Porto" can also give the user Porto). With UltraBERT, "you" in an assistant's turn can become an entity of its own.
Negation and reported speech are the weakest attributes. DeBERTa separates plans from assertions well ("I work at Acme. Next month I'm joining Northstar." gives an asserted fact and a planned one); UltraBERT misses the plan in that example. But in our own spot checks, "I don't work there anymore" can still come back as a positive fact, and "Leon says I work at Northstar" is marked asserted, held by the speaker, rather than reported. Treat polarity and modality as signals to check, not guarantees.
The smaller models miss more, and say more. The students return more facts per message than the teachers, many with low margins, so filter on margin for precision. tiny and small trail the teachers by 4 to 17 points on NER, SRL, coreference, relations and entity types, medium by 2 to 13, and each card lists its gaps.
English only.
What Ships
Six models, Apache-2.0: tiny, small, medium, large, xlarge-d and xlarge-u.
Each repository holds:
the PyTorch weights;
calibration.json;
a label bank of 1,423 relations and 1,559 entity types with descriptions, as starting points for your schema;
the tokenizer;
ONNX graphs in fp32, FP16 and INT8;
the kniv_v7 runtime with a quick start;
GUIDE.md, which covers choosing between the models, tuning thresholds and working around the known failure modes.
pip install onnxruntime tokenizers numpy huggingface_hub
Try It, Break It
kniv v7 is our answer to the opening contrast: a local model that reads the schema you give it, at the cost of a tagger. The code to reproduce every stage is on GitHub.
We'd most like to hear about schemas that break it. Bring a domain we haven't tested, a relation it confuses, or a conversation it misreads, and open an issue or reach out directly.
kniv is part of the Rustic AI initiative, built by Dragonscale.

items.title: How do we get to plug-and-play robots?
items.summary:
Back to Articles
How do we get to plug-and-play robots?
Community Article Published
October 30, 2026 Upvote 5
Luca Cilio lucakae Follow projectsim
At Long Horizon in San Francisco, I listened to Felipe Chavez Cortes, co-founder and CEO of Robot.com, talk about what it takes to deploy a robot. One of his slides compared policies running as is with systems that added planning, memory, outcome checks or safety mechanisms around them.
A simple summary of the talk would be: even with a generalist model as the starting point, there is still so much manual work around fine-tuning, testing, integration and system engineering before the robot can be deployed.
Reading the papers behind the talk, alongside the recent generalist-model releases, made me wonder how much of that work will still fall to the team deploying the robot. Policies are carrying more knowledge into unfamiliar situations, while AI agents are beginning to take on some of the diagnosis and experimentation that engineers do today. Progress in both directions brings us closer to plug-and-play robot systems. It also raises a question for the labs building them: how do we give those models enough experience, and test them thoroughly enough, before asking customers to rely on them?
The work between a policy and a deployment
Some of that manual work goes into something that sounds simple: deciding when an action is finished. VoLo combines π0.5 with a vision-language model that plans and monitors execution, plus grasp and placement tools. In its hardware evaluation, the full system completed 18 of 42 trials across 14 tasks, compared with 6 of 42 for the standalone policy. That is a substantial improvement, although it still leaves more than half the trials unsuccessful.
One of the paper's simulated failures shows why checking the outcome is a problem of its own. The monitor concludes that an orange is in a white bowl while the orange is still on the table. The system has a mechanism for checking progress, but the answer it receives is wrong.
The monitor reports that the orange is in the white bowl. The orange is still on the table. Image from the VoLo paper, showing a simulated trial.
This is where keeping track of the scene can help. POT-VLA maintains persistent 3D records of task objects, using them both to guide actions and to check relations such as whether one object is inside another. When an object becomes occluded, the system keeps track of the uncertainty and can request another observation. The policy is also fine-tuned to use this information, so improving the outcome check involves changes to both the controller and the information available to it.
Even a correctly executed action can leave the robot stuck, though. In a simulated example from BATON, a top grasp lifts a can successfully, but the combined height of the can and gripper prevents placement inside a microwave. A side grasp works. The grasp has to serve the placement, which is why BATON records constraints on skills and their transitions: the next operation needs to influence the choice the robot makes now.
For that coordination to work, the policy must reliably follow the planner's instructions. Tool-Aligned VLA post-trains policies to execute bounded subtasks, follow precise instructions and report progress. In several of its simulated comparisons, putting a planner above a conventionally trained policy actually reduced success. Training the executor for the way it would be called helped the two work together.
These are some of the decisions a deployment team has to get right: what the robot remembers, how its actions fit together, and what evidence allows it to move on. A model with a large repertoire of skills helps enormously, but the team still needs to turn that repertoire into a system that completes the job.
What is beginning to carry over
The encouraging change is how much learned competence can now carry over to a new setting. In Figure's Helix 2.5 evaluation, three behaviours—tidying, towel folding and bedmaking—were each fine-tuned on task data collected elsewhere, then tested in 30 unseen homes with unseen objects. Each task used one fixed checkpoint across the homes. With the task data, architecture and training procedure held constant, pretraining on Figure's Index human dataset raised full-task completion from 9% to 56%. The tasks had been taught, but teaching them did not have to start again in every home.
Something similar is happening across robot hardware. PI's π0.7 folds laundry with a dual-arm UR5e setup despite having no laundry demonstrations for that robot. The robot was present in training on other tasks. The result brings together knowledge about the embodiment and about folding without demonstrations of that particular robot-task combination.
When the task itself changes, the question becomes how much new experience is needed. Generalist's GEN-1.5 accepts physical demonstrations as prompts: sensor observations and action trajectories recorded with handheld grippers or a robot. Across ten short tasks, one 3–12 second demonstration produced 59% average success without gradient updates. Five minutes of data per task and ten fine-tuning steps produced 83%. Both the data budget and adaptation method changed, but the small amount of task-specific experience is what makes these results interesting.
Two adaptation settings across ten short tasks. Chart based on Generalist's reported results; whiskers show the reported standard deviations.
Skild's S1 uses an egocentric video of a person performing the task. Its selected demonstrations include plant potting, pancake preparation and kit assembly, with tasks lasting up to ten minutes that the company reports were absent from training. These longer sequences suggest how a demonstration can communicate the organisation of a job, drawing on skills the robot has already learned.
In these prompting results, a demonstration can specify a job using skills the model already has. That makes a few seconds of task-specific data useful, while leaving the result dependent on a much larger body of prior learning.
Generalist demonstrates physical prompting and adaptation with GEN-1.5.
The remaining difficulty is what happens when the robot tries the task and fails. A demonstration may communicate the intended sequence perfectly without explaining why the can will not fit through the microwave opening. Someone still has to diagnose the problem and find a change that works.
Adaptation can itself become a capability
Some of the research is beginning to put that responsibility on AI systems. In Recursive Harness Distillation, a more capable agent experiments with policy interventions and writes a playbook for a lighter agent. The playbook is refined using the lighter agent's execution. One illustrated revision develops a simple retry instruction into guidance to inspect a failed grasp, check the contact between object and fingers, and verify that the object follows the gripper. The result is reusable guidance for handling a failure that might otherwise require an engineer's attention.
Google's Gemini 4 Argon robotics demonstrations take on more of this preparation. In one example, the model constructs an articulated MuJoCo twin of a foot-pedal bin, practises balance and pedal stepping, then controls a Spot robot to dispose of a can. It uses an existing manipulation skill and explicit instructions to verify foot and hand alignment. A separate example has it inspect logs and video of a simple arm's pick-and-place attempts, test fixes and retry.
These are curated demonstrations with substantial instructions and tooling, but they show parts of the work from the deployment talk becoming things a model can do: inspecting an attempt, proposing a change and trying it. A stronger underlying policy gives this process more to work with. The fix may be a different grasp or subgoal, rather than an entirely new manipulation skill.
Finding that fix can still be hard. The last few failures may be precisely the ones the system cannot diagnose, and the orange on the table is a reminder that a confident explanation can be wrong. The system needs experience to learn from and a way to check whether its changes actually help.
The experience has to come from somewhere
That need begins long before deployment. The transfer results above depend on a model having already learned enough to handle a new room, robot or instruction. A lab trying to build that competence needs many more interactions than any one customer will ever see.
Collecting them physically means paying for robot time, operators and resets, with each new arrangement requiring another attempt. Simulation lets a team run many copies of a task, change the starting conditions and generate experience in parallel. For a task like the microwave example, that could mean practising across different can positions, openings and grasp choices before the policy reaches a real kitchen.
NVIDIA’s work on synthetic training data gives a sense of the volume simulation can provide. For GR00T N1, NVIDIA reports generating 780,000 simulated trajectories in 11 hours using DexMimicGen, covering 6,500 hours of trajectory time across its pre- and post-training datasets. The process transforms and replays segments of human demonstrations in new configurations, retaining successful attempts. Human examples still supply the behaviour; simulation expands the experience that can be built from them.
GR00T N1 combines several sources of experience. Its synthetic data includes both physics-simulated trajectories and generated videos. Figure from the GR00T N1 paper.
More experience also creates more choices: different datasets, training methods and checkpoints can all produce different policies. A lab needs to know which of those changes actually improves the robot. As the policy covers more tasks, testing every version on hardware becomes an increasingly expensive way to find out.
Simulation allows those versions to face the same held-out situations, repeatedly, while varying particular conditions to find where performance breaks down. In SIMPLER, simulated rollouts tracked real-world policy rankings more closely than action-prediction error on recorded demonstrations did on the tested Google Robot tasks. The robot's behaviour during execution revealed something that predicting actions in a dataset did not.
Those evaluations can then guide the next round of training. If a policy struggles with a particular placement or object arrangement, the team has a concrete target for additional experience and a test to run again afterwards. When a new deployment exposes another gap, the same process can extend to it. In some cases, simulation can supply the task example itself: GEN-1.5 used simulated rollouts as prompts for a real robot on a subset of tasks, without another training run. Experience from simulation could guide the action directly, as well as provide data for updating the policy.
Training, evaluation and adaptation are connected by this repeated use of experience: learning from it, testing what was learned, and finding what is still missing. Simulation can support that process while the foundation model is being built, while a team prepares it for a job, and as new failures appear.
The simulation has to preserve the difficulty
There is a condition on all of this: the simulated task must teach or test something that carries over to the real one. If the fingers pass through the microwave opening, or unrealistic friction keeps the can attached to the gripper, generating more attempts only reinforces the wrong lesson.
The same problem can invalidate an evaluation. In SIMPLER, replaying a real robot's actions initially produced a missed grasp in simulation. Calibrating the simulated controller made it track the real motion more closely and reproduce the grasp. Without that correction, a team could mistake a simulator error for a weakness in the policy.
Real execution on the left; simulated replay before and after controller calibration in the middle and on the right. The action sequence is the same. Figure from SIMPLER.
This is why useful simulation requires more than an attractive reconstruction. Geometry, appearance, articulation and physical properties determine what the robot sees and what its actions do. Which details need the most care depends on the task: clearance is central to the microwave example, while the can-pickup comparison exposes the importance of matching the controller's response. Real-robot checks establish which conclusions from simulation deserve to be trusted.
Creating those environments is itself a substantial part of the work. If every new task requires weeks of manual construction and calibration, simulation inherits the scaling problem it is supposed to help solve. Teams need to be able to build, vary and reuse interactive tasks without rebuilding the entire experiment each time.
How plug-and-play could arrive
The prospect that makes this research exciting is how much more of the preparation could carry into the next deployment. A foundation model can bring a larger repertoire of skills. Broad evaluation can uncover weaknesses before a customer encounters them. And an AI system can help work out what a particular job still requires. The customer may see a robot that gets to work quickly because a great deal of learning and testing has already happened elsewhere.
The measure of progress is whether this preparation produces robots that handle more jobs reliably, with less specialist effort for each new one.
This is what we are building towards with projectsim. The assets and scenes are the starting point; we want to turn them into simulations where teams can run policies, generate useful experience and understand how their robots behave. A team should be able to reuse an environment, vary its tasks and test a new policy without starting the simulation work again. Making that practical would give robotics labs more room to pursue the learning and testing that make the next deployment easier.
If you’re training, evaluating or adapting a robot policy, we’d love to hear what you’re working on. Reach out and tell us what you need to simulate.

items.title: Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams
items.summary:
Cost management for generative AI is a shared responsibility between the teams that build applications and the teams accountable for cloud spend. Many teams start by comparing per-model token rates and asking application teams to shorten prompts. Those steps help, but they don’t answer the questions that finance and engineering leaders ask as usage scales: which team spent this, on which workload, and was that spend inside an approved budget?
Agentic workloads make those questions more pressing. A conversational assistant typically issues one model invocation per user turn. An agentic workflow, such as an AI coding assistant that plans a change, reads files, calls tools, and iterates, issues many invocations per task and carries a larger context on each one. Token consumption therefore scales with the degree of autonomy you grant the workflow and the size of the context it carries, rather than with the number of user interactions. Because consumption is a function of how a workload is designed and operated, cost management for generative AI is an architectural and operational discipline. Published averages are a poor substitute for your own numbers: use the AWS Pricing Calculator and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page to model rates, and use Step 2 of this post to measure what your workloads actually consume.
The fix isn’t a cheaper model or a smaller prompt. It’s an operating model: a repeatable loop that attributes every dollar to an owner, makes every request observable, alerts on and enforces budgets before overspend compounds, optimizes the platform defaults that drive most waste, and reviews the whole system on a cadence.
In this post, you learn how to manage Amazon Bedrock cost in five steps. You attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, control spend with budgets and enforcement, optimize the platform defaults that drive most avoidable spend, and operate a review cadence that turns data into decisions. This approach is built from AWS building blocks, and you can customize it and apply it to your own environment. The post is written for two audiences: FinOps practitioners who own attribution, chargeback, budgets, and anomaly review, and platform engineering teams who own logging, request metadata, enforcement, and routing defaults.
The operating model in one view
Five stages, run as a loop. Attribute: every Amazon Bedrock dollar lands on an identity, team, and application in the billing pipeline. Observe: every request is logged with enough metadata to explain what generated the spend. Enforce: budgets have teeth, with alerts at minimum and hard blocks where the risk demands them. Optimize: the platform defaults (model routing, caching, token limits) remove waste centrally instead of asking every team to be careful. Operate: a small scorecard and a review cadence turn the data into decisions. FinOps leads stages one and five. Platform engineering leads two through four. The review is joint. The stages are sequenced deliberately. Each one depends on the ones before it, and teams that jump straight to optimization without attribution and observability are guessing.
Figure 1: The five-stage operating model, run as a continuous loop
Stage 1: Attribute every dollar
You can’t manage what you can’t attribute, and everything downstream (chargeback, budgets, enforcement, anomaly detection) depends on this stage. The foundation is the granular cost attribution of Amazon Bedrock (see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock): Amazon Bedrock automatically attributes inference costs to the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal that made the call, across all models, with no resources to manage. The caller’s ARN lands in the line_item_iam_principal column of the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0, and coverage spans IAM users, roles, federated identities, and API keys.
Setup is four steps:
Turn on IAM principal data in your CUR 2.0 data export.
Tag your IAM principals with business dimensions such as team, application, and cost center. For federated access, configure your identity provider to pass session names and tags through OIDC or SAML claims.
Activate those tags as cost allocation tags in AWS Billing (console or the UpdateCostAllocationTagsStatus API).
Analyze the tags: they surface in CUR 2.0 with an iamPrincipal/ prefix (for example, iamPrincipal/team) and appear in AWS Cost Explorer under the IAM category within 24–48 hours of activation, ready for filtering and grouping by team, application, or cost center.
This is invoice-grade, per-identity attribution with no custom infrastructure.
The shared-role problem
The pattern that deserves the most attention is the shared-role problem, because it is where most platforms silently lose attribution. A large language model (LLM) gateway that calls Amazon Bedrock through a single IAM role attributes every dollar to that one role, eliminating per-user visibility entirely. The fix is per-user session management. The gateway assumes the Amazon Bedrock invocation role once per user, passing the user’s identity as the role session name and their attributes as session tags, then caches those credentials for up to an hour (one AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) call per user per hour, not per request).
This needs two roles: a gateway execution role holding sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession permissions, and the Amazon Bedrock invocation role it assumes. The result is line_item_iam_principal entries like assumed-role/BedrockRuntimeRole/gw-alex, each carrying its user’s tags: per-user and per-tenant attribution restored behind a shared gateway.
import boto3
sts = boto3.client("sts")
# One call per user; cache the returned credentials up to 1 hour
response = sts.assume_role(
RoleArn="arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/BedrockRuntimeRole",
RoleSessionName="gw-alex", # the user, not the gateway
Tags=[
{"Key": "team", "Value": "sales-ai"},
{"Key": "application", "Value": "renewal-agent"},
{"Key": "costCenter", "Value": "CC-2041"}
]
)
A note on application inference profiles and Projects
Amazon Bedrock offers two more attribution mechanisms, each suited to a different pattern. Application inference profiles are pre-created, per-application resources on the bedrock-runtime endpoint that carry cost allocation tags. You create one profile per application per model per AWS Region, and callers reference the profile ARN, which fits teams with a small and stable set of applications and models. Projects and workspaces serve the bedrock-mantle endpoint (Responses API, Chat Completions API). A project isn’t tied to a specific model, so a single project ID spans many models, which fits teams whose model usage changes frequently. You pass the project ID at client initialization, and its tags flow to CUR 2.0 and Cost Explorer (see Manage AI costs with Amazon Bedrock Projects). Projects are the attribution path for OpenAI-compatible workloads on Amazon Bedrock.
For bedrock-runtime workloads, we recommend IAM principal attribution through session tags as the primary mechanism. It scales with your identity system, requires no pre-created resources, and covers every model and API operation. Application inference profiles work well when a small, stable set of business units needs invoice-grade billing separation without changes to identity design. Use projects for bedrock-mantle workloads that use the Responses API or Chat Completions API.
Stage 2: Make every request observable
CUR tells you who spent. Invocation logs tell you what happened. Amazon Bedrock supports model invocation logging of request data, response data, and metadata to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), or both. Use Amazon CloudWatch for fast operational queries and S3 plus Amazon Athena for long-term business intelligence (BI) access. Treat logging as infrastructure, not a manual toggle: provision the log group or bucket through code, define retention and encryption policies, and validate delivery during environment setup. If logging exists only in development or only in one Region, your cost program becomes fragmentary the moment usage grows.
Logging also closes the latency gap: CUR attribution lags roughly 24 hours, but CloudWatch plus OpenTelemetry can power near-real-time dashboards showing per-developer spend within minutes (Analyzing Claude Code usage with CloudWatch and OpenTelemetry demonstrates this end to end).
Request metadata for workload-level attribution
Raw logs answer identity-level questions. To answer workload-level questions (which feature, workflow, or tenant generated the tokens), stamp request metadata on every call. Amazon Bedrock captures this metadata in the invocation logs for later analysis:
The following example uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock through the US cross-Region inference profile. For the full list of models, see Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock. For availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
response = client.converse(
modelId="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5",
messages=[...],
requestMetadata={
"application": "renewal-copilot",
"workflow": "renewal-risk-summary",
"tenant": "enterprise-sales",
"agent": "renewal-agent"
}
)
Amazon Bedrock doesn’t enforce request metadata, and teams drift into inconsistent schemas quickly when every application does its own thing. The platform team should inject mandatory metadata centrally in a shared SDK wrapper or gateway, normalize the key set, and treat metadata coverage as a platform health metric.
Diagnostic queries
With logs and metadata in place, CloudWatch Logs Insights answers the standing questions. Who consumes the most tokens:
fields @timestamp, identity.arn as caller, modelId,
input.inputTokenCount as inTokens,
output.outputTokenCount as outTokens
| stats sum(inTokens + outTokens) as totalTokens,
count(*) as calls
by caller, modelId
| sort totalTokens desc
| limit 25
The same query grouped by requestMetadata.application and requestMetadata.workflow instead of caller produces the workload-level leaderboard: the view product and engineering teams will ask FinOps for the moment chargeback conversations start.
Note: Field paths shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema, which may vary by model, API operation, and logging configuration.
Stage 3: Enforce budgets
With attribution and observability in place, enforcement becomes an architecture choice rather than a wish. There are three viable tiers. The right one depends on your spend velocity, your risk tolerance for overspend, and how your tools connect to Amazon Bedrock.
Tier 1: Monitor and alert (no blocking)
Amazon Bedrock writes principal identity into the billing pipeline automatically. You put AWS Budgets on top for threshold alerts, with the OpenTelemetry dashboards from Stage 2 closing the 24-hour CUR gap for day-to-day visibility. Nothing to deploy, native AWS billing, and no added latency on inference calls. It works with tools that call Amazon Bedrock directly. Nothing can hard-stop spend, so you see the problem after it happens. Right for early adoption, where alerting plus human intervention is sufficient. Two builder guides walk through it: Limiting Bedrock usage and controlling costs, and Deep dive on managing Bedrock in Claude Code with AWS Budgets and Tags.
Tier 2: IAM tag enforcement (deny on breach)
An aggregator AWS Lambda function tallies per-user token and dollar counters in Amazon DynamoDB from invocation log data. When a user breaches their threshold, the function adds their identity to a shared IAM deny policy (denying bedrock:*) until a monthly reset or admin override. This enforcement runs entirely on IAM and Amazon Bedrock logging, with no third-party component in the inference path, and it works with tools that call Amazon Bedrock directly. The Guidance for Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock in the AWS Solutions Library provides a deployable variant. It checks each user’s usage against per-user and per-team limits when it issues credentials, and withholds credentials once a user exceeds their limit. Because that check uses usage telemetry emitted by the client, its figures can differ from CUR. In either form, enforcement is asynchronous. A block takes effect seconds to minutes after the breaching call for an IAM policy update, or at the next credential refresh for the credential check. Your platform team owns the pipeline. This tier is right for teams that need real enforcement, can tolerate that lag, and want to keep third-party software out of the data path.
Tier 3: Gateway enforcement (synchronous block)
A gateway sits in the inference data path and enforces budgets synchronously, returning HTTP 429 the moment a user or team exceeds their limit. You get sub-second blocking, per-user model allowlists, token rate limits, and centrally enforced routing rules. The trade-off: a component in the data path that must be deployed, scaled, and security-reviewed. Clients must be configured to send their requests through the gateway.
For Claude Code and Claude Desktop fleets, the Claude apps gateway for AWS is the official recommendation. It ships inside the CLI binary and runs as a single stateless container backed by PostgreSQL. It provides OIDC identity, centrally managed policy, OpenTelemetry telemetry, multi-Region Amazon Bedrock routing, and per-user/group/org spend caps out of the box. For mixed-model workloads spanning multiple providers, general-purpose gateways remain the right choice: LiteLLM through the Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate reference architecture, or a serverless alternative described in Build a proactive AI cost management system for Amazon Bedrock, Part 2.
Choosing a tier
Two factors dominate.
Connectivity: If developers call Amazon Bedrock directly with no proxy, only Tiers 1 and 2 are viable.
Spend velocity: If spend is already in the millions per month, build enforcement now. If alerts can hold the line for another quarter, invest in Stages 1 and 2 first and add enforcement when the data demands it.
Most organizations should phase it: observe at Tier 1, then step up. Treat all three as bridges, not destinations: the Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens already codifies agent cost governance as a first-class architectural concern, and the attribution foundation from Stage 1 is what any managed enforcement will sit on.
Stage 4: Optimize the defaults
Most Amazon Bedrock waste is not individual carelessness. It is platform defaults nobody set. The two highest-impact levers are both platform-controlled.
Model routing
Not every task needs a frontier model. Routine completions (boilerplate, linting suggestions, small refactors) can run on smaller, cheaper models with quality reserved for complex reasoning, through intelligent prompt routing within a model family or routing rules at the gateway (see Reduce costs and latency with Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing and prompt caching for the full walkthrough). Which workflows can downshift is an empirical question: pull the workload leaderboard from Stage 2, run a quality evaluation on the cheaper model for the top entries, and route what passes. For agentic coding fleets, where boilerplate dominates call volume, more than half of calls landing on cheaper models is an achievable target.
Prompt caching
Prompt caching rewards stable repeated prefixes. As of October 2026, the published Amazon Bedrock pricing for Anthropic Claude models in US East (N. Virginia) bills a cache write at 1.25x the base input rate with the 5-minute time-to-live (TTL) (2x with the 1-hour TTL). A cache read is billed at 0.1x the base input rate on Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and at 0.05x on Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5. Check the pricing page for your model and Region, because these multipliers vary by model and can change. The break-even math is friendlier than teams assume. With the 5-minute TTL, a single reuse already pays for the write, and ten calls against a stable prefix cost roughly a fifth of the uncached price (about 22 percent at a 0.1x read rate, 17 percent at 0.05x). The only losing case is writes that are never re-read, which cost 25 percent extra with the 5-minute TTL and double with the 1-hour TTL. So the platform dashboard should track cache-read volume against cache-write volume per workflow. A low read ratio means the prefix is not actually stable (usually a timestamp or session ID embedded before the cache point).
Candidates surface directly from the invocation logs:
fields requestMetadata.workflow as workflow, modelId,
input.inputTokenCount as inTokens
| stats count(*) as calls,
avg(inTokens) as avgInputTokens,
sum(inTokens) as totalInputTokens
by workflow, modelId
| filter calls > 50 and avgInputTokens > 2000
| sort totalInputTokens desc
| limit 25
Note: Field paths shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema, which may vary by model, API operation, and logging configuration.
Application-level optimization
A third class of savings (just-in-time retrieval instead of stuffed context, compaction of long conversations, distilling stable high-volume workflows onto smaller models) belongs to application teams rather than the platform. The platform’s job is to make those savings visible: publish the per-workflow token leaderboard, set token limits per model and workflow, and let the teams that own expensive workflows see exactly where they stand.
Stage 5: Operate the loop
The first four stages produce data. This one turns it into decisions. The platform team runs a standing health dashboard with four signals:
Model mix: Which models are called and how often, the direct measure of routing discipline.
Failed request rates: Errors, throttles, and timeouts. Each retry adds latency, and a client-side timeout on a request that still completes on the service side can be billed twice, once for the abandoned call and once for the retry.
Cache effectiveness: The read-versus-write ratio from Stage 4.
Metadata coverage: The percentage of production calls with complete metadata. Every uncovered call is an attribution blind spot that quietly degrades every other number.
When a signal drifts, the remediation is a policy change (routing rules, token limits, metadata enforcement), not an email asking teams to be careful.
The money loop
FinOps runs the money loop on the same data. When attribution is clean, anomaly detection becomes an investigation stream rather than a panicked all-hands: a spike in a tagged team or application triggers a lookup in the Stage 2 leaderboard, not a war room. Chargeback runs from CUR groupings by team and application.
Scorecard
The following thresholds are starting points, not prescriptions. Calibrate them against your own fleet data and pricing tier before adopting them as policy.
Dimension
Metric
Green
Yellow
Red
Unit economics
Cost per successful outcome
≤ budget
1–1.5x budget
>1.5x budget
Per-dev cost
Daily spend per developer
<$100
$100–$300
>$300
Model routing
% of calls to cost-efficient-models
>50%
30–50%
<30%
Cache efficiency
Cache-read hit ratio
>60%
30–60%
<30%
Green means the workload operates inside its economic envelope. Yellow means routing or caching discipline is slipping. Red means spend is concentrating in premium models or uncached context, and the Stage 3 and 4 controls are the remediation path. Review this scorecard on a regular cadence (weekly for high-velocity fleets, biweekly otherwise) and treat it as the joint FinOps-plus-platform decision surface.
Conclusion
In this post, you learned how to build a five-stage operating model that takes Amazon Bedrock spend from uncontrolled to fully governed:
Attribute every dollar to an owner using IAM principal tags, session tags, and CUR 2.0.
Observe every request through model invocation logging and stamped request metadata.
Enforce budgets at the tier that matches your risk: monitor-only, IAM deny on breach, or synchronous gateway blocking.
Optimize platform defaults with intelligent prompt routing and prompt caching to remove waste centrally.
Operate a scorecard and review cadence that turns telemetry into policy decisions.
Notice the first row of that scorecard: cost per successful outcome, not cost per call. That distinction is where this playbook hands off. Everything here makes Amazon Bedrock spend visible, attributable, capped, and efficient, but a workflow can be perfectly efficient and still not be worth running. Deciding that requires measuring the agent against the human process it replaced, which is a product and analytics discipline rather than a FinOps one. What the cost platform contributes is the foundation: clean attribution and per-workflow cost data are exactly the inputs that outcome measurement joins against.
Build the five stages and you can answer, end to end: who spent it, why, and whether it was controlled. That is what it means to manage Amazon Bedrock cost, and it is the difference between a monthly bill review and an operating model.
To get started, deploy the Guidance for Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock reference architecture for Stages 1–3, then use the cost attribution best practices documentation to configure your tagging strategy.
