items.title: Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
items.summary:
Coding agents now build working web apps: a dashboard, a product page, a prototype that a product team wants to try. The fastest way to review that work is to open the app, use it, ask for a change, and check the result. That loop works well when the app keeps running where the agent edits it, so each change shows up in the browser within seconds. When the app must be copied out and deployed somewhere else first, every change waits for a deployment, and the review slows down to that pace.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with your choice of agent framework and foundation model (FM). AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, runs each agent session in its own isolated microVM. With Session endpoints, you can open an app running in that session from your own browser. Session Endpoints give each session an authenticated URL that forwards each request’s HTTP method, path, query string, and body, and WebSocket connections, to the ports you allow. You can watch the page update as the agent saves each file.
In this post, you deploy a coding agent that keeps a Vite website running in its session, then open one local page with a chat on the left and the live website on the right. You ask the agent to switch the site to a dark color theme, follow its steps as they stream in, and watch the website change without a refresh. Finally, you look at what happens internally: a second port in the same session, and the requests the Session endpoint refuses.
The complete sample, including the notebook this post follows, is in the 14-remote-access folder of the agentcore-samples GitHub repo.
How Session endpoints work
Each session gets its own Session endpoint, and six details shape how you use it.
You choose which ports it reaches. You set allowedPorts when you call CreateAgentRuntime: 1–5 entries, each a single port or a range within 8000–12000, excluding the reserved platform ports. Allowing a port doesn’t start a server, so your application must listen on it, bound to 0.0.0.0.
The URL arrives with the session. The InvokeAgentRuntime response carries it in the X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Endpoint-Url header, which SDKs that model it expose as sessionEndpointUrl.
Every request is authenticated. For a runtime that uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), each HTTP request, HTTP/2 stream, and WebSocket handshake carries a Signature Version 4 (SigV4) signature. The caller also needs bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on the runtime and its runtime endpoint. For a runtime with an inbound JSON Web Token (JWT) authorizer, each request carries a bearer token instead. Knowing the URL doesn’t grant access.
The host name selects the port. Your client connects on port 443 regardless of the target port, and a prefix on the host name chooses the port inside the session:
https://8090--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/index.html
https://8081--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/status
It carries the protocols your server speaks. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 requests, including server-sent events and gRPC, and WebSocket connections all pass through. This walkthrough uses HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket.
It’s scoped to one session. The URL needs credentials on every request and lasts only as long as the session, so use it to build, test, and review what your agent produces. To serve an app to your users, deploy it to a hosting service such as AWS Amplify Hosting.
A browser can’t add a SigV4 signature or a bearer token to the requests a page makes on its own, so the Session endpoint client in the bedrock-agentcore SDK can open a local endpoint on your machine. Your browser opens http://localhost:8088, and the local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and WebSocket handshake before forwarding it.
A Session endpoint is different from a runtime endpoint, which AgentCore runtime already provides. Use a runtime endpoint, such as DEFAULT, to reach your agent, which controls which version of it callers will reach. InvokeAgentRuntime calls resolve through it, so you can keep development and production on different versions and promote or roll back without changing callers. Use a Session endpoint to see what your agent runs in its session, such as a web preview. It’s an authenticated URL that reaches only the ports you allow, works with whichever version the session runs, and stops working when the session ends. For complete documentation, refer to Connect to runtime sessions through a session endpoint.
Solution overview
The sample has four parts. A coding agent runs in the session on port 8080 and edits the website’s files with four tools: list, read, write, and edit. The agent starts a Vite development server on port 8090, which serves the website and pushes each saved change to the browser over its hot-reload WebSocket. On your machine, PreviewApp serves the preview page, sends your prompts to InvokeAgentRuntime, and opens a local endpoint for the website. As Figure 1 shows, the preview page loads the website from the Vite development server on port 8090 through the local endpoint and the Session endpoint, and sends your prompts through InvokeAgentRuntime to the agent on port 8080. The numbers show the order of the steps for one request.
Figure 1: Solution architecture
Before step 1, PreviewApp has already called InvokeAgentRuntime once to start the session, which starts the agent and the Vite development server. PreviewApp read the Session endpoint URL from that response and opened a local endpoint for port 8090. The numbered steps in Figure 1 then follow one request for a change:
The site pane of the preview page loads the website from the local endpoint on localhost:8088. The local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and the WebSocket handshake, and forwards them to the Session endpoint. The Session endpoint checks the signature and the port against allowedPorts, then forwards them to the Vite development server on port 8090. The page keeps the Vite hot-reload WebSocket open.
You send a prompt from the chat pane. PreviewApp sends it to InvokeAgentRuntime as a standard AWS API call signed with your AWS credentials, and the runtime delivers it to the agent on port 8080. The agent’s steps stream back to the chat pane as it works.
The agent calls Claude Haiku 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock to decide what to change.
The agent reads the site’s files and saves the ones it changes. The Vite development server serves those files and watches them for changes.
When a file is saved, Vite pushes the change over the WebSocket opened in step 1, back through the Session endpoint and the local endpoint, and the site pane updates without a refresh.
From the notebook, PreviewApp reads the agent’s /status route on port 8081 through the same Session endpoint. Only the port changes.
Port 8080 isn’t in allowedPorts, because InvokeAgentRuntime reaches the agent without going through the Session endpoint.
Prerequisites
To follow the walkthrough, you need:
An AWS account in an AWS Region where AgentCore runtime Session endpoints are available, with credentials configured.
Permissions to create an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, upload to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and create a runtime, plus bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime and bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on that runtime and its DEFAULT runtime endpoint. For details, refer to IAM permissions for AgentCore runtime.
Python 3.10 or later, with bedrock-agentcore 1.25.2 or later and boto3 1.43.122 or later.
Git, to clone the sample repo, and a Jupyter environment, such as JupyterLab or Visual Studio Code with the Jupyter extension, to run the notebook.
Access to Claude Haiku 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock. For model availability by Region, refer to Regional availability by models.
Node.js 22 or later with npm, which the deployment script uses to package the agent and the website.
The sample deploys the agent as a zip file in Amazon S3 with direct code deployment for Node.js, so you don’t need Docker or an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository. Session endpoints work with microVM runtimes, not with the Instances compute type, and Session endpoint URLs are reachable over public HTTPS. AWS PrivateLink isn’t supported for inbound connections.
Deploy the agent and its website
First, you deploy the runtime, and the configuration you choose here decides which ports the Session endpoint can reach. The deployment script bundles the agent into one file, adds the website and its dependencies for the runtime’s Linux on Arm64 system, uploads the zip to Amazon S3, and creates the runtime.
The following excerpt from deploy.py shows the two settings that matter for this post. protocolConfiguration says where the agent listens for InvokeAgentRuntime, and allowedPorts lists the ports the Session endpoint can reach: 8090 for the website and 8081 for the agent’s status route. Port 8080 isn’t in the list, because InvokeAgentRuntime reaches the agent without it. For the port and path settings, refer to Configure your agent’s serving port and invocation path.
agentRuntimeArtifact={"codeConfiguration": {
"code": {"s3": {"bucket": code_bucket(), "prefix": S3_PREFIX}},
"runtime": "NODE_22",
"entryPoint": ["app.js"],
}},
protocolConfiguration={"serverProtocol": "HTTP", "port": 8080, "path": "/invocations"},
allowedPorts=[{"port": 8090}, {"port": 8081}],
The website’s Vite configuration makes the development server reachable from the Session endpoint. It listens on 0.0.0.0 at port 8090 and doesn’t restrict the Host header (server.allowedHosts is true), because requests arrive under a host name the runtime assigns rather than localhost. The Session endpoint authenticates every request before it reaches the server, so the server doesn’t need its own host check.
To deploy the runtime:
1. Clone the sample repo and change to the sample folder:
git clone https://github.com/awslabs/agentcore-samples.git
cd agentcore-samples/01-features/02-host-your-agent/01-runtime/03-advanced/16-session-endpoints
2. Open session_endpoints_preview.ipynb from the sample folder.
3. Run the install cell, which installs the Python dependencies.
4. Run the %run deploy.py cell. Deployment takes a few minutes, mostly waiting for the runtime to reach the READY status.
Open the preview
With the runtime ready, you start the preview. One call does three things: it starts a session (which starts the website), opens a local endpoint for port 8090, and serves the preview page on localhost:8087.
from preview_app import PreviewApp
app = PreviewApp().start()
print("Open", app.url)
Inside start(), the calls that use Session endpoints are short. The first InvokeAgentRuntime call returns the URL in a response header, session_endpoint_url reads it, and the Session endpoint client opens a local endpoint for port 8090:
answer = client.invoke_agent_runtime(
agentRuntimeArn=runtime_arn, runtimeSessionId=session_id,
payload=json.dumps({"prompt": ""}).encode(), contentType="application/json",
)
endpoint = client.session_endpoint_client(session_endpoint_url(answer))
local = endpoint.open_local_endpoint(port=8090, local_port=8088).start()
To open the preview:
Run the cell that starts PreviewApp.
Open the printed link, http://localhost:8087, in your browser.
The page shows the website on the right, served from port 8090 in the session, and a short guide with suggested requests on the left.
Ask the agent for a change
Now you ask for a change and watch it arrive. Each prompt goes to the agent through InvokeAgentRuntime. The agent reads the files it needs, writes the ones it changes, and reports each step as it happens. When a file is saved, the Vite development server pushes the change over its WebSocket, through the Session endpoint and the local endpoint, and the website updates in place.
To ask for a change:
On the preview page, choose Switch this website to a dark coffee-house color theme.
Follow the agent’s steps in the chat pane as it reads and saves files.
Watch the site pane. It changes when the agent saves the stylesheet, and a banner names the file the change came from.
The following video shows the preview page while the agent works through several requests. Choosing a suggested request sends it to the agent, the chat pane lists each file the agent reads and saves, and the site pane on the right updates without a refresh, from the dark theme to a green Order ahead button.
Figure 2: The preview page as the agent works
The steps stream because the agent answers with server-sent events when you ask it to. You can send the same prompts from Python with app.ask, which reads the stream with iter_events from the bedrock-agentcore SDK. The open page updates in the same way:
for event in app.ask("Make the Order ahead button green"):
if "step" in event:
print(" ", event["step"])
elif "done" in event:
print(event["done"]["reply"])
The output of this Python script should resemble the following:
Looking at the site's files
Reading src/main.js
Reading src/style.css
Reading index.html
Saved src/style.css
The Order ahead button is now green instead of brown, with white text kept for contrast. You can see it in the hero section, just below the "Small batch coffee, roasted every morning" heading at the top of the page.
Reach a second port in the same session
The website isn’t the only server you can reach. The agent serves /status on port 8081, which lists each prompt and the files it changed. The same Session endpoint reaches it, and the only difference is the port argument.
status = app.endpoint.request("GET", "/status", port=8081)
print("GET /status on port 8081: HTTP", status.status)
for edit in status.json()["edits"]:
print(" ", edit["prompt"], "->", ", ".join(edit["files"]))
The output of this Python script should resemble the following:
GET /status on port 8081: HTTP 200
Make the Order ahead button green -> src/style.css
What the Session endpoint refuses
When the runtime refuses a request, it answers with an HTTP status, an empty body, and an error code in a response header, so you can tell its refusals from errors your application returns. The notebook sends a request to a port outside allowedPorts and a request without credentials, and the runtime refuses both with 403 AccessDenied.
The following table lists the refusals you’re likely to meet while you build with Session endpoints.
Request
Response from the runtime
A port that isn’t in allowedPorts
403 AccessDenied
A request without valid credentials
403 AccessDenied or 401 AuthenticationRequired
An allowed port with nothing listening on it
502 PortNotReachable
A URL whose session no longer exists
404 SessionNotFound
How access to your session is protected
The runtime removes its own authentication headers before it forwards a request, so the website doesn’t receive your signature. Requests are recorded in AWS CloudTrail as InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy events, with the event source bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com. The local endpoint acts with your credentials, so it limits who can use it. It listens on 127.0.0.1 only, answers only requests addressed to its own local address, and refuses WebSocket connections opened by pages from other origins. Run the local endpoint only while you use the preview. For more information, see Log session endpoint requests in CloudTrail.
The access controls don’t separate the website from the agent. Both run in the same session, so give the execution role only the permissions the agent needs. If the runtime replaces the session’s compute, open connections close, and the agent’s edits might not survive unless the session uses persistent storage. Refer to File system configurations for AgentCore runtime if you need the files to outlast the compute.
The agent’s file tools resolve every path inside the site folder and refuse paths outside it, so a prompt can’t make the agent change other files in the session. If other people can send prompts to your coding agent, consider Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful prompts and responses, and review the agent’s changes before you publish them.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, stop the preview and delete the resources the sample created. The website the agent edited lives in the session, so it goes with the session.
To clean up:
1. Run the stop cell, and press Enter when the notebook asks. This stops the preview page, the local endpoint, and the session.
2. Run the %run cleanup.py cell, which deletes the runtime, the uploaded code, and the IAM role.
Conclusion
Session endpoints give you authenticated access to the applications in an AgentCore runtime session from your own tools over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and WebSocket, on the ports you allow. In this post, you deployed a coding agent with a Vite website in its session, opened the live website in your browser through a local endpoint, asked the agent for a dark theme, and watched the change arrive as the agent saved the file. You also reached a second port in the same session and confirmed what the Session endpoint refuses.
To go further, run the notebook with your own site in the site folder, or change the agent’s tools to match how your coding agent works. For the full set of options, including port ranges, OAuth, HTTP/2, and gRPC, refer to Connect to runtime sessions through a session endpoint.
To change the port or path that InvokeAgentRuntime uses in your own agent, refer to Configure your agent’s serving port and invocation path. If your agent also needs to run build or test commands in the same session, refer to Execute shell commands in AgentCore runtime sessions. To deploy your own Node.js agent from a zip file the way this sample does, refer to Direct code deployment for Node.js. For everything else the service offers, start with Host agent or tools with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, and find more examples in the agentcore-samples GitHub repo.
About the author
Sundar Raghavan
Sundar is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS on the Agentic AI Foundations team. He leads the developer experience for Bedrock AgentCore, owning the SDK and CLI, and drives the framework and ecosystem integrations strategy. He focuses on how developers build, deploy, and scale production AI agents on AWS. He is also bringing the same agent developer experience to Physical AI through Strands Robots.

items.title: How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock
items.summary:
Worldwide Express (part of ShipStation Global) had built something big: approximately $5 billion in systemwide revenue, over 75 less-than-truckload (LTL) carriers and more than 130,000 customers. But that same scale had a hidden cost. Every month, $15 million in free cash flow sat frozen, locked in billing exceptions no one had resolved yet. Each one had to be chased down by hand, carrier by carrier, with its own rules to check. Worldwide Express outsourced to a team that worked cases one at a time, calling customers and carriers for each dispute. The exceptions piled up, cash stayed stuck, and every order took longer to turn into money.
Worldwide Express worked with AWS and LTM to build a multi-agentic AI solution with Amazon Bedrock that plugs directly into their transportation management system (TMS), SpeedShip. Six months after launch, the company reported a 75 percent reduction in active exceptions, a 4-week improvement in time-to-cash, $1M annual savings, and a one-time $10M free cash flow infusion.
In this post, we describe the challenge, explain how Worldwide Express designed the multi-agent solution, and share the results.
The challenge
In LTL freight, roughly 14 percent of invoices fail the standard three-way match between the purchase order, the goods receipt, and the carrier invoice. When a match fails, the invoice enters exception handling. For Worldwide Express, exceptions fell into three categories:
Line-item mismatches: Quantities or service codes that didn’t align with the shipment record.
Pricing variances: The carrier billed a rate different from the contracted price.
Unexpected accessorial charges: Liftgate fees, residential surcharges, or reweigh adjustments that weren’t on the original quote.
Each exception triggered a five-step manual process:
Identify the exception type by cross-referencing the invoice against the purchase order, goods receipt, and pricing.
Research the root cause in vendor records.
Send email to the carrier or warehouse with dispute details.
Wait for a response.
Execute the resolution in the TMS.
With each carrier operating under its own tariff structure and dispute workflow, this process consumed most of the FinOps team’s bandwidth.
Rule-based process automation (RPA) can handle structured, predictable workflows. However, exception resolution requires contextual judgment: interpreting a carrier’s accessorial policy, comparing charges against shipment data, and deciding validity given a carrier, exception type, and dollar amount. That variability is what made the problem a fit for the agentic AI framework.
From assessment to production
In June 2025, Worldwide Express engaged the AWS Business Transformation & Value Advisory team to identify 19 automation opportunities across the Order-to-Cash lifecycle. Knowing the business value of exceptions automation, Worldwide Express moved from assessment to production in less than 6 months.
How it works
The solution runs on AWS. Amazon Bedrock provides AI reasoning, and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is the engine. The design calls for fine-grained control over how each agent reasons, where decision boundaries sit, and how exceptions are routed between agents. Building the framework directly on Amazon EC2, with Amazon Bedrock providing inference, keeps that orchestration logic fully in the team’s hands and supports open source agent libraries. Production controls of business logic make each agent’s role, inputs, and decision boundaries explicit and auditable. In a billing-dispute workflow, every automated decision needs to be explainable.
Agents
When an invoice exception is detected, the system routes it to one of three specialized AI agents, each handling a specific type of billing dispute:
Invoice Matching Agent finds the matching shipment record and flags what doesn’t line up.
Pricing Variance Agent compares the carrier’s charge against the contracted rate and determines whether the difference is valid.
Accessorial Validation Agent checks whether unexpected fees (such as residential delivery or liftgate charges) are supported by the actual delivery events.
Each agent pulls specific carrier billing rules and policies before making a recommendation. After the exception is resolved, the system generates a plain-language note explaining what was found and what action was taken.
Each custom agent has an instruction prompt (defining its role, decision boundaries, and output format), a set of actions (integrations into SpeedShip), and access to carrier-specific knowledge bases. By using Amazon Bedrock, each agent accesses a suitable foundation model through a single API while inheriting existing AWS governance. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
Actions
The agents connect to SpeedShip through the same APIs that analysts use. That means the AI sees exactly what a human reviewer would see (contract rates, shipment details, delivery proof) and writes its resolution into the same workflow. SpeedShip has APIs on AWS, so the agents wire into the same endpoints as other existing systems.
Carrier knowledge base
Every carrier has different billing rules, fee definitions, and dispute procedures. Worldwide Express stores each carrier’s documentation: tariff rules, surcharge definitions, dispute steps, and variance thresholds. When an agent processes an exception, it retrieves that specific carrier’s policies and standard operating procedure (SOP) documents before deciding, so each decision is grounded in the carrier’s own rules. The same three agents handle all carriers without any carrier-specific code.
Human-in-the-loop
The approval step was necessary for FinOps adoption during the initial rollout. Initially, a human reviewer would use the existing SpeedShip UI to approve recommendations before they’re finalized. Eventually when accuracy exceeded 99 percent, bulk approval became the default.
Observability
Worldwide Express’s team built dashboards tracking automation rate by carrier, error rate by exception type, resolution time, and human override frequency. When a reviewer rejects a recommendation, the system logs the feedback. The team refines instruction prompts and knowledge bases based on rejection history, steadily increasing automation coverage.
End-to-end flow
The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow, from exception detection through the three specialized agents to human approval. In the diagram, exceptions from the data sources (the SpeedShip TMS, a shipping system, an electronic data interchange (EDI) server, and carrier and vendor portals) are detected and routed to one of three agents. Each agent runs on Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling, uses an agent framework with its own prompt, tools, and carrier knowledge base, and calls Amazon Bedrock for model inference. The agents produce a resolution report. Cost finalization and an AI-written note then go to a human reviewer for approval in the SpeedShip analyst UI.
Figure 1: Worldwide Express’s AI-powered exception handling architecture on AWS
Results
Six months in, Worldwide Express has deployed the solution across over 40 LTL carriers. The agents currently close 10,000 (approximately 50 percent) exceptions weekly with a less than 1 percent error rate. This shifted the FinOps team’s time from routine resolution to complex, high-value disputes.
The impact shows up most clearly in the backlog of active exceptions, which fell from $15M in June 2025 to $4M six months later, a 75 percent reduction. Worldwide Express unlocked $10M in freed-up cash flow, over $1M in annual cost savings, and 60x first-year ROI. The company reports time-to-cash improving by four weeks.
“With AWS, we’ve automated more than 40 percent of weekly billing exceptions, significantly reducing costs and accelerating billing cycles from days to minutes. Today, we release approximately $10 million more in customer billings each week at a speed that simply wasn’t possible before.”
— Nathanael Pearson, VP of FinOps, Worldwide Express
Looking forward
Worldwide Express is already expanding this approach to other parts of the Order-to-Cash cycle. For logistics companies managing high carrier volumes, the path forward is to start small. Automate the most repetitive exception type first, prove accuracy, then scale across the rest of the portfolio.
Conclusion
Worldwide Express’s exception automation shows what’s possible when agentic AI meets a well-scoped business problem. The combination of Amazon Bedrock, carrier-specific knowledge bases, and a human-in-the-loop approval design let Worldwide Express move from assessment to production in less than 6 months while maintaining financial controls. The company is now expanding automation to other Order-to-Cash processes.
To explore whether a similar approach might work for your organization, request a conversation with your account team or learn more about Amazon Bedrock. Partners like LTM can run a Proof of Value sprint with your own data.
About the authors

Saumya is a Customer Solutions Manager at AWS for four years. She helps Transportation & Logistics enterprises accelerate AI adoption from proof of concept to production.
Nikhil Bhagat
Nikhil is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS. With over a decade of experience architecting WAN, DNS, and data center networks, he specializes in cloud infrastructure, networking, and GenAI. He helps customers design, build, and optimize their cloud solutions, and build agentic AI frameworks. He brings the same discipline that underpins resilient networks, including reliable connectivity, isolation, and thoughtful traffic design, to the distributed systems behind modern AI.
Lynette Woolfolk
Lynette is an account executive in the Transportation & Logistics vertical with 6 years at AWS. She serves as an advisor to enterprise customers, helping them unlock measurable business value through transformative technical solutions and AI-driven innovation.
Arjun Srinivasan
Arjun is an enterprise AI executive and SVP of AI & Data Science at ShipStation Global, with over 20 years of experience driving data, analytics, and AI transformation across distribution, logistics, energy, manufacturing, and retail. He has led large-scale AI strategy, governance, and productization efforts spanning GenAI, Agentic AI, Intelligent Automation, Predictive Analytics, Computer Vision and Physics-based Simulations. Known for translating emerging technologies into measurable business outcomes, Arjun partners with executive teams to scale AI from pilots to enterprise adoption. He is also a frequent speaker, advisor, and ecosystem builder focused on practical, trusted, and value-driven AI innovation.

items.title: Configure the ChatGPT desktop app with Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)
items.summary:
The ChatGPT desktop app is now available on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US), providing access to OpenAI’s frontier models through two components. Work completes complex, multi-step tasks and delivers review-ready results, and Codex is a coding agent for developing, testing, and reviewing software.
This walkthrough is intended for organizations whose security architecture requires model inference to use AWS GovCloud (US) identities, endpoints, and Regional controls. It configures Codex to route model requests through Amazon Bedrock Mantle in us-gov-west-1, where access can be governed using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and existing AWS GovCloud (US) network controls.
Codex is the OpenAI coding agent for AI-powered software development. With GPT models powering inference, Codex introduces a new class of intelligence optimized for complex, long-horizon developer workflows. You can use the ChatGPT desktop app, the Codex CLI, and IDE integrations with Visual Studio Code, JetBrains, and Xcode. Model inference is routed through the Responses API on Amazon Bedrock.
For customers with data residency requirements, processing stays within the Amazon Bedrock AWS Region that you select. You pay per token with no seat licenses and no per-developer commitments. Zero data retention (ZDR) is also supported. In this configurable mode, prompts and responses are processed without being written to durable storage by AWS or shared with model providers. This helps you protect sensitive information and meet stringent data-governance, privacy, and security requirements.
This post walks through a controlled local deployment of the ChatGPT desktop app that sends model inference to Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US-West). The configuration uses API-mode sign-in, a managed device policy, a named AWS profile, and network restrictions. These restrictions allow access only to the approved Amazon Bedrock endpoint while disabling other external connections and network-enabled capabilities. The result is a deployment that an agency security team can test and document before approving broader use.
Using AWS GovCloud (US) and following this guide do not, by themselves, authorize your workload. Your organization remains responsible for reviewing the selected model, AWS services, Region, endpoint, workstation controls, repositories, credentials, and data flows against its system security plan and authorization process.
Solution overview
You can use the ChatGPT desktop app in two ways:
Work for larger tasks that need planning, research, files, and a finished result.
Codex for technical work such as editing code, running tests, and reviewing pull requests.
The ChatGPT desktop app runs on an organization-managed computer through the desktop app or CLI. It uses the configured AWS credentials to securely send requests to the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint in us-gov-west-1. Because this setup uses AWS directly, ChatGPT workspace rules and user roles don’t control it. The main security controls are the computer’s policies and the AWS identity and permissions being used.
Walkthrough
The configuration has three main steps: set up authentication, set up the ChatGPT desktop app configuration files, and then launch, initialize, and verify the deployment.
Prerequisites
Before setting up the ChatGPT desktop app with AWS GovCloud (US), make sure your version of the ChatGPT desktop app supports Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US). You need an approved AWS GovCloud (US) account, an IAM identity and approved credentials, access to the approved model, AWS Region, and endpoint, and permission to use them. You also need to set up the requirements.toml and config.toml files.
Step 1: Set up authentication
Select the approved AWS GovCloud (US) account and IAM identity or role with access to the approved model in us-gov-west-1. Obtain credentials through your organization’s approved mechanism. This walkthrough uses the named profile codex-il5. Keep credentials, bearer tokens, session tokens, and other secrets out of TOML files.
Protect the profile configuration, credential source, SSO token cache, and any credential helper from ChatGPT desktop app task writes, while allowing approved authentication tools to maintain and refresh credentials.
The ChatGPT desktop app supports two Amazon Bedrock authentication pathways: an Amazon Bedrock API key or the AWS SDK credential chain. AWS SSO through AWS IAM Identity Center is supported within the credential-chain pathway.
The app first checks for AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK in its environment. For desktop use, this variable can be supplied through %USERPROFILE%\.codex\.env on Windows or ~/.codex/.env on Linux and macOS. When present, the bearer token takes precedence over profile-based authentication.
If no bearer token is available, the app falls back to the standard AWS SDK credential chain. The chain can read AWS credentials from ~/.aws/credentials and related profile settings from ~/.aws/config. On Windows, the corresponding default paths are %USERPROFILE%\.aws\credentials and %USERPROFILE%\.aws\config. The chain also supports SSO profiles. For SSO, it uses the profile settings in the AWS config file and the cached SSO session to obtain temporary role credentials. These credentials don’t need to be manually stored in the AWS credentials file. See OpenAI’s Bedrock authentication documentation and the AWS IAM Identity Center credential provider documentation.
Step 2: Set up ChatGPT desktop app configuration files
You must create two ChatGPT desktop app configuration files: config.toml and requirements.toml.
Important: the configuration files need to be set up before the application is launched. The following table shows the file locations.
Operating system
User config.toml
Admin requirements.toml
Windows
%USERPROFILE%\.codex\config.toml
%ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex\requirements.toml
Linux
~/.codex/config.toml
/etc/codex/requirements.toml
macOS
~/.codex/config.toml
/etc/codex/requirements.toml
Start from the requirements.toml file. requirements.toml is an administrator-controlled rules file. It sets security limits that users can’t override, for example, restricting which permission levels, tools, or settings the ChatGPT desktop app is allowed to use.
Use the following baseline for the supported AWS GovCloud (US) Amazon Bedrock deployment. The [windows] section applies only to Windows, and sandbox_private_desktop must be supported by the approved runtime.
allowed_login_methods = ["api"]
allowed_sandbox_modes = ["read-only", "workspace-write"]
allowed_approvals_reviewers = ["user"]
allowed_approval_policies = [
{ granular = { sandbox_approval = false, rules = true,
mcp_elicitations = false, request_permissions = false,
skill_approval = true } },
]
allowed_web_search_modes = ["disabled", "cached"]
allow_browser_and_computer_use = false
allow_appshots = false
allow_remote_control = false
allow_login_shell = false
allow_managed_hooks_only = true
check_for_update_on_startup = false
mcp_servers = {}
[feedback]
enabled = false
[features]
network_proxy = true
in_app_chat = false
in_app_dictation = false
in_app_browser = false
browser_use = false
browser_use_external = false
browser_use_full_cdp_access = false
computer_use = false
in_app_updates = false
image_generation = false
memories = false
chronicle = false
external_agent_memory_import = false
guardian_approval = false
guardianv2 = false
guardian_ext = false
apps = false
enable_mcp_apps = false
plugins = false
remote_plugin = false
plugin_sharing = false
recommended_plugins = false
skill_mcp_dependency_install = false
skill_search = false
workspace_dependencies = false
hooks = false
standalone_web_search = false
[experimental_network]
enabled = true
managed_allowed_domains_only = true
domains = {}
unix_sockets = {}
allow_upstream_proxy = false
dangerously_allow_non_loopback_proxy = false
dangerously_allow_all_unix_sockets = false
allow_local_binding = false
[application.network]
enabled = true
[application.network.domains]
"bedrock-mantle.us-gov-west-1.api.aws" = "allow"
"api.openai.com" = "deny"
"chat.openai.com" = "deny"
"chatgpt.com" = "deny"
"ab.chatgpt.com" = "deny"
"platform.openai.com" = "deny"

allowed_sandbox_implementations = ["elevated"]

Next, configure the config.toml file. config.toml tells the ChatGPT desktop app how to operate, including which model provider to use (amazon-bedrock), which model to select, and settings such as permissions or context limits.
Replace the model ID and named profile (for example, codex-il5) with approved values.
model = "REPLACE_WITH_APPROVED_MODEL_ID"
model_provider = "amazon-bedrock"
forced_login_method = "api"
approval_policy = { granular = { sandbox_approval = false,
rules = true, mcp_elicitations = false,
request_permissions = false, skill_approval = true } }
approvals_reviewer = "user"
sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"
web_search = "cached"

check_for_update_on_startup = false
[model_providers.amazon-bedrock]
base_url = "https://bedrock-mantle.us-gov-west-1.api.aws/openai/v1"

requires_openai_auth = false
supports_websockets = false
supports_standalone_web_search = false
[model_providers.amazon-bedrock.aws]
region = "us-gov-west-1"
profile = "codex-il5"
[sandbox_workspace_write]

[features]

[analytics]
enabled = false
[feedback]
enabled = false
[otel]
exporter = "none"
trace_exporter = "none"
metrics_exporter = "none"
log_user_prompt = false
[memories]
generate_memories = false
use_memories = false
[skills.bundled]
enabled = false
[apps._default]
enabled = false
[windows]
sandbox = "elevated"
Step 3: Launch, initialize, and verify
Download the app from the ChatGPT site and install it. Leave the app closed after installation. If it opens automatically or if the app has been launched previously, fully exit ChatGPT and end any lingering ChatGPT or Codex processes.
Make sure requirements.toml and config.toml are in place before the first app launch.
Start the app to load the requirements.toml and config.toml settings. Make sure it shows amazon-bedrock as the model provider.
In the Codex CLI, you should see a /status tab that looks like this:
Figure 1: The Codex CLI /status tab confirming amazon-bedrock as the model provider
In the ChatGPT desktop app, you can also confirm amazon-bedrock as the model provider.
Figure 2: The ChatGPT desktop app settings showing amazon-bedrock as the model provider
Troubleshooting
The application prompts for an OpenAI account. Verify that requirements.toml and config.toml use the exact locations and file names shown in the preceding table, terminate all ChatGPT and Codex processes, and relaunch. The files must precede app launch.
AWS GovCloud (US) endpoint is reported as unsupported. Confirm the exact desktop or app-server release, endpoint, and model with OpenAI. Changing the URL alone does not establish support.
The wrong AWS identity is used. Inspect the effective credential source and named profile. Check whether an Amazon Bedrock API key takes precedence over the profile.
Capability restrictions are missing. Inspect the full effective requirements after restart. The API-only sign-in setting doesn’t apply the capability policy.
Rollback and cleanup
If a validation check fails, stop the rollout. Return the affected devices to the previously approved policy and provider settings, then restart the ChatGPT desktop app. Revoke any temporary AWS credentials or API keys, and confirm that those devices can no longer connect to Amazon Bedrock. Keep a record of the test and clearly document what failed before trying again.
Conclusion
The ChatGPT desktop app on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) gives you a controlled way to use OpenAI frontier models and coding assistance. Inference stays in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. By validating the configuration, confirming the approved AWS identity and endpoint, and verifying security controls, you can confidently prepare the deployment for broader use. This approach supports innovation while aligning deployment decisions with each organization’s security, authorization, and data-handling requirements.
Ready to explore the ChatGPT desktop app with Codex on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)? Start with a controlled deployment, validate your security controls, and work with your security team to prepare for broader adoption.

OpenAI’s Bedrock authentication documentation – Amazon Bedrock API key and AWS SDK credential-chain authentication, including SSO.
AWS IAM Identity Center credential provider documentation – SSO profile configuration and temporary AWS credentials.
About the authors
Virgil Ennes
Virgil is a Senior Partner Solutions Architect at AWS and a GenAI and AI/ML specialist. He helps partners and customers integrate OpenAI technologies with AWS services, transforming innovative ideas into scalable, real-world business solutions.
Sean Phuphanich
Sean is a Principal Technologist of Applied AI and segment lead for ISVs. Sean is focused on solving major challenges for industry with frontier AI and optimizing the pareto curve. Sean is also a development and cyber security SME, and program manager for AWS Zero Trust Accelerator for Government (ZTAG).

items.title: Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.summary:
Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With Web Answer, agent builders get a synthesized, source-cited answer to a natural-language question with a single tool call. They no longer build a search, retrieve, synthesize, and citation pipeline themselves.
If you have built agents that need to answer questions from current web sources, you know the pattern: call a search API, decide which results to trust, retrieve and clean page content, prompt a model to synthesize, and engineer citation extraction so the output traces back to a source. Every step is code you maintain, and every step is another place things can go wrong: hallucination when evidence is insufficient, stale content when the index moves, and broken attribution when a claim and its source drift apart.
The Web Answer collapses that entire pipeline into one request. You send a question. You get back a cited answer in seconds. In this post, we explain what Web Answer does, compare it with Web Search on AgentCore, show how it works and what it returns, and walk through adding Web Answer to a gateway and calling it from an agent.
What Web Answer does
Figure 1: Request flow from an agent through the Gateway to Web Answer and back
Your agent sends a question to your AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The Gateway authenticates the call with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) or a JSON Web Token (JWT). The Gateway calls Web Answer, a managed connector that AWS owns, using its own service role. Web Answer plans its searches, runs several in parallel, and reads key pages to check the facts. When the evidence is insufficient, it searches again. It then writes an answer that ties each claim to its source URL. The Gateway returns the answer and its citations to your agent as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool result.
Web Answer is a managed AgentCore Gateway tool that takes a natural-language question and returns a synthesized answer in seconds grounded in current web sources. Here is what you get back:
A grounded, cited answer, where each grounded claim maps to a citation, with a source URL where one is available.
Current sources. Web Answer runs new searches for every question, and its model is given today’s date so it can search for up-to-date information.
Agentic search: Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, reads pages to verify facts, and decides when it has enough evidence to answer.
Responsible AI safeguards: Web Answer is designed and tested with responsible AI safeguards.
Figure 2: Demo video showing how to add Web Answer to an AgentCore Gateway, from setup to a finished, cited answer
How it differs from Web Search
Web Answer and the Web Search tools both support retrieval use cases, with different levels of integration complexity. The dividing line is who runs the model:
Web Search: Returns ranked URLs, titles, snippets, and metadata. You keep your own model and control the synthesis. Use Web Search when you want full control over how results are processed.
Web Answer: Runs the model, the agentic retrieval loop, synthesis, and attribution for you. You get a finished, cited answer. Use Web Answer when the question is a sub-task inside a larger agent and you do not want to own a retrieval pipeline for it.
Many customers will use both. An agent might use Web Search for broad research tasks where it needs raw results, and Web Answer for specific factual questions where it needs a quick, cited answer.
Set up and invoke Web Answer
Web Answer is a connector that AWS owns. You reference it by ID, and the Gateway handles the tool schema, parameter governance, endpoint resolution, and authentication to the backend. In this walkthrough, you give your Gateway’s service role permission to call Web Answer, add a Web Answer target, and call it from a Strands agent.
Getting started
Getting started takes minutes. A Gateway administrator adds Web Answer as a target on an existing AgentCore Gateway, and the tool appears to any attached agent over MCP through tools/list and tools/call.
Prerequisites
An AWS account with AgentCore Gateway access.
An AgentCore Gateway in us-east-1 that uses IAM (AWS_IAM) inbound authentication. To create one, see Create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway in the Developer Guide.
AWS credentials for an identity that has bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway on the Gateway, and Amazon Bedrock access to the model your agent uses.
Python 3.10 or later, with the required packages:
pip install boto3 strands-agents mcp mcp-proxy-for-aws
Note: Following these steps creates AWS resources that incur charges. The Gateway and Web Answer invocations are billable. See the Pricing section that follows for details, and when you finish, delete the resources you created (see “Clean up resources”).
Step 1: Grant the Gateway service role access to Web Answer
The Gateway uses its service role to act on your behalf. The role’s trust policy allows bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com to assume it, scoped to your account. For Web Answer, the role needs:
bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebAnswer, to call Web Answer. The Gateway checks this permission on every request against the ARN that AWS owns, arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:aws:tool/web-answer.v1.
Attach the policy to the service role as an inline policy:
import json
import boto3
iam = boto3.client("iam")
iam.put_role_policy(
RoleName="<gateway-service-role>",
PolicyName="WebAnswerGuide",
PolicyDocument=json.dumps({
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "InvokeWebAnswer",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebAnswer",
"Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:aws:tool/web-answer.v1",
}
],
}),
)
The role controls only the Gateway’s outbound calls. Who can call your Gateway is set by its inbound authorizer. The role also doesn’t need bedrock:InvokeModel: your agent’s model runs under your agent’s own identity.
Step 2: Create the Web Answer target
Add Web Answer as a connector target. The connectorId tells the Gateway which managed integration to provision: in this case, an agent that searches the web and writes a cited answer.
import boto3
gateway_client = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore-control", region_name="us-east-1")
target_response = gateway_client.create_gateway_target(
name="web-answer-tool",
gatewayIdentifier=gateway_id,
targetConfiguration={
"mcp": {
"connector": {
"source": {"connectorId": "web-answer"},
"configurations": [{"name": "WebAnswer", "parameterValues": {}}],
}
}
},
credentialProviderConfigurations=[
{"credentialProviderType": "GATEWAY_IAM_ROLE"}
],
)
target_id = target_response["targetId"]
Outbound authentication is automatic for connectors. With GATEWAY_IAM_ROLE, the Gateway calls the Web Answer backend with the service role from Step 1, so you don’t create or store any credentials for the tool. Wait until get_gateway_target reports the target status as READY before you call it.
As the Gateway administrator, you can also set a domain filter on the target. The filter applies to every call that goes through the target. To limit the target to a set of domains, set parameterValues to {"domainFilter": {"include": ["bis.org"], "exclude": ["unreliable-source.net"]}}.
Step 3: Invoke Web Answer from a Strands agent
Your agent discovers Web Answer through the Gateway’s tools/list and calls it with tools/call, like any other MCP tool. This works with Strands Agents, LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, or any other MCP-compatible client.
from strands import Agent
from strands.models.bedrock import BedrockModel
from strands.tools.mcp import MCPClient
from mcp_proxy_for_aws.client import aws_iam_streamablehttp_client
gateway_url = "https://gateway-<id>.gateway.bedrock-agentcore.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/mcp"
mcp_client = MCPClient(lambda: aws_iam_streamablehttp_client(
endpoint=gateway_url,
aws_region="us-east-1",
aws_service="bedrock-agentcore",
aws_profile="<aws-profile-id>", # identity with bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway on the Gateway
))
model = BedrockModel(model_id="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5", max_tokens=1024)
with mcp_client:
tools = mcp_client.list_tools_sync() # Web Answer tool discovered from the Gateway
agent = Agent(model=model, tools=tools)
result = agent("What are the Basel III minimum requirements for Tier 1 capital?")
print(result.message)
When a question needs current information, your agent calls the Web Answer tool (web-answer-tool___WebAnswer). Web Answer runs the agentic search and returns a finished answer with citations.
Besides the question, the Web Answer tool takes optional arguments that your agent can set on each call: a domain filter to include or exclude sites, a published-date range, and a country to localize results. The agent’s domain filter is combined with the target’s filter. The agent can exclude more domains, or limit results to some of the target’s included domains, but it can’t add a domain that the target’s filter blocks.
Response format
Web Answer returns an MCP tool result with both content and structuredContent fields. The answer is markdown text with inline citation markers like [1], and structuredContent.answer carries the same text alongside a structured citations list:
{
"content": [
{
"type": "text",
"text": "Under Basel III, banks must hold Common Equity Tier 1 capital of at least 4.5% of risk-weighted assets [[1](https://www.bis.org/...)]..."
}
],
"structuredContent": {
"answer": [
{
"text": "Under Basel III, banks must hold Common Equity Tier 1 capital of at least 4.5% of risk-weighted assets [[1](https://www.bis.org/...)]...",
"citations": [
{ "domain": "bis.org", "url": "https://www.bis.org/..." }
]
}
]
},
"isError": false,
"_meta": {
"latencyMs": 5210
}
}
structuredContent.answer normally holds a single block. Each citation carries the source url and, when available, the domain.
Clean up resources
Delete the Web Answer target when you no longer need it:
gateway_client.delete_gateway_target(gatewayIdentifier=gateway_id, targetId=target_id)
If you created the Gateway only for this walkthrough, delete its targets first, then the Gateway (delete_gateway), and then the service role and its policy. There is no persistent infrastructure on the AWS side beyond these resources. After they are removed, you stop incurring charges.
Enterprise controls, built in
Web Answer inherits the same enterprise controls as other AgentCore tools:
Gateway authentication. No separate API key to provision, rotate, or manage for Web Answer. Callers authenticate to the gateway with the inbound method you configure, such as AWS IAM (SigV4) or a JSON Web Token from your identity provider. The gateway then calls Web Answer with its own service role, which needs the bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebAnswer permission.
VPC and AWS PrivateLink. Your agents can call the gateway through an interface virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint (com.amazonaws.us-east-1.bedrock-agentcore.gateway), so traffic stays off the public internet.
Zero data egress. Your queries and results stay within your AWS environment.
Amazon CloudWatch metrics. Operational metrics publish to CloudWatch from the first call.
Per-account rate limits. Enforced from launch, with 10 transactions per second per account in US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1). To request an increase, contact AWS Support.
Admin-time policy bounds. The Gateway administrator sets domain filter bounds at target setup. Agents can narrow the filter bounds on each call but can’t widen them.
Queries stay within AWS. Web Answer searches an Amazon-operated web index and Amazon’s knowledge graph, and doesn’t send your question to third-party search engines or external websites.
Use cases
Web Answer helps agents retrieve current, cited information to support a range of knowledge-intensive workflows. Example scenarios include:
Financial services. Regulatory Q&A agents answering questions about compliance requirements, market regulations, and policy changes, where every answer must trace to an authoritative source.
Healthcare. Clinical support agents grounding responses in current medical literature and treatment guidelines published on the web.
Customer service. Support agents answering product and policy questions in real time, where ten ranked links are not useful and a cited answer is.
Legal and compliance. Research assistants answering questions about case law, regulatory filings, and policy interpretations with auditable citations.
Enterprise knowledge workers. Internal copilots that answer questions from current public information without requiring employees to build their own search and synthesis workflow.
Availability
Web Answer is available in US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), with more AWS Regions coming soon.
Pricing
Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is priced at $10 per 1,000 tool calls.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how Web Answer gives your agents current, cited answers through agentic search, with no search pipeline for you to build or maintain. We granted a Gateway service role access to Web Answer, added a Web Answer target, called it from a Strands agent, and read the answer and its citations from the response. Use Web Search on AgentCore when your own model should reason over raw results, and Web Answer when your agent needs a finished, cited answer.
To get started, see:
Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation
Web Answer structured output schema
Adding Web Answer to an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
Supported regions

items.title: How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI
items.summary:
A+ Content is the rich media widget on the Amazon product detail page. Through visual assets, brands communicate unique product and brand value to help customers make informed purchase decisions. Selling partners using high-quality A+ Content boost their sales by 8–20 percent compared to those without it. A wide variety of brands, from established brands with large in-house design teams to bootstrapped brands with limited resources, use A+ Content, creating inconsistency in content quality. A typical A+ Content project combines text, images, and video into a cohesive product story. Evaluating each asset in isolation misses the quality that emerges from how those assets work together. When your content spans multiple heterogeneous modules and you need a holistic quality signal rather than per-asset checks, the multi-model fusion approach described in this post can help. In this post, we examine this problem in the context of A+ Content.
A+ Content provides creative freedom for selling partners to express their authentic selves on their product detail pages, without strict content specifications such as image ratio and text word count.
Although this flexibility allows compelling brand storytelling, it also creates substantial variation in content composition and quality.
With quality evaluation and improvement recommendations, brands can transform average content into high-quality content that is more coherent, relevant, and useful. This improved content helps customers make more informed purchasing decisions and build lasting relationships with brands, leading to improved revenue for selling partners.
To achieve this goal, an evaluation system must assess the complete content experience, provide actionable recommendations beyond numeric scores, and reflect the nuances across product categories. Existing approaches struggle to meet all these requirements simultaneously, so in this post, you will see a new approach using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to understand and evaluate content holistically, and a diffusion-based generation component that produces improved visual assets from the resulting quality signals.
In this post, you will learn how to:
Render complete ecommerce content as a single snapshot and evaluate it holistically with a VLM.
Combine VLM semantic scores with OCR readability signals in a lightweight CatBoost classifier trained on expert annotations.
Use SHAP to explain quality decisions and generate actionable improvement recommendations for selling partners.
Implement the end-to-end pipeline on Amazon SageMaker AI, from data ingestion and annotation through model hosting, explainability, and production monitoring.
Opportunities and challenges in VLM-based evaluation
A vision language model (VLM) pairs an image encoder with a large language model (LLM). The encoder, often a vision transformer (ViT), splits an image into patches and turns them into embeddings, and a small connector maps those embeddings into the language model’s input space (Flamingo, LLaVA). Many VLMs reuse the image encoder from CLIP, which learned to match images with their captions. Because VLMs are trained to follow instructions, you can give one an image along with a rubric of evaluation criteria and get back a written assessment without task-specific training. When you need closer agreement with human reviewers, you can fine-tune the model on labeled examples. This makes VLMs a practical starting point for checking product images against your content guidelines at scale.
Conventional computer vision models can already score individual assets, for example flagging a blurry image or a grammar error in a bullet list. Using a VLM to grade each asset separately adds little beyond that. A product detail page, however, combines images, text, and layout modules into a single story, and its quality depends on how those pieces work together. Our approach renders the full page as a single snapshot and asks the VLM to evaluate it as customers see it.
Consider a blender page with a hero image, a bulleted feature list highlighting blade speed and capacity, and a lifestyle photo of the blender in a modern kitchen. Checked one by one, each asset passes: the image is sharp, the bullets are grammatical, and the photo is well lit. Viewed together, problems appear. The bullets might advertise a 64-oz pitcher while the lifestyle photo shows a single-serve model, or the lifestyle photo might sit above the hero image so customers see the kitchen before the product. Because an asset’s meaning depends on where it appears and what surrounds it, these issues only show up when the page is evaluated as a whole. The snapshot gives the VLM that complete view. Using it in production adds three requirements: scores must match expert quality standards, evaluation must be accurate and efficient at scale, and each result must explain what to fix.
As shown in Figure 1, we address these considerations through a VLM-based multi-model fusion architecture designed around adaptability, performance, and explainability. The following sections describe each component.
Figure 1: Block diagram of the VLM-based multi-model fusion approach, including VLM, OCR, and classifier models
Adaptive VLM content evaluation with expert annotations
A pretrained VLM prompted with a rubric scores content from its general knowledge, and those scores don’t always match ecommerce quality standards. Fine-tuning the VLM to close that gap would require GPU training infrastructure and, with only a few thousand labeled examples, carries a real risk of overfitting. Instead, we keep the VLM and rubric prompt fixed, use the VLM’s structured outputs as features, and train a CatBoost classifier on them to predict expert quality labels. CatBoost, a gradient-boosted decision tree library, performs well on small tabular datasets like this one. Because only the classifier is retrained, updating the system as annotations accumulate or criteria change takes a short CPU-only job rather than a foundation model fine-tuning run.
The VLM receives the page snapshot and a rubric prompt covering four quality dimensions: Visual Storytelling, Feature Presentation, A+ Layout, and Conversion Optimization. Each dimension has explicit criteria and point-deduction rules. For each dimension, the VLM returns a score from 0 to 10, a confidence value, and a natural-language rationale. For example, it lowers the score and explains why when a page lacks diverse modules or lifestyle imagery, or repeats information. The scores and confidence values become the classifier’s features, and the rationales help selling partners understand the result.
To build the training labels, one ecommerce marketing expert and four professional annotators independently rated 5,478 product detail pages from 10 product categories as high or low quality, using the same criteria. We assessed their ratings and took the majority vote to create a consensus label. The classes are nearly balanced (49.6 percent high quality), so a classifier can’t score well by predicting the majority class. To measure label reliability, we used Cohen’s kappa, which measures how often two raters agree after accounting for the agreement they would reach by chance. A score of 0 means agreement is no better than chance, 1 means perfect agreement, and values above 0.8 are generally considered strong. Each annotator scored between 0.845 and 0.915 when compared against the consensus label.
Figure 2: Annotator performance and content difficulty distribution. The near-even class split rules out majority-class bias (left), and the difficulty distribution explains the residual disagreement (right)
We compared the classifier with a baseline on a 20 percent holdout set (about 1,100 pages). The baseline averages the four VLM scores and applies a fixed threshold, so every dimension counts equally. The baseline reached 0.80 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.84 on the high-quality class. The CatBoost classifier, trained on the same scores, reached 0.89 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.90. Because the classifier learns how much each dimension matters and how the dimensions interact, its predictions match expert decisions more closely.
High-performance VLM content evaluation with OCR
VLMs capture the overall meaning and visual composition of a page well, but they are less reliable at fine-grained readability issues, such as how crowded the text is or how much space separates lines. Because of their language-model foundation, they can also favor long, detailed descriptions even when customers prefer concise text they can scan quickly. On a text-heavy page, a VLM might rate dense product information as helpful while customers struggle to read long sentences packed into a small area. To capture these issues, we use an optical character recognition (OCR) model hosted on SageMaker AI Inference to extract each block of text and its position, then calculate four quantitative signals: Text Density, Character Density, Spacing, and Overall Readability. Combining these OCR scores with the VLM’s semantic and visual assessment adds complementary information that improves quality classification.
From that output, we calculate four readability scores:
Text Density: The share of the page area covered by text.
Character Density: The number of characters per unit of page area.
Spacing: How consistent and sufficient the whitespace is between words, lines, and paragraphs.
Overall Readability: A combined signal from the three preceding scores.
Because these scores depend on layout rather than wording, two pages with identical text can score differently.
The fusion model combines the four VLM rubric scores and the four OCR scores into eight features and trains a CatBoost classifier on the same expert labels. Table 1 compares it with models trained on each feature set alone, using the same 20 percent holdout set.
On the same 20 percent holdout set, the CatBoost model using only OCR features achieved 0.82 accuracy and a 0.83 F1 score, while the model using only VLM features achieved 0.89 and 0.90. The fused OCR-VLM-CatBoost model outperformed both standalone models, reaching 0.94 accuracy and a 0.95 F1 score. The 0.05 improvement in both metrics over the VLM-only model demonstrates that OCR isn’t a replacement signal. It complements the VLM’s holistic judgment with fine-grained text-readability information.

Explainable VLM content evaluation with SHAP
A quality label alone doesn’t tell selling partners what to fix first. To find which dimensions drove each decision, we use SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), which assigns each feature a value showing how far it pushed a prediction toward high or low quality. Because the VLM and OCR scores feed the same classifier, SHAP measures both on a common scale. Raw scores can’t do this: a Visual Storytelling score of 6 and a high Character Density don’t tell you which one mattered more to the decision.
Across the holdout set, the most influential features were OCR Character Density (mean absolute SHAP value 1.1), OCR Overall Readability (1.0), and VLM Visual Storytelling (1.0). They were followed by A+ Layout (0.8), Feature Presentation (0.6), and Conversion Optimization (0.4). Both OCR and VLM features rank near the top, so the classifier depends on both sources.
Figure 3: Global SHAP value distributions for all VLM and OCR features
For an individual page, SHAP shows which features lowered the decision. For each page classified as low quality, we rank the eight features by SHAP value, then pass the most negative features, the product category, and ecommerce best practices, along with the VLM’s rationales, to an LLM, which turns them into prioritized, specific actions.
Figure 4 shows two local SHAP plots with the LLM reasoning grounded in the SHAP results, for a low-quality and a high-quality A+ Content sample. For example, if A+ Layout has a SHAP value of -1.2 and Visual Storytelling has -0.3, the system prioritizes restructuring the layout and rebalancing text and images, followed by improvements to the imagery.
Figure 4: Two local SHAP value distributions for all VLM and OCR features: (a) a low-quality case, where most features contribute negatively and drive an improvement-requested recommendation; (b) a high-quality case, where most features contribute positively
We validated the effectiveness of these explanation-based recommendations by measuring quality scores after selling partners revised their content. The average post-revision quality score increased by 1.4 points on a 10-point scale on a statistically significant sample. SHAP contributions can therefore be translated from decision explanations into actionable improvement priorities and methods. Explainability is therefore not merely an auxiliary capability for understanding the model. It functions as a feedback mechanism that materially improves content quality.
Results
The complete system scores each page snapshot with the VLM and OCR, combines the four VLM scores and four OCR scores into a single feature vector, and passes it to a CatBoost classifier trained on expert labels. SHAP then identifies which features drove each decision. To measure what each component adds, we compared four configurations on the same 20 percent holdout set. The holdout set comes from 5,478 product detail pages across 10 product categories, including Furniture, Shoes, Grocery, Beauty, and Apparel.
The baseline averages the four VLM scores and applies a fixed threshold, so every dimension counts equally. It reached 0.80 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.84. Training a CatBoost classifier on the same scores lets the model learn which dimensions matter most and how they interact, which raised accuracy to 0.89 and F1 to 0.90. A classifier trained on the OCR scores alone reached 0.82 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.83. Combining the VLM and OCR scores gave the best results, with 0.94 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.95. That’s 14 percentage points higher accuracy and 11 points higher F1 than the baseline.
Figure 5: Accuracy and F1 comparison across VLM and OCR evaluation configurations
Examining each performance gain separately makes the value of the integrated approach clearer. CatBoost calibration first reduces the limitations of a fixed threshold by learning dimension-specific weights and nonlinear decision boundaries. Adding OCR features then supplies text-readability signals that the VLM can miss. Overall, the final fusion model improves accuracy by 0.14 and F1 by 0.11 over the baseline.
We also changed the VLM backbone in an additional experiment on a single-category dataset containing 499 content projects. With a lighter VLM variant, the baseline achieved 0.74 accuracy and a 0.72 F1 score, while the OCR-VLM-CatBoost model achieved 0.90 for both metrics. With a more capable VLM variant, the baseline achieved 0.79 accuracy and a 0.84 F1 score, while the fusion model achieved 0.94 and 0.95. The fusion approach improved accuracy by 0.16 and 0.15 for the two VLMs, respectively, demonstrating that complementary OCR features deliver consistent gains without depending on a particular foundation model.
To reduce development costs while retaining access to high-performance foundation models, the system freezes the VLM and trains only the low-overhead classifier. In production, a worldwide A/B experiment that adjusted the visibility of low-quality A+ Content based on the model’s quality decisions produced a statistically meaningful improvement in Ordered Product Sales (OPS). Beyond aligning closely with expert judgment, the integrated system provides a quality signal that can support customer-experience and business decisions at scale.
Implementation on Amazon SageMaker AI
This section describes how the architecture is implemented end-to-end on Amazon SageMaker AI. Each stage of the pipeline from content rendering and expert annotation through VLM scoring, OCR extraction, feature aggregation, classifier training, SHAP-based explainability, and production monitoring maps to a managed SageMaker AI capability. This design keeps the operational overhead low. The following steps walk through how each component is deployed, connected, and maintained in production.
Figure 6: Architecture of the content-quality system on Amazon SageMaker AI
1. Content snapshot rendering and data ingestion: The complete A+ Content experience is rendered, capturing how customers actually see the page.
SageMaker Processing Jobs run containerized rendering jobs at scale, decoupling data preparation from training and inference compute.
2. VLM scoring and model hosting: Annotators independently label content using the quality rubric. Their aggregated consensus labels become the training targets. The frozen VLM receives each snapshot plus a rubric prompt and outputs four scores from 0 to 10 (Visual Storytelling, Feature Presentation, A+ Layout, Conversion Optimization), each with a confidence value and rationale. SageMaker AI Inference hosts the VLM with the deployment option that fits the workload:
Real-Time Endpoints for synchronous, low-latency scoring of individual listings.
Asynchronous Endpoints for large payloads such as high-resolution snapshots, where a slight delay is acceptable.
Batch Transform for offline bulk scoring at catalog scale.
These options support automatic scaling, managed infrastructure, and GPU instance selection.
SageMaker Training Jobs can optionally be used to further tune or distill the VLM (for example, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters, knowledge distillation into a smaller model) if teams want a specialized, lower-latency variant. Avoid this to keep recalibration cost-effective and VLM-agnostic.
3. OCR readability extraction: In parallel, OCR extracts text and bounding-box positions from each snapshot and computes four readability signals: Text Density, Character Density, Spacing, and Overall Readability.
SageMaker JumpStart provides pre-trained, single-action deployable models from its model hub, avoiding the need to source, package, and benchmark models from scratch. Teams select a model, optionally fine-tune it without managing infrastructure using SageMaker Serverless Model Customization on ecommerce content, and deploy directly. SageMaker AI Inference then hosts the chosen OCR model as an endpoint.
4. Feature aggregation and storage:
SageMaker Feature Store provides both online (low-latency inference) and offline (batch training) access to the same features, avoiding training-serving skew. Teams can share features across the organization, so downstream consumers can reuse the same curated features.
5. Classifier training: A CatBoost classifier is trained on the eight-dimensional feature vector against expert annotations to learn non-uniform dimension weights and nonlinear decision boundaries. SageMaker Training Jobs can be used here again. You can register trained models directly to SageMaker Model Registry for versioning, approval workflows, and production deployment.
6. SHAP explainability and recommendations: SageMaker Processing Jobs support Bring Your Own (BYO) processing code, which you can use to derive SHAP values and model explainability metrics.
7. Production monitoring and re-training: In production, ML models naturally degrade over time. Customer aesthetics shift, new A+ module types launch, product categories evolve, and seller behavior changes. The scoring patterns the classifier learned from historical annotations gradually fall out of alignment with what quality means today, leading to silent accuracy erosion if left unchecked. Continuous monitoring closes this gap by detecting when the live data distribution or model predictions have drifted far enough from the training baseline to warrant recalibration.
SageMaker AI ModelOps provides a collection of examples and resources to help you operationalize generative AI and machine learning workloads on SageMaker AI.
SageMaker AIOps provides the tool to track data quality, model quality, and feature-attribution drift. SageMaker Pipelines also automates the re-training workflow end-to-end when drift thresholds are breached.
8. Diffusion-based content generation: Closing the loop, the quality scores and SHAP-derived recommendations condition a diffusion model that generates improved A+ image assets. Rather than leaving sellers to interpret recommendations and create new content from scratch, the system produces ready-to-use visual assets (upgraded lifestyle imagery, rebalanced layouts, or enhanced product shots) that directly address the dimensions SHAP flagged as most negatively contributing. These generated assets and natural-language improvement suggestions are surfaced to sellers, so they can upgrade their listings on amazon.com.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to evaluate product detail pages as customers see them by rendering each page as a single snapshot and scoring it with a VLM. We also walked through implementing the system on Amazon SageMaker AI. We built the system around three goals. For adaptability, we keep the VLM fixed and train a CatBoost classifier on its rubric scores, so the system matches expert judgment and can be updated with a short CPU-only job. For performance, we add OCR readability scores that catch dense or poorly spaced text the VLM misses. For explainability, SHAP identifies which features drove each decision, and an LLM turns those results into prioritized recommendations for selling partners.
On 5,478 product detail pages from 10 product categories, the fused model reached 0.94 accuracy and a 0.95 F1 score, 14 and 11 percentage points above the averaged-score baseline. Pages revised using the recommendations improved their quality score by an average of 1.4 points on a scale of 10.
Content quality standards differ across product categories, languages, and marketplaces, and our expert annotations can’t fully represent every context. Next, we plan to evaluate more efficient VLM backbones and inference methods to run the system on a global catalog.

He is a recognized expert in AI Agent, Generative AI, Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and Reinforcement Learning (RL).

Harsh is a Sr. Worldwide Generative AI Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS specializing in ML theory, MLOps, and Generative AI frameworks. His background is in Applied Data Science with a focus on operationalizing AI workloads in the cloud at scale.

He is also a subject matter expert in SageMaker Model Deployment, Inference Optimization for cost saving, performance and latency improvement for customer’s open weights models in SageMaker Managed Inference and HyperPod. He also oversees Voice AI and Video AI 3P model SageMaker and Marketplace hosting.
